£3,500 and no work done: the offer to help that’s really a roofing scam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
06:00:51 UTC
15:00:51 KST

The builder who calls at your door says they are doing some work in the area and has spotted a loose tile on your roof. They offer to fix it for a good price that you agree to.
But when they go up on their ladder to inspect the problem, they see another problem. Rain has been splashing out of the gutters and the wood around them is getting damaged. The only solution, the builder says, is to have rigid PVC trays installed to divert the water.
More rain is forecast and you are worried about what damage could be done so you pay the builder via bank transfer to get the job done there and then. They are gone within an hour, having apparently completed the work.
But nothing was done because there was no problem with your guttering. Instead you were one of a growing number of people who have been targeted by criminals posing as roofers, only to make off with payment after doing unnecessary or no work.
The charity Citizens Advice says suspected roofing frauds were the top scam it heard from consumers about in the last year. It received more than 2,200 complaints of suspected roofing scams in the year to August in England and Wales, about 10% more than the previous year.
“The vast majority of cases is … somebody just knocking on your door saying that they’ve noticed that there’s something wrong with your roof and they’re in a position to help you,” says Ruwani Purcell, the director of external affairs at Citizens Advice.
“The difficulty is [that] your roof is out of sight and out of reach. You can’t fully see what’s going on.”
Purcell says the fraudsters use really persuasive tactics to offer you confidence and reassurance that they know what they’re talking about. “And you might not be familiar with [the] terms,” she says. “In the worst case scenarios, they’ve been quite intimidating to compel people to hand over money there and then.”
What it looks like
While more than three-quarters of the roofing scams reported to Citizens Advice start with someone knocking at the door, some criminals look online for potential victims.
In one case dealt with by Citizens Advice, a 65-year-old woman posted on an online platform that she needed someone to fix a dripping sound in her gutters. A builder phoned her to say that it would cost £250 but when he and another man came and examined her roof they said they had discovered more problems and the price quickly grew. At one point they showed her a bucket of cement and said it was crumbling from under the tiles.
The woman said the man and his accomplice said the work needed to be done immediately and once they claimed to have finished they wanted the payment straightaway.
“I was afraid, two men in front of me in the dark, demanding money and making it clear they weren’t moving,” the victim told Citizens Advice. “They knew I was alone, I didn’t feel like I could deal with anything that might happen after, so I paid £3,500.”
She paid it using bank transfer. “The next day there was no trace that any work was done,” she said. “I felt stupid, and tried to contact them, but couldn’t get through.”
What to do
Be wary of anyone offering unsolicited work by cold calling and demanding confirmation of a job and payment there and then. No reputable builder will do that, says Purcell.
To check the roofer’s authenticity, ask for references and for all proposed work to be confirmed in writing. Treat it as a red flag if they refuse this or if they insist on being paid in cash.
To see if a trader is reputable, you can check your local council’s website as it often lists trusted traders. The government runs the TrustMark scheme which lists approved tradespeople.
Citizens Advice says that if a trader has done a poor job without reasonable care and skill, the victim is entitled to ask for the problem to be fixed or get a refund under the Consumer Rights Act 2015. Keep any paperwork and receipts, take photos and document what happened to make your case.

WASHINGTON – It is dealmaking time: Despite the roiling geopolitical tensions embroiling Washington on several fronts, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio headed to Central and South Asia late on Oct 17 to boost commercial ties – and gain an edge over Russia and China.
With the United States mired in its war with Iran, and the conflict in Ukraine showing no signs of abating, Rubio has stepped up his foreign travel with recent trips to Europe and Latin America, smack in the middle of the US midterm election campaign.
He has largely ceded control of the contentious Iran, Ukraine and Gaza situations to US President Donald Trump’s special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Rubio was instead leading a massive delegation of 200 business leaders to Uzbekistan, where he will take part in a ministerial meeting of five Central Asian countries on Oct 19.
“This is an important relationship,” Rubio said shortly before his departure, calling the trip a strategic visit. “There’s countries you’d like to get to because we want to build our relationships with them.”
A senior State Department official told reporters on Oct 16 that Rubio was demonstrating Washington’s goodwill toward the “deepening partnership across Central Asia”, especially in the energy sector.
Central Asia is a resource-rich region as vast as the European Union but only boasts a population of about 80 million people.
“We’ve been planning this for several months, and it’s an incredible opportunity to bring the United States into a region of the world that is vitally important,” said a second senior US official, on condition of anonymity.
During his visit to the Uzbek city of Samarkand, an emblematic stop on the historic Silk Road, Rubio will participate in a C5+1 meeting with ministers from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.
In November 2025, Trump welcomed the leaders of those countries to the White House.
The former Soviet republics remain linked to Moscow by energy pipelines, as well as security and migratory networks, but Russian influence has eroded since the start of the war in Ukraine – with China reaping the benefits.
Beijing is the main trade partner of all five Central Asian nations.
Chinese companies have signed a number of energy-related deals, seeking to buy natural gas in Turkmenistan, uranium in Kazakhstan and rare earths in Tajikistan.
The United States also has made sourcing rare earths and improving its energy mix key parts of its foreign policy.
The US Ambassador to India, Sergio Gor – who also serves as the special envoy for Central and South Asia – has repeatedly emphasised the need for Washington to have better ties across the region.
Trade deal
After his visit to Uzbekistan, Rubio will head to India, with stops in Mumbai and Jamnagar in Gujarat state. Both are industrial hubs and major international port cities.
It will be the Secretary of State’s second official visit to India in 2026, after a May trip to New Delhi and Kolkata, signifying Washington’s push in the region.
“We’re very close” to a trade deal with India, the second senior US official said of negotiations that have dragged on for months.
In February 2025, the two sides reached a provisional agreement aimed at reducing US tariffs on Indian products.
But just a few days later, the US Supreme Court struck down many of Trump’s tariffs, which fuelled uncertainty about when a bilateral trade deal could take effect.
Ever since, Washington and Delhi have been locked in negotiations.
Relations were rattled when Trump imposed 25% tariffs on Indian goods in retaliation for Delhi’s purchases of Russian oil, but those duties have since been lifted.
In Mumbai and Jamnagar, Rubio will offer the new US brand of so-called “commercial diplomacy” in his meetings with Indian business leaders.
He will notably raise plans by the Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries to finance a refinery in Texas. Reliance is led by billionaire Indian tycoon Anant Ambani. AFP

Leisure out of reach for one in eight people in the EU: Where is the problem biggest?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:54:13 UTC
14:54:13 KST

From sport to cinema trips, regular leisure activities are out of reach for around 46 million people in the EU. Income helps explain the gap between countries, but it does not tell the whole story.
About 46 million people in the EU miss out on regular leisure activities because they cannot afford them, according to Eurostat. In Greece, more than one in four people face this barrier — the highest share in the bloc.
The figures reveal wide differences across Europe, even between countries with similar income levels.
Several studies link social and leisure participation to better mental well-being and fewer symptoms of depression and anxiety. Eurostat also highlights the role leisure and social interactions can play in improving quality of life.
So, where are costs most likely to prevent people from taking part, and how much does income explain the gap?
In 2025, the share of people who couldn't afford to participate regularly in a leisure activity ranged from 3.9% in Croatia to 27.3% in Greece, compared with an EU average of 12.1%, according to Eurostat.
Figures cover people aged 16 and over. With about 381 million people in this age group in 2025, this means around 46 million people in the EU faced this financial barrier.
This share was also above 15% in Romania (23.3%), Lithuania (17.9%), Latvia (16.2%), North Macedonia (15.9%) and Hungary (15.8%).
France and Spain are above the EU average
More than 13% of people in France (13.9%) and Spain (13.4%) also reported that cost prevented them from taking part regularly in leisure activities. Switzerland (13%) was also above the EU average.
Germany (11.7%) was just below the EU average. In Italy, regular leisure activities were out of reach for 10.7% of people because of the cost.
Czechia (4.1%), Luxembourg (5.4%), Norway (5.7%) and Slovakia (5.7%) were also close to Croatia (3.9%) at the lower end.
The share was also higher than in Croatia in the Nordic EU countries: Denmark (10.4%), Sweden (9.7%) and Finland (7.9%).
Elsewhere, it stood at 6.7% in the Netherlands, 8.7% in Turkey and Portugal, 9.2% in Ireland and 9.7% in Belgium.
Leisure activities are less affordable for women
Except for Malta, where the difference was slight at 0.1 percentage point, leisure activities were less affordable for women than men. In the EU, the share was 13% among women, compared with 11.1% among men.
The gender gap was particularly large in several countries: 5.1 percentage points (pp) in Lithuania, 4.7 pp in Romania, 3.9 pp in Denmark and 3.7 pp in France.
Is income linked to leisure affordability?
Analysis by Euronews Business covering 33 European countries shows that income plays a role, but it does not tell the whole story. There is a moderate link between median income and the share of people who miss out on regular leisure activities because of the cost. Income data come from Eurostat and show median equivalised income in purchasing power standards (PPS).
Income accounts for less than a fifth of the variation between countries. Czechia, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania had almost identical median incomes, all between 17,097 and 17,190 PPS. Yet only 4.1% of people in Czechia couldn't afford to take part regularly in a leisure activity, compared with 10.7% in Estonia, 16.2% in Latvia and 17.9% in Lithuania.
The same pattern appeared among wealthier countries. France and Cyprus had virtually the same median income, at 23,792 and 23,782 PPS, respectively. But the share of people facing this financial barrier was more than twice as high in France (13.9%) as in Cyprus (6.3%).
Greece had the highest rate at 27.3%, with a median income of 13,612 PPS. Turkey (8.7%) and Serbia (9.9%) had lower incomes but much lower rates. Croatia, Czechia and Slovakia had some of the lowest rates despite incomes below the EU median of 22,638 PPS.
The role of inequality within countries
Across the EU, people below the poverty line were more than three times as likely to miss out on regular leisure activities as those above it, with 29% unable to afford them.
While inequality within countries may play a role, Euronews Business analysis finds only a weak link between income inequality and leisure affordability, which is not statistically significant.
The analysis uses Eurostat’s Gini coefficient, a measure of how unevenly income is distributed.
How people answer the survey may affect the results
How people answer the survey matters. A Eurostat working paper by Anne-Catherine Guio and colleagues found that “poor people may report that they do not want things, simply because they cannot afford them”. They found that leisure was the item most often not seen as a necessity.
What is a leisure activity?
According to Eurostat, leisure activities include sport, cinema and concerts, among others, and should take place outside the home. These activities involve spending money on entrance fees or travel, such as for swimming; on equipment, such as a bicycle; or on participation in organised activities, such as football club fees.

ROME, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Protests against the rising cost of living turned violent on Saturday in several northern Italian cities, including Milan, Bologna and Turin, leaving dozens of people injured, according to Italian media reports.
In Milan, hundreds of young people dressed in black besieged Piazza del Duomo in the city center, throwing firecrackers and bottles at police. Vietnam, EFTA sign free trade agreement
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:53:34 CST
14:53:34 KST

HANOI, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Vietnam and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), which comprises Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein, signed a free trade agreement in Hanoi on Sunday, the Vietnam News Agency reported.
Under the agreement, EFTA countries will maintain zero import tariffs on industrial and seafood products originating from Vietnam once the agreement enters into force, while Vietnam will gradually reduce or eliminate tariffs on most such products from EFTA countries within 11 years, the government portal reported on Saturday.
Selected agricultural products, including cheese, coffee and chocolate, will also gain duty-free access to Vietnam, subject to a transition period of up to 16 years.
The agreement also seeks to simplify and modernize customs procedures. It provides for national treatment of investors in designated non-service sectors, including agriculture, mining and manufacturing, subject to certain exceptions, and promotes transparency and reduces technical barriers to trade.
Bilateral trade between Vietnam and EFTA member countries averages nearly 2 billion U.S. dollars annually. Vietnam mainly exports seafood, footwear, textiles, machinery and electronics, while importing industrial equipment, chemicals, pharmaceuticals and production materials, according to the Vietnam News Agency. ■

From spreadsheets to autonomous tractors: AI's growing role in farming
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:43:00 UTC
14:43:00 KST

From spreadsheets to autonomous tractors: AI's growing role in farming
Artificial intelligence primarily helps farmers process data in their daily operations, but autonomous agricultural robots and drones are no longer the stuff of science fiction either.
According to Airika Verrev, crop and livestock production manager and consultant at Pajo Ranch, AI's capabilities have improved significantly even in the short time she has been using it. This spring, the food producer tried using AI to compile data in Excel, but the technology was not yet up to the task. By the grain harvest season, however, that had changed.
"These days, I no longer create a single Excel spreadsheet myself. I tell AI what I want and what it should look like, and that's it," Verrev said.
She also uses AI to analyze data and find relevant provisions in legislation. Nevertheless, she said the information it provides must be constantly checked.
Marten Madissoo, assistant professor of agricultural engineering at the Estonian University of Life Sciences, confirmed that the technology does not relieve farmers of the responsibility to evaluate its answers.
"We have to bear in mind that AI is simply a useful tool that allows us to make decisions faster, but we still need to be experts ourselves," he said.
More broadly, Madissoo sees significant potential for machine learning and artificial intelligence in the agricultural sector. Potential applications include logistics, organizing the storage and processing of agricultural products and analyzing fields. However, he said there is no one-size-fits-all solution as the potential applications depend largely on the problem being addressed.
One possibility is to make better use of data that farmers already collect for field records, registers and reports.
"We have the advantage of having data spanning several years. By bringing this data together and developing a model to analyze it, we can achieve those gains," Madissoo said.
At the same time, he reiterated the need to combine agricultural and technical expertise. The relevant indicators must be assessed by people familiar with the fields who can define what they want to learn from the data.
From chat bots to field drones
However, chatbots are just the tip of the iceberg. Marten Madissoo coordinates the work of the AI and Robotics Center AIRE at the Estonian University of Life Sciences. The center focuses on opportunities to improve the competitiveness of industrial companies through artificial intelligence and robotics.
As an example of AI's industrial applications, Madissoo pointed to an AIRE demonstration project at meat producer Nõo Lihatööstus, which tested the use of AI for quality control of packaged products moving along a conveyor belt. The system was designed to detect problems such as poorly attached labels, incorrect dates or defects in a product's appearance.
Researchers at the University of Tartu have also used artificial intelligence to identify field islands in aerial photographs and sort grain. Novaator has previously reported on the Estonian University of Life Sciences' experiments with autonomous agricultural machinery.
New solutions involving agricultural drones could soon emerge. An amendment to the Plant Protection Act is currently being considered by the Riigikogu that would allow plant protection products to be sprayed from unmanned aircraft under certain conditions.
According to Madissoo, several autonomous solutions already exist, but their deployment is hindered by both legal restrictions and the need to ensure safety. For example, he said the Estonian University of Life Sciences' field robot is still firmly in the testing phase. The machine needs to be taught the boundaries of fields and where it can operate.
"It's not exactly science fiction, but it will still take some time before we can put all these technologies and capabilities to use," he said.
In his assessment, repetitive tasks with clearly defined procedures are particularly well suited to automation as machine learning can make them more efficient.
Trust but verify
Airika Verrev believes that, in the future, combining data with the help of AI will make farming significantly more precise. For example, AI could analyze aerial and drone photographs to help determine how much fertilizer or plant protection products need to be ordered for the upcoming season. This could help avoid unnecessary spending.
"The savings could actually be quite substantial. Right now, though, we're still estimating how much to order," she said.
According to Verrev, many producers currently use AI primarily as a more advanced search engine. However, she said a lack of time makes it difficult to keep up with new developments.
Madissoo said businesses' willingness to adopt new technology depends primarily on whether the benefits are clear and the investment is justified.
"How much do I need to invest and how quickly will that investment pay for itself?" he said, summing up the key question facing producers.
However, Madissoo believes that an initial experiment does not have to be expensive. Farmers can start with a chatbot and a specific question, then try analyzing their own data and testing the resulting recommendations on a smaller field, for example. For more complex ideas, he recommends seeking support from universities or AIRE.
"At one conference, someone gave a good example of AI adoption: Horses are still around today, but they have absolutely no significance in the transportation sector. It's the same with AI. You can manage without it, but you'll simply fall behind the mainstream. So I encourage people to use it: Trust, but verify," Madissoo said.

Trump will need up to 60 days to consider sanctions against Russia — Rubio
Kyiv • UNN
Trump suspended sanctions and tariffs against Russia but has not made a final decision. Rubio said the review would take up to 60 days.
The day after suspending sanctions and tariffs related to Russian exports, U.S. President Donald Trump said on Saturday that he had not yet made a final decision on the matter. At the same time, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said officials needed more time to assess the situation, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
On Saturday, Rubio said the president would take up to 60 days to analyze the economic consequences of the sanctions and tariffs related to Russia, which he had suspended the previous day.
"Many of you still do not know what my decision will be, but we will figure it all out — and you will find out too," Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida.
The decision to suspend the measures was made just weeks before the midterm elections in November. Trump is under pressure over high energy prices, while the war with Iran is disrupting global oil supplies.
On Friday, Trump signed an executive order suspending key sanctions and tariffs provided for under a law known as the "Graham Act." He signed the law last month under pressure from lawmakers seeking to pressure Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
The measures, which include tariffs on Russian goods and penalties against countries purchasing Russian oil and gas, were due to take effect next week. Friday's order did not specify how long the suspension would last; however, Rubio said Trump had decided to allow 60 days to review the matter.
"I think the president wants to use this 60-day period to analyze what imposing the sanctions and tariffs would mean for the global economy, as well as for the U.S. economy itself," Rubio told reporters before departing for Uzbekistan.
The situation is complicated by the fact that the "Graham Act" provides not only for sanctions against Russia, but also tariffs on goods from countries that import Russian energy. Rubio cited India as an example — an important U.S. partner that, although it has diversified its energy sources, remains heavily dependent on Russian oil.
The executive order signed on Friday drew criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He warned that such a move would give Russian dictator Vladimir Putin more confidence and prolong the war. Senator Lindsey Graham, a Republican from South Carolina, whose late brother Lindsey Graham was the initiator of the bill bearing his name, said she disagreed with Trump's decision. She plans to discuss it with him next week, when he comes to support her election campaign.
"Personally, I believe the pressure on Russia should continue," she told reporters on Saturday. "After all, I trust neither Putin nor Russia."
In addition
Rubio also defended a separate agreement between the United States and Russia to increase diesel fuel supplies to global markets. The move is intended to lower fuel prices, which have risen amid the war with Iran and disruptions to energy supplies.
According to Trump, under the agreement, Russia will initially ship more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel fuel to the United States; further deliveries are expected in November and thereafter.
"This diesel fuel will be sold one way or another," Rubio said. "The only difference is how much of it will go to the United States."
Rubio added that the diesel fuel agreement and the decision to grant exemptions from the sanctions demonstrate how difficult it is to resolve the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, which have caused disruptions to global energy supplies.
"These conflicts in different corners of the world are beginning to intersect and overlap," he said.

AI tool helps stranded protesters find their way home in the Indian capital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:37:36 UTC
14:37:36 KST

AI tool helps stranded protesters find their way home in the Indian capital
A digital lifeline that connects people detained and dropped off at distant locations with volunteers who ensure a safe return.
New Delhi, India – A 19-year-old woman was detained by police during the youth-led antigovernment protests in the Indian capital over the weekend.
The young woman, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of further reprisals from the authorities, said she was detained on Sunday as thousands of people congregated in central New Delhi. They were demanding the resignation of India’s Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls, which saw the removal of 133 million people from the voter lists.
After the woman’s detention, she and several other demonstrators were taken on a police bus to a location about 50km from the protest site. With no cash and her phone battery drained, the woman spent nearly an hour wandering along a dark road, trying to figure out what to do next.
A car pulled up and the driver asked if she needed any help.
“I was frightened and completely lost. When those volunteers finally helped me get back safely, it felt like a miracle. I had never imagined that someone I had never met would come forward to help me like that,” she told Al Jazeera.
For a young woman in New Delhi, notoriously referred to as the “rape capital of India”, being alone in the middle of the night and getting into a car with strangers is not an easy decision. The city records an average of three rapes a day.
But the young protester said she immediately recognised one of the volunteers in the car. She had seen his videos online, in which he had asked the detained protesters whether they needed help. Recognising a familiar face reassured her that the people offering the ride could be trusted.
The woman was rescued using an AI-assisted tool developed by 25-year-old Rajiv Choudhary, who is helping protesters get home safely after being detained and dropped off by the police far away.
Called the Detainee Gharwapsi Yojana, the initiative combines a digital dashboard with a network of volunteers who track information about police buses carrying detainees and arrange transport for those left stranded.
“Gharwapsi” in Hindi means “to return home”. It is also a play on a campaign by India’s right-wing Hindu groups which want to bring the country’s Muslims and Christians back into the Hindu fold, claiming that their ancestors converted to “foreign” religions from Hinduism. “Yojana” means a plan.
Since the beginning of this month, India has seen near daily protests over alleged electoral fraud by Kumar and his commission. Led by the satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a number of left-leaning student groups as well as the main opposition Congress party, the protests have seen tens of thousands of people hitting the streets in New Delhi and other cities.
In response, authorities in the Indian capital have imposed a sweeping crackdown, blocking roads, closing metro stations and detaining thousands as Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government faces the biggest challenge to its power after 12 years of rule.
Choudhary said his network’s primary focus was to help minors, elderly people and women, mainly first-time protesters.
The initiative operates through a private digital dashboard that uses AI-assisted data processing, live mapping and information shared by volunteers on the ground. Volunteers send details, including police bus numbers and locations, through WhatsApp, helping the team coordinate assistance and rides home.
Choudhary said he and his associate, journalist Meghnad, who goes by a single name, initially worked with a small group of volunteers to connect detainees with transport, legal assistance and medical support. The network has since expanded to more than 130 volunteers, who have offered their time and resources to assist detained demonstrators.
“For people caught up in these demonstrations, the ordeal doesn’t end with detention. They can be taken far from the protest site and left trying to find their way home from unfamiliar locations, often struggling to contact friends or arrange transport,” he said.
The idea grew out of Choudhary’s experience during an earlier protest called by the CJP at Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in New Delhi that has now been denotified by the authorities. Initially, he helped organise supplies and volunteers.
As demonstrations continued, he recognised that protesters needed more systemic support, particularly those who were detained by the police and left fending for themselves far from the city limits.
As renewed protests began on October 2 , Choudhary built a digital system around the same volunteer network using AI tools. It began with a simple spreadsheet.
“The whole aim behind the application was that I had to systemise things that are not systemised,” he said. “We just wanted to become a support system that could help our people in their fight for their demands.”
Choudhary recalled receiving a distress call from a woman who had been detained in central New Delhi and released on the outskirts of the city. Stranded alone near a railway station, with metro services shut and no clear way to get home, she was frightened and unsure which way to turn.
She reached out to Choudhary’s network for help and he arranged for a nearby female driver to take her home safely. “It is heartbreaking to see people left helpless in an unfamiliar city, frightened and unsure of how they will get home,” he said.
For now, the Detainee Gharwapsi Yojana operates only in New Delhi, but Choudhary plans to expand it to other cities.
“I am overwhelmed by the response from volunteers and drivers who have come forward to help without charging anything. They are offering their services for free because they want to support the protesters,” he said.
The 19-year-old woman who was helped by Choudhary’s team described the initiative as “a lifeline for protesters”. She said the team not only arranged her return, but also offered reassurance and emotional support.
“I cannot thank them enough. As long as we have people like them in our society, no authority can stop us from demanding our rights and protesting peacefully,” she said.

France rocked by nationwide clashes, fires and looting as cost-of-living protests turn violent

2026-10-18
05:35:31 UTC
14:35:31 KST

France woke up Sunday to devastated streets after clashes between police and protesters, mass looting and fires erupted nationwide as marches against rising costs of living degenerated into "extreme" violence.
The widespread unrest followed weeks of student protests and comes just six months ahead of elections to replace President Emmanuel Macron.
Whole streets in Paris "have been devastated", the city's mayor Emmanuel Gregoire said as groups of masked young men torched parked cars and ransacked shops.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, who had condemned the "extreme intensity" of the violence, said 1,200 people had been arrested and 150 police officers hurt.
It was "a miracle the toll isn't higher", he said.
The violence began on the sidelines of marches in the capital and other cities over the cost of living that the interior ministry said were attended by 550,000 people.
The CGT union, which took part, said 800,000 people participated.
Police used tear gas and water cannon against protesters who threw projectiles and aimed fireworks.
A 17-year-old boy had his right hand blown off by a crowd-control grenade in the southern city of Saint-Etienne.
Looting
During and after those demonstrations, gangs of youths roamed city streets, sporadically confronting police, while setting fires and attacking shuttered stores to break in and empty their shelves.
Scores of shops, supermarkets, pharmacies, luxury boutiques, clothing retailers, opticians, cosmetic vendors and consumer electronics stores, were looted in Paris, Marseille, Nice, Nantes, Bordeaux, Limoges, Lille, Toulouse and Strasbourg.
AFP reporters in Paris saw groups of half a dozen young men attacking the shops in an organised way. Wearing masks and gloves, they first disconnected security cameras before smashing windows to get in.
The looting added to a day of destruction and vandalism, with town halls in several cities targeted.
The town hall in the city of Limoges, more than 140 years old, was largely destroyed by a blaze set by masked protesters who broke in, according to the region's top official. Two others were broken into and vandalised in Marseille and Lille.
A police compound in Bordeaux was also vandalised, while in Lyon protesters set ablaze a tourist office.
The violence has drawn global headlines, in the United States, Vice President JD Vance blamed immigration for the unrest.
"Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion. They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility," he said on X.
President Macron said that "those who carried out vandalism, attacked administrative offices or businesses, or carried out looting, even in our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished".
Opposition politicians vying to replace Macron in presidential elections in April and May have seized on the chaos.
Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen condemned "the rioters" and claimed that the party of her far-left rival for the presidency, Jean-Luc Melenchon, had "legitimised the violence".
She vowed to protect the French "from the violence of the extreme left".
Melenchon, who had prominently supported the demonstrations and the student protests preceding them, urged demonstrators to stay away from any looting, describing it as "contrary to our methods".
'Revolution'
France's Yellow Vest movement, which staged street protests eight years ago against Macron's government over planned fuel tax hikes, had called for Saturday's "yellow and youth" demonstrations.
The principal grievance was the cost of living, pushed up in part by the war in the Middle East that has helped send inflation soaring in Europe as elsewhere.
"We're sick of slaving away for poverty wages while our rents keep going up," teacher Regine Monfroid told AFP in the eastern city of Strasbourg.
But there were other issues.
In Paris, tens of thousands marched across the east and north of the city in one major march, some shouting "Everyone hates the police" and "Macron, resign".
High school student Kamil Alahyan, 18, said he was protesting "for so many reasons -- the elections coming up in 2027, politicians who lie, the ultra-rich who've been taking more and more wealth over the past 10 years".
Several protesters sought to draw parallels with the French Revolution of 1789.
"It's the Revolution, we're taking the Bastille!" some shouted in Marseille as they forced their way into the mayor's offices.
In the western city of La Rochelle, marchers streamed behind a placard reading: "Revolution or death."
And in the southern city of Montpellier, a giant blue sign reading "The people will win" was unfurled above a central square.
"The government is trembling and it's right to tremble because when the French people are angry, they never let up," Ryad Rani, the head of the LSU high school student representative body, told journalists in Paris.

I’m a Russian Fashion Designer – Vladimir Putin Is Terrified of Me
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:34:00 UTC
14:34:00 KST

Less than five years ago, her life could hardly have been more glamorous or safer. Anastasia Vistorobska worked in Paris for two of the world’s best-known fashion houses. Today her life could hardly be more challenging or dangerous: working as a combat medic for Ukraine’s armed forces on the front line of its brutal all-out war with Russia.
Anastasia’s story is all-the-more remarkable because of her nationality – she is Russian, which means she has volunteered to risk her life fighting against her homeland. For more than two-and-a-half years, she has worked as a combat medic, treating her comrades close to the front line, while also seeing countless others die on the battlefield.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
It is physically and mentally exhausting work. Typically, Anastasia’s days are full of both good and bad news. She fought back tears as she talked about the recent death of a close comrade. “The constant death is terrible. It builds up and it makes me sad and angry. I have seen 42 comrades go on a mission but only 38 came back,” she reflects.
However, there are rewarding days too. “On one occasion, a wounded soldier passed on a message through a comrade: ‘Thank you for saving my life.’ That was very inspiring. I am fortunate, too, that I have never had anyone die in my arms.”
On Feb. 24, 2022, when Russia began its all-out invasion, Anastasia was sleeping in a beautiful house in rural France, when suddenly friends started messaging her that the war had started. “They all said the same: that Ukraine was under bombardment. My immediate reaction was: ‘this cannot be happening!’”
Olesia Avramenko: ‘Ukrainian Art Preserves What the World Is Gradually Losing’
At that time, Anastasia, then aged 36, had lived in France for 15 years, for the last seven working in the fashion industry for Chanel and Givenchy as an embroidery designer. With friends and relatives in Ukraine, she typically visited the country twice a year. “After the all-out invasion, I wanted to join the Ukrainian army straightaway but I felt helpless. I was conscious that I had a Russian passport and no previous military experiences. I feared that I would be useless and that no one would take me seriously. But I do have an ability to act decisively. I wanted to go and start killing these invaders.”
As she pondered how to get involved, the Russian massacre of some 500 people at Bucha, near Kyiv, in March 2022, was the final straw. “For me, this was the most horrific moment of the whole war,” she said. Anastasia initially wrote a letter to a military committee in Ukraine explaining: “I know I am Russian but I want to go and defend Ukrainian children. Can you please accept me?”
Her offer was rejected but friends advised her to look into the Freedom of Russian Legion, Russians fighting against their homeland. “I looked at their videos and documentaries and I was astounded by the way they thought and spoke. They seemed to be the best of people and, four years on, having met them, I still feel the same.”
Fearing she was too old and too weak, Anastasia first got herself fitter and stronger over six months before going to Texas, in the US, for a two-month military training course. Eventually, she passed a long vetting procedure and was successful in joining the legion. “The process is strict: Every potential recruit’s background is scrutinized down to the smallest detail to completely eliminate any possibility of FSB [Russian security] infiltration,” she said.
It was not until February 2024, on the second anniversary of the full-scale invasion, that she finally arrived in Ukraine and started undergoing four months of training at a secret location. “It was horrible – really, really hard – but at the end of it I could shoot five different weapons and I learned a lot about the battlefield and communications. I also learned medical skills and evacuation techniques.”
At the end of her training, she chose to work as a combat medic and is now head of a tactical evacuation team. Typically, she operates some six miles from the front line. The aim is that an injured soldier is given basic first aid and evacuated by his comrades, so he or she can receive fuller medical attention from combat medics in slightly safer locations.
I asked Anastasia, who is 5 feet 8 inches (173 cm) tall and of slim build, how she felt fighting a war against her homeland. “I prefer to judge people on their actions rather than their passport. People either do good things or bad things and I want to be on the side of right versus wrong. Stealing land, killing civilians, harming children – they are all wrong.” Strangely perhaps, Anastasia considers it more dangerous to be in Kyiv on leave than she does working close to the front line. The capital is hit almost daily by ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones.
“In the war zone, I am wearing body armor, I am surrounded by comrades, I am always on alert and I trust my commanders to keep me safe. But in Kyiv this summer I was sleeping in my pajamas on the 14th floor of an apartment building when the area was being hit by missiles and drones. That was terrifying.”
Her worst times have come when comrades are being killed or wounded on the front line. “When you hear someone screaming [for help] on the radio that’s probably one of the hardest moments,” she said.
Anastasia, who left Russia aged 23, has signed a three-year contract with the legion. She does not know yet if she will stay in the army longer because she also has a yearning to go back to her artistic roots. Even now, she applies her talents by creating artistic projects, including making art works from the uniforms of dead soldiers and their belongings. It is intended as a memorial to their sacrifice and, in time, she hopes to exhibit her work. Hundreds of Russians are currently fighting for Ukraine and Anastasia admires them all.
“I am soaked in the stories of my comrades, their chivalry and bravery,” she said. “But what upsets me is that after they die in battle and are cremated, no one [from their family] will come and visit their grave. So I hope my work will commemorate their death, their memory. The huge power of war and art often go hand in hand.”
For security reasons, Anastasia prefers not to discuss details of her family. However, she says all her family members, including her mother, now live outside Russia, which is why she is willing to be identified by name, without fear of reprisals in her homeland.
“I am not scared by the reality that I might get killed. I am just proud to have done a little bit to make the situation better for Ukrainians. Putin is scared of the Legion of Russia which means he is scared of me.”
Her hatred of the Russian president has no limits. She says: “He is one of the biggest war criminals in history. He has been compared to Hitler but he is much worse than Hitler. Putin is destroying Russia even more horribly than he is Ukraine. He stole my pride and my joy at being Russian. He has stolen the right of the Russian language to be the beautiful language it once was.”
She hopes that, once the war ends well for Ukraine, she will be able to divide her time between France and Ukraine. Now aged 41 years old, she is engaged to a Russian man who also serves in the legion. Anastasia says Ukrainians have been largely supportive, rather than suspicious, of her and other Russians fighting for their cause, but she added: “If a Ukrainian was to spit in my face, I would not say a word because I would understand the anger. The reality is that Russia owes a huge debt to Ukraine.”
Lord Ashcroft KCMG PC is an international businessman, philanthropist, author and pollster. For more information on his work, visit lordashcroft.com. Follow him on X/Facebook @LordAshcroft.

Ukrainian drone attack causes fire at oil terminal in St. Petersburg

Ukrainian drone attack causes fire at oil terminal in St. Petersburg
A blaze has broken out at an oil terminal in St. Petersburg as a result of a major Ukrainian drone attack on Russia’s second-largest city, local governor Aleksandr Beglov has said.
One person was killed and five others wounded in St. Petersburg during the aerial raid by “the Ukrainian Nazis,” Beglov said in a social media post on Sunday. Twelve apartment blocks and two private homes sustained damage, with repairs already being underway, he added.
Emergencies services have been tackling fires at the Petersburg Oil Terminal in the Great Port of St. Petersburg, the Ruchyi oil depot and industrial warehouses in Kolpinsky District, the governor said.
The affected oil terminal is the largest facility of its kind in the Baltic Region, handling 125 million tons of liquefied product per year.
Ukraine continues to target Russian oil infrastructure despite demands by US President Donald Trump to curb the attacks, which he blames for surging global energy prices. He accused Vladimir Zelensky of “making problems” for the US and the whole world and suggested that Ukraine needs a “new president.”
In an attempt to alleviate the fuel shortage ahead of the midterm election on November 3, Trump eased restrictions on Moscow’s diesel exports and waived “the bone-crushing” sanctions championed by the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, which proposed 500% tariffs on imports from Russia and 100% tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.
Flights have been delayed at St. Petersburg’s Pulkovo International Airport due to the raid, according to Beglov.
At least 144 UAVs were shot down by air defenses overnight, Aleksandr Drozdenko, the head of Leningrad Region, which surrounds St. Petersburg, said on social media.
Four people have been hospitalized for smoke inhalation from a blaze caused when debris from an intercepted UAV fell on an apartment block in the town of Vsevolzhsk, he said.
Residential areas were also hit by debris in Gatchina, Kirovsk and several other settlements, according to Drozdenko.
Some 20,000 people remain without electricity in Leningrad Region; two transformer substations in the community of Yanino, servicing some 50 apartment blocks, went offline during the Ukrainian raid, the governor said.
Russia’s leading social media platform VK said in a statement that one of its data centers in Leningrad Region has been targeted by Ukrainian UAVs.
According to the Downdetector website, the number of reports from users about issues with VK’s services increased following the attack.
The major Russian online retailer Ozon said that one of its warehouses was attacked during the raid. There were no injuries, as staff were evacuated, according to the company.
The Russian Defense Ministry has said that a total of 1,015 Ukrainian drones were destroyed above 16 regions overnight.
Moscow has accused Kiev of deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure and residential areas with long-range drones in an attempt to compensate for setbacks on the battlefield, where Russian forces have continued to advance.
Russia has responded to Kiev’s terrorist attacks by intensifying its long-range missile and drone campaign against Ukraine’s military-industrial facilities and logistics infrastructure. The Defense Ministry in Moscow maintains that it does not target civilians and that its strikes are directed solely at military targets and infrastructure supporting Kiev’s forces.

People increasingly not paying hospital fees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:28:00 UTC
14:28:00 KST

People increasingly not paying hospital fees
Since patient visit fees increased last year, more and more people have been falling behind on payments to hospitals. Patients with outstanding debts can no longer see a specialist.
A year and a half ago, the cost of visiting a doctor quadrupled, with patient visit fees rising from €5 to €20 and daily hospital bed fees doubling from €2.50 to €5. Since then, the number of patients owing money to North Estonia Medical Center (PERH) has doubled, while the total amount owed has tripled.
"Daily hospital bed fees account for about 70 percent of the debt, while visit fees, mainly for emergency department visits, account for the remaining 30 percent," said Anneli Habicht, PERH's head of customer service.
According to Habicht, in about half of cases patients simply forget to pay, while the other half have no intention of paying. Before turning to a debt collection agency, the hospital spends a couple of months trying to recover the money itself.
"When we look at which groups are more likely to owe us money, it seems to be older people approaching retirement age, as well as very young adults. In terms of gender, men tend to be more likely to fall behind on payments," Habicht said.
Last year, nearly 2,200 people owed money to Narva Hospital. The amounts involved are generally small and are usually paid after a reminder.
"In the first nine months of this year, the number of debtors has increased by about 25 percent. At the same time, we haven't seen any behavior that would require us to take aggressive action through debt collection agencies or any signs that people are deliberately trying to avoid their obligations," said Narva Hospital CEO Üllar Lanno.
Tartu University Hospital has not experienced the same problems as its counterparts in northern Estonia.
"The hospital still receives most of its revenue for medical treatment through its contract with the Estonian Health Insurance Fund. Patients' out-of-pocket payments account for less than 3 percent of that. We have half a million outpatient visits a year and perhaps 200 to 400 patients need to be sent payment reminders," said Joel Starkopf, a member of Tartu University Hospital's management board.
According to debt collection agency Julianus Inkasso, the number of claims submitted by hospitals has increased by a few percentage points, although some medical institutions have submitted 10 percent more claims.
"When the visit fee was €5, it was a little easier to pay. If you're in a difficult financial situation, €20 is harder to afford. And if you forget to pay on time, finding that extra money later can be more difficult when you're working with a tight household budget," said Merle Laurimäe, CEO of Julianus Inkasso.
More than half of debtors settle their debts within a year of receiving a letter from the collection agency. However, they must also cover late-payment interest and collection fees of up to €30.
"I think the total could rise to around €55 at most, provided you act in time," Laurimäe said.

EU Commissioner wants to see the long queues at Brussels Airport sorted before Christmas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:26:00 UTC
14:26:00 KST

“We face a number of challenges, like at Zaventem in Belgium,” European Commissioner for Migration Magnus Brunner told US news outlet Politico. He wants the long queues at European airports to be resolved before Christmas. The office of Minister Bernard Quintin (Francophone liberal MR) has announced that Belgium has submitted an action plan to the European Commission.
EU Commissioner wants to see the long queues at Brussels Airport sorted before Christmas
A year ago, EU countries began rolling out a new Entry/Exit System (EES) that records the fingerprints and facial images of non-EU visitors entering the Schengen area or leaving the EU. The system has been fully operational since April.
Instead of having their passports stamped by a border guard, travellers must register via an EES kiosk. This involves, amongst other things, having their fingerprints and photographs taken.
At many airports, the new system led to long queues, also at Brussels Airport. Waiting times were particularly long during the summer months. But even last month, travellers sometimes had to queue for up to five hours.
The solution? To suspend the collection of fingerprints and facial images at busy times. “But since 6 September, that suspension is no longer possible,” Quintin’s office states.
“Some Member States are lagging behind a little,” acknowledges European Commissioner Brunner. “We are facing a number of challenges, for example at Zaventem, but also in other Member States. They must do their job. They have agreed to the new system, and now it is up to the Member States to carry out their tasks.”
Brunner emphasises that he has “a great deal of confidence” that the problems will be resolved before the next holiday period, at Christmas.
Whether that is feasible remains to be seen.
Quintin’s response
Quintin’s office tells VRT NEWS that “the federal police have been manning the 12 checkpoints in the arrivals hall at Brussels Airport for months and that, in addition, dozens of police officers are currently undergoing training to further strengthen the border control teams on a permanent basis”.
“Belgium, like several other Member States, submitted an action plan to the European Commission in September for the phased introduction of the EES at Brussels Airport, in order to avoid additional waiting times for travellers,” the office added.
Quintin’s spokesperson also told news outlet Politico that the airport can only process between 500 and 600 passengers from outside the Schengen area per hour, compared with nearly 3,500 passengers who may arrive between 6.00 am and 10.00 am on busy days.
The airport’s infrastructure “cannot cope with that demand”, the spokesperson is reported to have said, and the company must “implement far-reaching changes”.
Brussels Airport has not responded directly to the criticism from Brunner or Quintin but has stated in a written response that “all parties involved” are working to resolve the delays, including by testing new e-gates and pre-check-in kiosks and training more police officers. “The need for additional infrastructure is also being investigated,” the statement reads.
The airport also emphasises that changes have already been implemented. For example, two additional federal police checkpoints have been added, both in the departures and arrivals areas. In addition, 60 pre-registration kiosks are available, allowing travellers to enter certain details in advance before passing through border control.
ACI Europe (the European airport association) has also hit back in response to the criticism. According to them, there are structural flaws in the system. They are proposing a six-point plan to, for example, eliminate duplicate checks and to reintroduce the exception in the event of excessive waiting times.
‘It really works’
Brunner, meanwhile, remains convinced of the new system’s usefulness. "The entry and exit system has recorded nearly 230 million entries and exits via around 1,500 border crossings. The authorities have refused entry to around 80,000 people, including 2,000 who were considered a security risk due to links to activities such as terrorism or organised crime.”
“As you can see, it really does work. And it pays off,” the Austrian European Commissioner tells Politico.
“This is the most modern border management system in the world,” he adds. “We are compared to the US, to Canada, to other countries, and they are all jealous.”

Artists celebrate their professional holiday on October 18

On October 18, artists celebrate their professional holiday. The day is closely associated with the Christian Church and the memory of the Holy Apostle and Evangelist Luke. According to church tradition, St. Luke was the first Christian icon painter, credited with creating the earliest images of the Virgin Mary with the Child Jesus and of the apostles Peter and Paul. He is regarded as the patron saint of artists, painters and iconographers. The Union of Bulgarian Artists, art galleries and art academies mark the occasion each year with exhibitions, award ceremonies and community gatherings.

The project explores questions of borders, migration, identity, humanity’s relationship with nature, and the interplay between the digital and physical worlds

====================================================================================================

Denmark and Vietnam at 55: From Development Cooperation to a Green Partnership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:21:00 UTC
14:21:00 KST

Two of Denmark’s best-known brands, LEGO and Pandora, now have factories in the same industrial park outside Ho Chi Minh City. Their arrival shows how far the relationship has come since Denmark opened an embassy in Hanoi 55 years ago.
The anniversary comes with a state visit. On 19 October, King Frederik and Queen Mary receive Vietnam’s President Tô Lâm at Copenhagen Airport. Over the three days of the state visit, the programme takes him to the quantum laboratory at the Niels Bohr Institute, a business conference at the Confederation of Danish Industry (DI), and a boat trip past the Lynetteholm island project and the Middelgrunden wind turbines.
The Royal House says the visit is a chance to highlight shared interests in green solutions, health and food, and that it also reflects strong commercial interests on both sides. Denmark’s new ambassador, Lina Gandløse Hansen, presented her credentials to Vietnam’s General Secretary and President Tô Lâm in Hanoi on 3 October, as the two countries mark the 55th anniversary.
How it began
Denmark and Vietnam established diplomatic relations in 1971, and the Danish embassy in Hanoi opened that year. It was closed from 1983 until 1994. After that, development aid became the main channel of cooperation, with Vietnam as a partner country until the aid ended in 2015.
By then the relationship had a new frame. In 2011 the two foreign ministers signed a strategic partnership on climate change, environment, energy and green growth. In 2013, during a Vietnamese state visit to Denmark, the governments signed a Comprehensive Partnership.
On 1 November 2023 the two prime ministers declared a Green Strategic Partnership, which builds on cooperation in climate, energy, trade and business, food and agriculture, health and education.
Fireworks over the Saigon River and the Landmark 81 tower in Ho Chi Minh City. Photo: SGGP
What Danish business does there
More than 150 Danish companies now operate in Vietnam, the Danish ambassador said in June 2026. By the end of February 2025, Danish investment had passed USD 2 billion in 174 projects, according to Vietnam’s Ministry of Finance. That put Denmark 21st among foreign investors in Vietnam and first among the Nordic countries.
The most visible projects are factories.
- LEGO opened its plant in the Vietnam-Singapore Industrial Park III in April 2025. It is the company’s sixth factory in the world, represents an investment of more than USD 1 billion, and the company has said it will run on renewable energy.
The opening ceremony of LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam, 9 April 2025. Photo: VGP (Vietnam Government Portal)
- Pandora opened its USD 150 million crafting facility in the same industrial park on 1 October 2026, its first production site outside Thailand. It is designed to make up to 60 million pieces of jewellery a year and to employ 7,000 people when fully staffed. The company says it runs on renewable electricity, and the Danish ambassador was at the opening.
The inauguration of the Pandora Vietnam plant, 1 October 2026: Ho Chi Minh City leaders and Pandora representatives on stage. Photo: SGGP
- Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners signed a joint development agreement with Petrovietnam in 2025 for one of Vietnam’s first offshore wind projects.
Trade grew in 2025. Danish exports to Vietnam rose about 20%, to DKK 1.8 billion, according to Statistics Denmark, while imports from Vietnam were DKK 4.0 billion. From Vietnam come mostly electronics, clothing, furniture, machinery and footwear. Denmark sends mainly machinery, fish, and measuring and medical instruments.
Getting there has become simpler. Vietnam Airlines has flown direct between Ho Chi Minh City and Copenhagen since December 2025, and Danes can stay in Vietnam for 45 days without a visa.
Where Danish companies and experts can take part
The 2023 Green Strategic Partnership names the areas. The two governments say they will strengthen trade and investment cooperation in onshore and offshore wind, energy efficiency solutions, food, agriculture, water and wastewater management, and maritime solutions, and hold dialogue on green shipping.
They also commit to work on a circular economy, sustainable food, feed and aquaculture production, and health and life science. For Danish companies, consultants and researchers, those are the open doors.
Energy is the furthest along. The Danish Energy Agency has run an energy partnership programme with Vietnam’s Ministry of Industry and Trade since 2013, and offshore wind became part of it in the third phase.
In 2023 the two governments agreed to continue it. Vietnam’s revised power plan, approved in April 2025, provides for 6,000 to 17,000 MW of offshore wind to come into operation between 2030 and 2035, and Vietnam has committed to net zero emissions by 2050.
At sea, Maersk’s chief executive told Vietnam’s leader in Hanoi in November 2025 that the group is exploring investments in large, modern, low-carbon container ports. Maersk and the Vietnamese firm Hateco opened a deep-water port in Hải Phòng in April 2025, according to The Investor.
Vietnam asks for something in return. On 29 September, Denmark’s ambassador raised proposals from Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, Vestas and Carlsberg with Vietnam’s Ministry of Industry and Trade.
The deputy minister said the ministry would consider them under Vietnamese law, and encouraged Danish investors to transfer technology, train Vietnamese workers and strengthen local supply chains.
Danish companies can start with the Danish Trade Council, which has offices in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City. The business conference at the Confederation of Danish Industry on 20 October focuses on green solutions, health and food.
What comes next
Big projects take time, and these two are now finished. LEGO broke ground in November 2022 and opened in April 2025. Pandora broke ground in May 2024 and opened in October 2026.
The partnerships signed since 2011 give both countries a framework. What gets built under them, such as turbines, factories, research projects and exchange programmes, will show how far they go. A practical question for a Danish reader is which of the areas above could involve their own company, university or hospital in the next five years.
Sources

11 still missing after boat capsizes off Baja California
Rescue crews are continuing the search for 11 people missing after a boat carrying 27 people sank off Mexico's Baja California coast, according to U.S. Coast Guard officials, Qazinform News Agency cites Al Jazeera.
Sixteen Mexican nationals were rescued on Friday after the vessel capsized about 225 kilometers west of Ensenada. Survivors told authorities that 27 people had been on board when the boat went down.
The U.S. Coast Guard said several rescued passengers suffered serious injuries consistent with suspected shark bites and received emergency medical treatment while being transported to San Diego.
The search operation involves U.S. Coast Guard and U.S. Navy aircraft and vessels, as well as support from the Mexican Navy. Officials said an additional helicopter would be deployed to assist in locating the missing individuals.
A distress call was received around 1 a.m. Friday, prompting an immediate response. A rescue helicopter reached the scene roughly two hours later, and crews spent about 90 minutes pulling survivors from the water.
Although the incident occurred outside U.S. territorial waters, American authorities joined the operation due to the emergency nature of the situation.
The waters off Baja California are popular with recreational boaters and fishing vessels but are also known routes used by migrant and smuggling operations. Similar maritime tragedies have occurred in the region in recent years, including fatal boat accidents involving migrants attempting to reach the United States.
Authorities have not yet determined the cause of the sinking, and the search for the remaining passengers remains ongoing.
At least 13 people, most of them children, died after a boat capsized in eastern India’s Bihar state, officials said late Tuesday.

Why Marco Rubio’s visit to Mumbai has ruffled feathers in India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:16:49 UTC
14:16:49 KST

Why Marco Rubio’s visit to Mumbai has ruffled feathers in India
The US secretary of state is skipping New Delhi on his second trip to India in six months, and opposition leaders say the arrangements are humiliating.
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio is to visit India in the coming week, but he will not set foot in the capital, New Delhi.
Instead, on Monday, Rubio will hold talks with Indian External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar in Mumbai, India’s financial hub, and then visit an oil refinery in Jamnagar in the western state of Gujarat, according to a statement from the US Department of State.
His itinerary sparked a political storm after the US ambassador to India said Washington expected Jaishankar to travel to meet Rubio, prompting opposition leaders to accuse the government of allowing India’s top diplomat to be “summoned” on home soil.
The spat comes as relations between the two countries are strained over trade, tariffs and India’s purchases of Russian oil.
So why is Rubio avoiding New Delhi, and why has it caused such upset? Here’s what you need to know:
What is Rubio doing in India?
He plans to discuss trade, energy and investment.
Rubio is arriving on Sunday from Samarkand, Uzbekistan, where he has been meeting with five Central Asian states at the C5+1 summit.
In India, he is due to meet senior officials to discuss the US-India strategic partnership and energy cooperation and hold talks with business leaders, the State Department said.
Indian Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal appeared to confirm the agenda, stating on Friday that the Mumbai talks would cover energy, trade and investment, defence, and critical and emerging technologies.
In Jamnagar, Rubio is to visit the world’s largest single-site refinery, operated by billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, and attend a reception hosted by the Ambani family, according to The Hindu newspaper.
Why isn’t Rubio going to New Delhi?
No official reason has been given.
Rubio was in the Indian capital in May for a meeting of foreign ministers of countries in the Quad, a group consisting of the US, India, Japan and Australia.
The State Department has framed his upcoming trip around energy and investment, and the second stop on Rubio’s India visit, Jamnagar, is one of the world’s most important energy hubs.
The visit also comes as fuel prices bite in the US before next month’s midterm elections.
Reliance, an energy, retail and telecommunications conglomerate, also sits at the centre of Washington’s wider oil diplomacy.
Business Standard, an Indian financial daily, said the Jamnagar stop was significant because Reliance is the biggest buyer of Venezuelan crude oil besides the US at a time when Washington has been urging India to buy more.
Since US forces seized Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January and took essential control of the country’s oil industry, the US government has marketed Venezuelan oil to buyers abroad.
Reliance is also investing in a new refinery in Texas, the first to be built in the US in 50 years, which Trump hailed as a $300bn deal when he announced it in March, Business Standard reported.
What did the US ambassador say, and why has it caused upset?
Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi on Thursday, US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said Rubio would meet Indian government officials in Mumbai, and Washington “expected” Jaishankar and others from New Delhi to travel there to see him.
Earlier in the week, however, Jaiswal had not confirmed the trip or explained why Rubio was skipping New Delhi, telling reporters the Indian government would announce it “at the appropriate time”, The Hindu newspaper reported.
Jairam Ramesh, a general secretary of the opposition Indian National Congress party, wrote on X that the ambassador’s statement was “quite extraordinary”.
Rahul Gandhi, leader of the opposition in parliament’s lower house, also took to X to comment, writing on Friday that Rubio had “summoned his employee to Mumbai”.
Congress MP Pawan Khera went further.
“A foreign government summoning India’s External Affairs Minister on Indian soil is a new low, even by the Modi Government’s standards,” he wrote on X, referring to Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
Why are US-India relations strained?
Mainly because of Trump’s tariffs and Russian oil.
In August last year after a round of trade talks broke down, the US hit most Indian goods with a 50 percent tariff. Under a framework the two sides agreed in February, that rate fell to 18 percent, however.
Since then, negotiations have stalled.
This month, Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said the talks had “plateaued”, according to The Hindu.
On Thursday, Trade Minister Piyush Goyal said the “first tranche” of a deal was in its final stages but India would not sign until its exporters had an edge over rivals such as Bangladesh, Vietnam and Indonesia, according to the Reuters news agency.
Other points of friction have emerged.
Last week, US Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling announced that his department was suspending eight companies – including the Indian IT giants Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro and HCL – from a labour certification scheme that is a key step for employers seeking green cards for their foreign staff.
Sameer Lalwani, a senior fellow in the South Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, wrote this week that Indian public opinion of the US has hit a record low, citing US engagement with Pakistan and the US-Israel war on Iran, which he said had pushed India back towards Russian oil.
Despite that, he argued, defence and technology cooperation has quietly deepened, and bilateral trade grew by almost 12 percent in 2025 to nearly $240bn.
In his view, “perceptions of the political relationship have deteriorated faster than its strategic foundations.”
A sanctions law had threatened to make matters worse.
Last month, Trump signed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which could impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on goods from the five largest importers of Russian oil or gas.
India, one of the world’s biggest buyers of Russian oil, had warned Washington that new tariffs could hurt bilateral ties. Trump signed an executive order seeking to waive the sanctions on Friday as he tries to ease high oil prices before the November 3 US elections.

Dozens of critically endangered orangutans have been rescued in recent weeks from rampant wildfires burning across Indonesia, conservation groups said.
The fires have triggered a months-long pollution spell that has closed schools, fuelled a surge in respiratory conditions both among humans and animals, and restricted outdoor activities in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and East Timor.
Pollution levels again ranged from unhealthy to very unhealthy across the region on Sunday, cloaking many areas across southern Southeast Asia in toxic haze.
Swiss-based air quality monitor IQAir again ranked Singapore and Kuala Lumpur among the world's top five most polluted major cities as fires on Borneo and Sumatra islands, intensified by a turbo-charged El Nino weather phenomenon, keep emitting smoke.
In Indonesia, groups are working to save wildlife from the fires, including orangutans.
On Saturday, the West Kalimantan conservation agency and Indonesian non-profit YIARI said a team evacuated 51 orangutans from locations in the province from August 6 to October 19.
And figures from Indonesia's forestry ministry suggested this week that the number rescued over recent months in Kalimantan could be as high as 96.
Officials could not be immediately reached to clarify the number.
The latest rescue came on Saturday, when three conservation agencies rescued a 20-year-old male orangutan in Hampangen village in Central Kalimantan, on Borneo island.
"The evacuation process was carried out with great caution," the agencies said.
"After the orangutan was sedated, the medical team immediately conducted a health examination before taking the animal to the... rehabilitation center," it said.
Indonesia's transport ministry also said around 2,400 flights across the country have been affected by the haze since mid-August.
"Haze reduces visibility around airports, which can lead to delays, disruptions, and even flight cancellations. Every operational decision is made with safety as the top priority," the ministry said.
All three orangutan species face a critical risk of extinction due to deforestation, wildfires, habitat loss and illegal hunting.

Israel's opposition will not defeat Netanyahu by focusing on October 7 - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:11:48 UTC
14:11:48 KST

The clock is ticking toward October 27, and tensions are running high. The central question is whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will manage to hold on to power, although most polls suggest that his chances are slim. Yet a closer look at the election campaigns of Gadi Eisenkot and Netanyahu reveals that each side has its own interpretation of why the 2026 election is critical to Israel’s future.
While Eisenkot and his fellow leaders of the center-left bloc, including Naftali Bennett, Yair Lapid, Avigdor Liberman, and Yair Golan, have placed the October 7 failure and the question of haredi (ultra-Orthodox) conscription at the center of their campaign, Netanyahu is seeking to highlight the achievements of the War of Redemption [the multifront conflict following Hamas’s 2023 attack] while downplaying his responsibility for the October 7 failure.
Alongside allegations that Netanyahu received two warnings of an impending attack, from the Emiratis and the Egyptians, the statements made by his former military secretary, Avi Gil, are regarded by the opposition as compelling evidence of Netanyahu’s failure.
Eisenkot’s camp has also continued to emphasize that Netanyahu’s inner circle is tainted by corruption and a lack of integrity. In addition to the alleged attempt to falsify the official record, Netanyahu presented a selective account of the State Comptroller’s Report on the October 7 failure.
The opposition’s claims are certainly open to debate, and a closer examination of Gil’s statements only reinforces the conclusion that the security establishment failed on that terrible night. Nevertheless, several questions arise when we analyze the arguments put forward by both sides.
Analyzing the arguments
First, although Netanyahu pursued a failed policy toward Hamas, motivated in part by a desire to avoid a confrontation that could derail efforts to normalize relations with Saudi Arabia, the fact remains that he received intelligence indicating an impending attack only after it had begun.
Unlike the hours preceding the outbreak of the Yom Kippur War, when then-prime minister Golda Meir was involved in the decision-making process and could have ordered a preemptive strike against Egypt, Netanyahu was not even given an opportunity to influence events that night.
Second, questions also arise regarding the claim that the alleged criminal attempt to change the time of a phone call in the official record, from 6:40 a.m. to 6:29 a.m., was intended to reinforce the bizarre conspiracy theory that a generals’ revolt had taken place. Netanyahu’s opponents argue that members of his inner circle sought to create the impression that the generals had deliberately failed to wake him.
An alternative explanation, however, is that the change was intended to demonstrate that Netanyahu had not been asleep while Hamas terrorists were infiltrating communities near the Gaza border. If Netanyahu’s associates had wanted to emphasize that the generals had kept him in the dark, it would have made more sense to leave the call time at 6:40 a.m., allowing them to argue that he had been informed only 11 minutes after the attack began.
Third, Netanyahu’s strained relationship with the security establishment’s leadership was shaped in part by his insistence, during the judicial reform debate, that the phenomenon of military refusal be confronted rather than tolerated. Critics argue that Netanyahu chose to disregard the security chiefs’ warnings about the implications of the proposed judicial legislation and the threat it posed to national security, as well as their less specific warnings of a possible war.
Others, however, argue that had the IDF responded to military refusal as it did during the Disengagement from Gaza, Yahya Sinwar and Mohammed Deif might have thought twice before launching their attack.
This raises another question: If the security establishment’s leaders had warned of an impending war, why was the IDF so unprepared on that fateful day and caught so completely off guard?
In conclusion, Netanyahu has effectively been campaigning continuously since the 2022 election, particularly in the aftermath of the October 7, 2023, massacre. Yet focusing on the alleged falsification of official records and the conduct of Netanyahu’s inner circle is unlikely to be the key to defeating him in the 2026 election.
Israel’s political history repeatedly demonstrates that corruption is not necessarily a decisive issue for voters. Arye Deri, for example, led Shas to 17 seats in the 1999 election despite having been convicted of bribery. Ariel Sharon led Likud to 38 seats in the 2003 election despite the cloud of suspicion surrounding the Cyril Kern affair.
Netanyahu, meanwhile, has consistently secured more than 30 seats in elections held since he became a criminal defendant. Rather than dwelling on the past, the opposition would be better served by persuading the public that Israel has a better future beyond Netanyahu’s leadership. That is how elections are won!
The writer is a lecturer and research fellow at the University of South Wales in the United Kingdom. He is the author of Collapse: The Israeli Labor Party, 1992–2024.
