Pope's surgeon details operating on the "ideal patient" after lung cancer discovery "entirely by chance"
The surgeon who operated on Pope Leo XIV earlier this week detailed in an interview with Vatican News how the pope's cancer was discovered, moments before and after his surgical procedure and the importance of prevention.
The pope was discharged from the hospital Saturday — four days after his surgery — to a large crowd of well-wishers cheering for him.
Dr. Stefano Margaritora, director of the thoracic surgery unit at the Agostino Gemelli University Hospital Foundation, spoke to the Vatican News in a lengthy interview and said the pope's lung cancer was discovered "entirely by chance."
"The Holy Father falls into the category of people who discover they have lung cancer entirely by chance — not because they are undergoing preventive screening, but because they undergo examinations for other reasons," Margaritora said.
Margaritora said the tumor was found at the base of the right lung, but if it had been "a little higher up, it certainly would not have been seen."
Unfortunately, the doctor said, in its early stages, cancers can show no symptoms — such as the lung cancer the pope was diagnosed with. That's why regular preventive checkups for other cancers are so important, he said.
"He had no respiratory symptoms and felt perfectly well," said Margaritora.
The 71-year-old pontiff revealed the news at the end of his Sunday noon blessing last week before thousands of people in St. Peter's Square.
Margaritora said the operation to remove a lung nodule was routine and went forward "without any complications." The pope was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, a common cancer, during the surgery.
The doctor said that for the four days the pope recovered at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, he was "an ideal patient."
"I am not saying that to flatter him. He truly did not cause the slightest problem for the team caring for him ... ," the doctor told Vatican News.
He said on the second day following the surgery, medical staff found the pope arranging the chairs in the hospital's makeshift chapel. Margaritora recounted that staff offered to move the chairs, "Holy Father, we can do that." And he replied, "It doesn't matter. I can do it, so I will."
The pope had already resumed some work activity on Thursday. By Friday, the pope had spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin over the phone. Pictures of the American-born pope standing at an altar in green vestments, celebrating Mass at a small hospital chapel, were released by the Vatican.
He also held separate meetings with Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, the dean of the College of Cardinals, and Cardinal Baldassare Reina, the vicar general of the Diocese of Rome. The pope is scheduled to travel Nov. 6-17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

At least 19 killed in stampede at religious gathering in India

At least 19 killed in stampede at religious gathering in India
Incident took place at festival in Kolkata, in India’s West Bengal state, amid large crowds and rainfall, police say.
A “stampede” during a Hindu religious festival in eastern India has killed at least 19 people and injured 25 others, officials said.
The stampede in Kolkata, the capital of West Bengal state, happened on Saturday night when a crowd near a pavilion ran for cover as it began raining during Durga Puja, an annual Hindu festival celebrating the goddess Durga.
According to police, some worshippers fell on the road and were trampled.
West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari, who visited Kolkata Medical College and Hospital where victims were taken, said 19 people had died and 25 were receiving treatment.
Among the dead was a seven-year-old girl, Adhikari told reporters.
He announced that a special investigation team to be headed by a judge of the state’s high court would look into the disaster.
Police detained some pavilion organisers, private security personnel and on-duty staff, and launched a probe into any crowd-control and safety lapses.
Police said the injured were taken to hospital from a Durga Puja pandal, a temporary pavilion housing idols of the goddess Durga at a festival which attracts thousands of devotees.
A police statement said the stampede happened in the evening due to “heavy crowds of pandal hoppers amid rainfall”.
A senior police official at the scene told the AFP news agency that an announcement caused “commotion” after it started raining and the “crowd waiting outside the pandal [pavilion] was pushing, pulling and rushing forward and fell on the ground, leading to the stampede.”
Prime Minister Narendra Modi described the incident as “saddening”.
“Condolences to the bereaved families. Wishing the injured a speedy recovery. The West Bengal Government is providing all possible help to the affected families,” Modi wrote on X.
Modi’s office announced compensation of 200,000 rupees ($2,106) for the next of kin of those who died and 50,000 rupees ($527) each for the injured.
Interior Minister Amit Shah said the “administration is ensuring that all possible medical facilities are being provided to the injured”.
About 3,500 Durga Puja pavilions have been set up across Kolkata for the festival. Following the stampede, authorities advised several of Kolkata’s most heavily attended venues to temporarily close to visitors.
Deadly crowd incidents happen frequently at Indian mass events, such as religious festivals, often due to poor management and safety lapses.
Last year, a stampede at India’s Kumbh Mela religious fair killed 30 people and injured several others. In Bengaluru, 11 fans were crushed to death during celebrations for the local cricket team’s first Indian Premier League title.
In southern Tamil Nadu state, 36 people were killed in a stampede at a campaign rally for a popular actor-turned-politician.
In 2024, 121 people were killed in northern Uttar Pradesh state during a Hindu religious gathering.

Salman refused to stay silent. His brother paid the price
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
19:39:45 UTC
04:39:45 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
Salman Shabbir was having breakfast at his Sydney home when his phone rang in the pre-dawn hours of 15 March 2024.
On the other end of the line, in Pakistan, his sister-in-law was in a panic.
"They're here. They're asking for you. They're taking your brother," she told Shabbir.
Then an unfamiliar man came on the line and asked Shabbir to confirm his identity.
Shabbir says he could hear his sister-in-law screaming in the background, pleading with the men not to take her husband. Then the screams fell silent.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
He was in Australia, thousands of kilometres from his family in Pakistan, a country he left 11 years earlier.
Hours later, Shabbir says, the callers demanded that he stop posting about Pakistan's politics on his X account.
SBS News has contacted the High Commission for Pakistan in Canberra for comment but did not receive a reply by the deadline.
The episode raises a disturbing question: can speaking out against a government from abroad put the people you love at risk? It is a question at the heart of transnational repression in which governments or their alleged proxies seek to silence critics beyond their borders.
Shabbir, his activism and his family
In the hours after the call, Shabbir tried to piece together what had happened to his brother.
He says several uniformed men arrived in a black ute known locally as a Vigo Dala. One was from the local police; the others wore commando-style clothing and carried what Shabbir describes as "huge guns”.
"They were sent by the [Pakistani] military," he alleges.
"I have no doubt."
Shabbir runs an X account called Citizen Action, which he initially used to advocate for overseas voting rights. He later turned to criticising Pakistan's elections and the treatment of former prime minister Imran Khan.
Shabbir alleges that, days before his brother was taken, Pakistan's then-information minister, Attaullah Tarar, criticised a petition he had launched. The petition addressed bodies within the European Union and highlighted the alleged mistreatment of Khan, arguing it breached human rights expectations embedded in trade agreements. Shabbir says the petition attracted more than 3,000 signatures.
Khan has been jailed since 2023 following a string of convictions and charges. He and his party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf, maintain the cases are politically motivated and aimed at keeping him out of power.
"I tweeted out that they have taken my brother, and the tweet started going viral," Shabbir says.
He says he also contacted Australia's Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT), the National Security Hotline, the Australian Federal Police (AFP), and Pakistan's then-high commissioner to Australia, seeking help. He also spoke to a Pakistani media outlet.
Within 12 hours, Shabbir received a second call. The caller asked where Shabbir was and whether he had an Australian passport. He demanded Shabbir's X username and password. Shabbir says he refused.
The caller then warned they would continue to hold his brother if Shabbir wouldn't comply, before ending the call.
Shabbir says he received a third call about half an hour later. SBS News obtained a recording of the calls, first published by Drop Site News.
The callers demanded that Shabbir stop posting on X about Pakistan's politics, initially for three months. When he refused, he says they reduced the demand to one month and then five days.
At one point, Shabbir alleges, the men tortured his brother during the call.
"The conversation got really heated.
They tortured my brother on the call, and he made sure that I heard his screams.
Not an isolated incident
Shabbir's experience is not the only alleged case of transnational repression involving people in Australia.
In recent years, allegations have included death threats linked to the Cambodian government, requests to spy on a neighbour allegedly made on behalf of the Chinese government, and stalking orders attributed to the Iranian government. Other reports have involved India, Myanmar, Rwanda, South Sudan, Vietnam and other countries.
Australians have also reportedly been targeted overseas. Melbourne-based Tran Hiep is currently being detained in Vietnam on terrorism and sabotage charges, which the United States-based pro-democracy group Viet Tan, designated as a terrorist group by Vietnam, alleges are unfounded.
In another case, last year, an Australian journalist was arrested in Thailand at Malaysia's request over a criminal defamation complaint, prompting criticism from human rights groups.
In September, a Senate inquiry was launched to examine the nature, scale and methods of transnational repression, including its impacts on diaspora communities and democratic processes. The inquiry was established by a Greens motion with support from the Coalition.
Newly elected Greens leader David Shoebridge tells SBS News: "The purpose of this inquiry is to surface this and force parliament to confront the reality that there are foreign governments, bad actors in other parts of the world that are actively trying to silence and stifle political discussion inside Australia."
Shoebridge says perpetrators can be "incredibly bold" and make little effort to hide their actions.
They're making the phone calls, they're sending the social media messages, they're having, sometimes somebody who's a consular official, turn up or attend a community rally and start taking photos and observe what's happening.
"Sometimes it's quite overt and there is a potentially quite significant evidentiary thread."
He says he's spoken to many Australians who've experienced transnational repression, including Shabbir, who contacted him after his brother was taken.
How transnational repression works
Transnational repression occurs when states or their proxies seek to control, intimidate or punish people for their activities beyond their own borders.
Tactics range from threats, surveillance and physical violence to pressure on relatives and the misuse of legal or law enforcement systems. They can also include denying passports or consular services, refusing re-entry into the country or revoking nationality. Some acts are criminal offences, while others can foster fear and mistrust within diaspora communities.
The issue has drawn growing concern from the United Nations. More than 100 UN special rapporteurs and mandate holders expressed "deep concern" over the "growing challenge" in a statement published last month.
At the 56th session of the UN Human Rights Council in June 2024, Australia joined with more than 45 other countries in a statement condemning transnational repression as a threat to sovereignty, democracy and human rights, and calling for stronger protections for those at risk.
For people living in exile, the effects can extend well beyond their own safety, reaching family members who remain in their country of origin.
Naung Naung, a refugee from Myanmar who studies transnational repression, says Myanmar people in Australia have reported threatening phone calls, surveillance, intimidation at pro-democracy events and restrictions on passports, as well as the alleged misuse of Australian law.
In 2021, the Myanmar embassy in Canberra was accused of transnational repression after it wrote to students demanding they pledge loyalty to the military junta.
Naung says his brother was doxed because of his alleged friendship with figures from the National Unity Government, an opposition administration formed after the 2021 military coup, in their hometown. He says a photo his brother had posted online was shared in a pro-military Telegram channel with calls for arrest.
"My parents had to move to a different town, and they have not been able to come back since then to my hometown," he tells SBS News.
For years, Naung used a pseudonym online, despite living in Australia.
He remains too worried about his family's safety to connect with his parents on social media.
I don't want to be a victim of the transnational repression. I don't want to be a victim of the subject I'm studying.
In a statement, the Embassy of Myanmar in Canberra denied all allegations it has engaged in transnational repression or foreign interference, calling them “entirely groundless” and saying it acts in accordance with Australian law and relevant diplomatic rules and regulations.
The embassy said it has never threatened, surveilled, or intimidated members of the Myanmar community in Australia, and that it has handled passport-related matters in accordance with applicable rules and regulations.
“It is a globally widespread phenomenon for individual with differing point of views to criticize and target one another on social media,” the embassy said.
How widespread is transnational repression in Australia?
The scale of transnational repression in Australia is difficult to establish, partly because there is no comprehensive public data tracking reported cases, according to Shoebridge.
"One of the reasons is when you go to, for example, the Australian Federal Police — and I've put many complaints in front of them about foreign interference — after a rudimentary review of it, they will say, 'Well, actually the core potentially criminal action is happening in another country and therefore they won't undertake a police investigation and therefore they don't gather the data,'" he says.
In recent years, the AFP has pursued several cases involving alleged transnational repression.
In one case, three Chinese nationals have been accused of covertly collecting information about a Canberra Buddhist association on behalf of a Chinese public security bureau.
The Australian Security Intelligence Organisation (ASIO) has also documented attempts to intimidate or harm critics living in Australia. In his 2024 annual threat assessment, ASIO director-general Mike Burgess said the Counter Foreign Interference Taskforce, established in 2020, had conducted more than 120 operations to mitigate threats to communities, Australia's political system and classified information.
The operations covered a range of foreign interference threats, Burgess said at the time.
"One involved an individual working on behalf of a foreign government who wanted to physically harm an Australian-based critic of the regime, including attempts to identify the target's home address and bank details, hiring a subcontractor to photograph the house, and requesting a quote for 'severe action' against the dissident.
"Even more recently, a foreign intelligence service tried to find an Australian who would be willing to make a different dissident quote 'disappear'."
When fear follows you abroad
Mubashar Hasan is a Sydney-based researcher on transnational repression whose work draws on both his own experience and accounts from diaspora communities. He was a political science professor in Bangladesh before relocating to Norway and later moving to Australia in 2020, after being forcibly disappeared by Bangladesh's military in 2017.
I remember on the first day of kidnapping when they blindfolded me, they were beating me. They put me in handcuffs.
"I heard people crying. I heard people begging. There was no freedom to even drink water as you want. There was a 24-hour high-voltage light," he tells SBS News.
Hasan says he was held at a secret detention site for 44 days, but after his release, he could no longer feel safe in Bangladesh.
"I became a kind of refugee in my own country, because the police, the intelligence, the judge, everyone knew there was a crime against humanity that took place against me, but no-one was doing anything," he says.
SBS News tried several times to contact the Bangladeshi embassy for comment but did not receive a response.
After relocating to Norway, Hasan began hearing similar accounts from other people, some of whom were living in exile.
He later turned to researching transnational repression, taking care with how he wrote about the subject because he feared attracting the attention of authorities back home. He has since moved to Australia, where he studies the issue and works with diaspora communities.
"In my experience of engaging with the community members from Myanmar, Iran, Rwanda, South Sudan, and a few other countries, we've found mistrust within the community," he says.
Some people fear they are being watched by others in their own community; others avoid community gatherings or posting on social media, worried about intimidation or harassment.
Hasan says more needs to be done to address the effects of transnational repression on migrant communities.
"Communities here need to find confidence in the authorities that yes, if I believe that I'm facing repression, I could go somewhere, and that could be a government department, an agency or even a counselling support system where I can go and talk about it and people will listen."
Calls for reform
In July, Independent National Security Legislation Monitor Jake Blight completed a statutory review of Australia's foreign interference laws.
He says evidence from ASIO, AFP, civil society and academics convinced him transnational repression is a "very serious and growing problem".
Blight says it can be addressed using diplomatic pressure, sanctions, and the visa system, as well as through criminal law.
"Many types of these actions are already crimes. Assaulting people, stalking people, using a telecommunication service to menace or harass: these are all offences," he tells SBS News.
"And while I found a few gaps in the offences, it's very challenging when you're talking about prosecuting people who are acting offshore."
Those who are outside the country are very difficult to prosecute under Australian law.
Blight's review identified four areas for reform: creating a new offence for coerced repatriation; extending an existing foreign interference offence concerning democratic and political rights from Australians to anyone in Australia; increasing penalties for people paid to commit crimes on behalf of foreign governments; and extending protections against foreign interference to judicial proceedings, royal commissions and independent inquiries.
A spokesperson for the Department of Home Affairs told SBS News the government takes the "persistent, evolving and increasingly complex threat" seriously.
They said the government is carefully considering Blight's recommendations and "is committed to ensuring Australia's robust criminal offences remain fit-for-purpose to address the risks posed by espionage and foreign interference, including transnational repression".
In May, the government launched the Counter Foreign Interference Community Support Hub, providing online resources in more than 23 languages to help recognise and respond to foreign interference.
But Shoebridge wants the law to go further.
"I think if somebody in a third country is threatening to harm somebody's relatives, threatening to potentially destroy their house, to coerce them, to change someone's behaviour in Australia, and if you can establish that causal connection, then I think it should be a crime on the Australian statute books," he says.
Shabbir encountered the limits of Australia's response firsthand when he tried to get help after his brother was taken.
"On the day I called DFAT, they asked me to call the National Security Hotline, who asked me to call AFP, who asked me to call DFAT," he says.
"It was a bit of ping-pong, to be honest, but in the end, I was forwarded a flyer that was made by Senator [David] Shoebridge's office, and it had guidelines on how to register such a case, and something called the category called foreign interference."
Eventually, Shabbir says he got a call from NSW Police, who discussed the case and conducted a risk assessment. An officer gave him a case number and told him to call if anything changes.
His brother was ultimately released within a day, and Shabbir continues his online activism, but he wants to see greater action to protect Australian citizens from alleged transnational repression.
Like Shoebridge, he wants Australian authorities to recognise what he calls the "extraterritorial proxy loophole" — where threats made through relatives overseas fall outside the reach of Australian law because the conduct occurred offshore.
They have to recognise it as a criminal offence because ultimately the target was an Australian citizen.

Ukrainian foreign minister says Russian-held town is a ‘death trap’ with starving residents
UKRAINE – Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Oct 17 that Russian occupying forces were turning the Ukrainian town of Oleshky into a “death trap” gripped by starvation, and urged international organisations to help evacuate its residents.
Sybiha made his comments on social media platform X a day after Russian President Vladimir Putin pledged, in a conversation with Pope Leo, to cooperate in delivering vital supplies into the town in southern Ukraine’s Kherson region.
“Russians are trying to turn the Ukrainian town of Oleshky into a death trap. The hospital has run out of medicine. Dozens of bodies lie in the streets or in homes, as Russians forbid residents from burying them,” Sybiha wrote.

Diplomats detail attack, call on Israel to protect Palestinians

"The whole world needs to know what's happening there," he said. "For me, I'll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here."
Baudoux said he did not suffer serious injuries. He said the attackers kicked him and beat him with iron bars, and threw him to the ground.
"It's the gratuitous nature of the violence that stuns me," he said. "They arrived completely enraged."
Netanyahu's office, in its statement, said Baudoux previously raised the Palestinian flag over the Aulnoye-Aymeries municipal building, "prompting French authorities to order its removal."
Poland's foreign ministry confirmed the incident on social media, saying in a statement that its representatives were unharmed and that based on information currently available, "there is no indication that they were specifically targeted."
It added: "According to preliminary information, Israeli settlers may have been responsible for the incident."
"We are deeply outraged by this incident and condemn it in the strongest possible terms," the statement on X said. "Poland has consistently opposed violence perpetrated by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank. Attacks against members of the diplomatic corps are absolutely unacceptable."
"We remain in close contact with our partners to establish the full circumstances of the incident," the statement said.
Settler violence has surged in West Bank
Violence by Israeli settlers against Palestinians in the West Bank has surged in recent years, particularly after the establishment of Israel's current hard-right government in late 2022, according to statistics released by the United Nations humanitarian office.
Activists say authorities do little to stop it, particularly during this year's annual olive harvest.
Netanyahu, in the past, has condemned the violence and vowed a crackdown against what he says is a small group of several hundred wayward youths responsible for attacks on Palestinians.
Human rights groups and critics say the government is complicit in the attacks and that Netanyahu's condemnation appears to be posturing since the Israeli military often intervenes on the settlers' side and the perpetrators are rarely prosecuted.
Saturday's attack follows a similar incident on Friday during which several people were seriously injured, including a freelance American photojournalist working with The Washington Post.
On Saturday, Heidi Levine, the veteran American journalist injured in the attack, was undergoing surgery on her finger, which was nearly detached from her hand, her daughter told the Associated Press.
Ashley Milner said Levine also has a broken rib and multiple broken vertebrae, as well as lacerations.
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee on Saturday called for a full investigation and the arrest and prosecution of anyone involved in the attack against Levine.
"Attacking a female photographer is despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards. Dishonorable act of senseless violence," he wrote on social media.
Israel's police and military said they had opened investigations into Friday's incident.

‘A sudden blow to my head’: Flydubai captain recalls cockpit attack that nearly downed the jet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
19:29:12 UTC
04:29:12 KST

Flydubai captain Smit Machchhar, who was seriously wounded when his Omani co-pilot attacked him during a flight to Israel, has spoken publicly about the terrifying moments inside the cockpit and his desperate efforts to prevent the aircraft from crashing.
In interviews published Saturday by the Emirati newspaper The National and Sky News Arabia, Machchhar described how he managed to reach the cockpit door despite severe injuries, allowing Israeli passengers and crew members to enter and help stop the attacker.
Both interviews were conducted at his hospital bedside in Abu Dhabi, where he remains under medical care. His head was still bandaged, although he appeared stronger than during an earlier televised conversation with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi several days after the September 30 attack. Neither interview devoted much attention to the significant role played by the Israeli passengers in preventing the disaster.
Machchhar described his brief interactions with the attacker, Omani co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami, before the assault, saying there had been nothing unusual about his behavior. The two had never flown together before.
Asked about Israeli passenger Yaniv Hayun, who made international headlines as the "plumber who saved the plane," Machchhar said he had little recollection of his involvement.
"To be honest, I don't know the plumber's story," he said. "But I do remember someone senior on the flight saying that the captain was in control. I didn't see him."
He then laughed when asked whether a plumber could land an aircraft. "Can a plumber land a plane? I don't want to speculate. All my memories and energy at that moment were focused on staying alive," he said.
Machchhar explained that he was drifting in and out of consciousness and that his vision had been severely impaired by the repeated blows he suffered.
In his interview with The National, Machchhar recalled initially believing that the violent blow to his head had been caused by a technical malfunction or an object falling from the aircraft's ceiling. "It was such a hard blow that I nearly fell onto the controls," he said.
The captain said he had met al-Hammami for the first time that morning. "We exchanged some small talk, but nothing particularly deep, just like on other flights. There was never anything that made me think something was wrong."
When the attack began, his first instinct was to release his seat belt and try to defend himself. "The first thing I did was free myself from the seat belts and try to block the blows as much as possible," he recalled. "The blows were directed at my head. After the first few, my vision narrowed dramatically, and I could only make out outlines."
Despite his injuries, Machchhar managed to reach toward the mechanism that opens the cockpit door. "My hand went to the handle that opens the door, and I shouted for my colleagues. That's when I believe I lost consciousness for the first time. I heard the door opening," he said.
The most frightening moment came when he realized the aircraft was losing altitude. "The scariest thing was hearing the engines slow down and feeling the nose of the aircraft dive," he recalled.
He said he repeatedly tried to reach the door, desperate to let others into the cockpit. "I kept looking for the door. People ask me whether I opened it. I tried to get to it. I pushed, tried to reach out. But the next thing I remember is lying face down. And thank God, the cockpit door was open."
Machchhar said he did not know whether he would survive the ordeal but refused to give up. "I wasn't sure I would come out of it alive, but I didn't give up. I thought about my son and daughter. It was as though a survival instinct had taken over, and fortunately it saved me and all the other passengers and my colleagues. I would say a higher power was involved."
Speaking separately to Sky News Arabia, Machchhar provided further details about the moments immediately preceding the attack. He said al-Hammami had indicated that he wanted to pray inside the cockpit.
"He wanted to pray, so he stood up and started praying," Machchhar recalled. "On our 737, the aircraft I fly, the cockpit isn't particularly large. Out of respect for someone who is praying, I try not to look at them."
The captain continued working, checking flight information on his computer. "I was doing my job, sitting there and checking the timings and everything else on my computer, when suddenly I received a very hard blow to the back of my head," he said.
"It was an extremely strong blow. I felt that whatever struck me was very hard and solid. At that moment, I had no idea what had hit me. As the incident continued, I kept losing and regaining consciousness."
Machchhar said the attacker appeared to say something while striking him, but he could not understand the words.
Asked by the Sky News Arabia interviewer whether there had been a moment when he thought he might not survive, Machchhar acknowledged that he was still struggling to process what happened. "I'm trying to get over it now, but yes, there was a moment when I realized I had to tell myself: Do something. You can't die like this," he said.
He stressed that he had not resigned himself to dying. Instead, he felt an overwhelming need to act before it was too late. "It wasn't that I had accepted my death. It was more a feeling that I had to do something. There was a moment when I realized that if nothing was done immediately..."
Then the cockpit door opened, and the situation changed dramatically. "When the door opened, the scene was completely different. I remember lying face down. There was panic, of course, and screaming," he said.
Machchhar reserved particular praise for the colleague who eventually took control of the aircraft.
"What happened afterward, the fact that another colleague of mine took over the controls and saved the situation, deserves enormous praise," he said. "It's something I will carry with me until the day I die."

Albanian police fire rubber bullets as protests against Rama escalate
Five days of clashes rock Tirana as students join a wider movement demanding Prime Minister Edi Rama’s resignation.
Police in Albania have fired rubber bullets at antigovernment protesters in the capital, Tirana, as violent clashes intensify over demands for Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.
The clashes continued on Saturday for a fifth consecutive day after high school and university students joined a broader movement against Rama, whose governing centre-left Socialist Party has held power since 2013.
The unrest has brought growing anger over education, unemployment and alleged corruption into a wider confrontation with the government.
Protesters threw stones, petrol bombs and fireworks at police near Rama’s office and elsewhere in central Tirana.
Some set cars and rubbish bins alight, creating burning barricades across streets.
Police responded with tear gas, water cannon and baton charges as demonstrators pushed against security lines.
The AFP news agency reported that officers used rubber bullets for the first time since the demonstrations began.
National police chief Skender Hita confirmed their use at a news conference on Saturday, saying they had been deployed “in a limited manner”.
The Ministry of Health and Social Welfare said nine protesters and four police officers received medical treatment on Saturday.
Hita said 167 people had been arrested over five days of unrest, while 132 officers had been injured.
Seven police officers were also suspended pending investigations into allegations that they had exceeded their authority.
Rama, who is serving his fourth term and has refused to resign, visited businesses damaged during the unrest on Saturday. He promised to listen to students and protect their right to demonstrate, while warning against further destruction.
He also accused his conservative political opponents of encouraging the violence.
Growing discontent
The students have complained about expensive university fees, poor educational facilities and limited employment opportunities, alongside allegations of government corruption.
At the start of Saturday’s demonstration, protesters set fire to a suitcase and threw it into the Ministry of Education’s courtyard. AFP reported that the gesture symbolised their determination not to leave Albania in search of better opportunities.
“We are demanding our rights, our future and a better country,” journalism student Sinan Billa told AFP.
The student demonstrations have added to months of antigovernment rallies organised by the Flamingo movement, which began as a campaign against a luxury tourism development on Albania’s southern coast.
The project is linked to an investment company founded by Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of US President Donald Trump.
The movement has since widened its demands to include Rama’s resignation amid allegations of corruption against his government.
The unrest has also spread beyond Tirana. Local media reported that protesters in the coastal city of Durres damaged a post office and blocked roads with burning barricades, extending the confrontations beyond the capital.

Poland asks EP to waive immunity of ex-CEO at state oil giant
Poland submitted on Thursday a request to the European Parliament (EP) seeking to waive the immunity of MEP Daniel Obajtek, a former CEO of state oil conglomerate Orlen, as well as to authorise his pre-trial detention, Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek announced on X.
The request relates to an investigation into the artificial lowering of fuel prices in 2023, a period during which Obajtek served as CEO of Orlen, said Zurek, who is also the country's Prosecutor General.
Investigators allege that Obajtek, while serving as CEO of Orlen and "acting on grounds unrelated to economic considerations", instructed subordinates to lower wholesale and retail fuel prices. The objective was to ensure that, between October 1 and October 15, 2023, the price of a litre of fuel would not exceed PLN 5.99 (EUR 1.4) at the pump.
The prosecution asserts that Obajtek acted in violation of established procedures and, "despite mounting problems and losses, personally monitored the operation and issued ongoing directives to maintain the artificially low rates", according to Zurek's post.
He argued that Obajtek's decisions led to a fuel shortage at over 600 service stations, causing damage to Orlen exceeding PLN 4.1 billion (EUR 938 million).
Zurek added that the acts covered by the request to lift immunity carry a potential sentence of up to 25 years in prison.
In early October, five current and former Orlen managers were charged in connection with the suspected manipulation of fuel prices.
Daniel Obajtek is currently a member of the European Parliament representing Poland's ex-governing socially-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party. He served as CEO of Orlen from 2018 to 2024. (PAP)

What Trump’s Waiver of New Russia Sanctions Means for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
19:17:33 UTC
04:17:33 KST

President Donald Trump signed an executive order Friday that waives many of the sanctions in the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which Congress passed in the late senator’s name last month. The waiver, coming a week after Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia, also underscores fraying relations between the U.S. and Ukraine.
The law, which was set to take effect Oct. 18, called for sanctions targeting Russian officials, financial institutions, and other entities, alongside tariffs of up to 100% on goods imported into the U.S. from major buyers of Russian crude oil or natural gas. Those measures were intended to restrict the financial resources supporting Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Read More: Lawmakers Argue Trump's Russia Diesel Deal 'Violates' the Law. Here's What Legal Experts Say
The U.K.’s Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office estimated in June 2025 that international sanctions had deprived the Russian state of at least $450 billion in war funds since February 2022, including through lost oil tax revenues and immobilized central-bank reserves.
While Trump’s waiver leaves existing sanctions in place, it blocks the additional pressure the new measures were intended to exert.
Trump has also pushed Ukraine to scale back its own campaign against Russia’s energy sector, repeatedly urging Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian fuel infrastructure and suggesting that those attacks are driving up U.S. fuel prices. But Ukrainian strikes are only one factor affecting fuel prices; disruptions linked to the war with Iran are largely responsible for constraining global supplies, while reduced Russian refinery activity has added pressure to diesel markets.
On Oct. 11, Trump claimed that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “energy ceasefire.” But Ukrainian officials reported Russian strikes on energy infrastructure hours after his announcement, and Zelensky said the purported agreement was news to him.
That same day, Trump called for Ukraine to replace President Volodymyr Zelensky. Withdrawing sanctions within a week of those statements, and thereby improving Russia’s financial position, points to an increasingly uneven display of support from the U.S.
Jeff Colgan, a professor of political science at Brown University, tells TIME that the decision is basically “is like trading [Ukrainian] democracy for diesel.”
A diesel deal with Russia, announced Oct. 9, is one of the many recent actions Trump has taken in an effort to reduce fuel prices for Americans ahead of midterm elections on Nov. 3. The deal came with an easing of sanctions as the Treasury Department issued a temporary license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel, including imports into the U.S., through April 7, 2027.
In his announcement of the deal on Truth Social, Trump said that Russia had agreed to supply global markets with more than 4.8 million tons of diesel, claiming that it would bring diesel prices down “IN RECORD NUMBERS.”
But experts question whether the deal would actually have any material impact on the price of fuel for American consumers.
“There could be a modest short-term effect on wholesale prices, but only a small and delayed benefit, if any, would reach consumers at the pump,” says Tatiana Mitrova, a fellow at Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy.
The waiver signed Friday, in comparison, could potentially prevent additional disruption to the global energy market. It allows Russian oil to continue flowing to importers like China and India, preventing further market volatility.
“The broader sanctions waiver may prevent additional market disruptions, but it does not itself create new supply,” Mitrova says. “The potential economic benefit to American consumers looks rather modest compared with the geopolitical cost of weakening sanctions pressure.”
Reducing that pressure—which has widely been interpreted as a component of the diesel deal, though it has not been explicitly identified as such—likely benefits Russia more than the monetary value of the diesel deal itself, Mitrova points out.
“The much bigger financial benefit for Moscow is avoiding additional sanctions that could have undermined its much larger crude oil export revenues,” she says.
And while Trump has touted the benefits of the deal, Colgan questions whether they will be tangible to any country other than Russia itself.
“Easing the sanctions probably won't move global prices very much (big market), but could mean substantial extra revenue for Russia,” he says.
But the potential consequences extend beyond Russia’s balance sheet. The waiver also raises questions about Washington’s commitment to Ukraine as relations between the two countries deteriorate.
How might the sanctions waiver affect Ukraine?
Beyond its impact on global diesel prices, Trump’s sanctions waiver could deepen a growing rift between the U.S. and Ukraine—raising further questions about Washington’s support for Kyiv.
Konstantin Sonin, a Russian economist and a professor at the University of Chicago Harris School of Public Policy, reads the move as a symbolic gesture of support for Russian President Vladimir Putin. He suggests that it could send a message to U.S. allies that extends beyond economic considerations.
“I think this will be read by Ukraine and Ukraine leadership—and European leadership—as another step in the United States withdrawing from being an active European player,” he tells TIME.
In addition to bolstering Russia’s finances and giving it latitude in its invasion of Ukraine, Sonin says that the waiver of additional sanctions could also “boost morale” for Putin.
“It’s another bit of signaling that the United States is not as supportive of Ukraine as they were historically,” he adds. “You still cannot say that the United States is on Putin's side, but it is another bit of diminishing support for Ukraine.”
Mitrova agrees that the biggest benefit to Russia might be more strategic than financial.
“For Putin, the most valuable outcome may not be additional diesel revenues but the perception that Washington is increasingly prioritizing domestic energy prices over sustained pressure on Russia,” she says. “That could reinforce the Kremlin’s belief that it can outlast Western support rather than make meaningful concessions.”
Zelensky criticized the decision to block the new sanctions.
“The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me,” the Ukrainian President wrote on X on Saturday. “And it definitely helps only the Russians. It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people. This certainly does not stop the war.”
Mitrova argues that in easing sanctions, the U.S. also compromises its position with European leadership that has continued to align closely with Zelensky and Ukraine.
“Europe is still tightening sanctions against Russia, while Washington is now moving in the opposite direction,” she says. “By suspending sanctions that were designed to discourage major countries from buying Russian energy, Washington risks undermining a central pillar of the Western strategy toward Russia.”
Why Republicans and Democrats are criticizing the waiver
Trump’s waiver earned a flood of criticism from both sides of the aisle, particularly since it undermined a widely supported act of Congress. The Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026 cleared Congress on Sept. 16 with overwhelming bipartisan support: a vote of 86-11 in the Senate and a vote of 262-159 in the House.
North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who is leaving office in January, called the decision “beyond irresponsible” on Saturday.
Suggesting that the Trump Administration is overtly snubbing the will of the legislative branch, Tillis wrote on X: “It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine.”
Texas Republican Sen. John Cornyn reacted by saying “Lindsey would be appalled,” referencing the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham—a staunch Ukraine supporter after whom the sanctions act was named. Graham had spent over a year petitioning for the move before his death on July 11.
Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat, said in a statement that Trump was “enabling Vladimir Putin to continue his war of aggression.”
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer released a statement Saturday saying that “by giving the Russian economy life support, Trump’s deal with the devil keeps getting dirtier.”
Trump was able to waive the sanctions through a safety valve provision embedded in the legislation. The law allowed Trump to waive its sanctions and tariffs after submitting a written certification to Congress that doing so was in the national interest, along with a report explaining that determination. In Friday’s order, Trump said he had submitted both.
“I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and duties provided for in the Graham Act,” Trump wrote in the order. “I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States.”
Trump has not yet publicly disclosed how the move served national interests, and the White House did not reply to TIME’s request for comment.
Darline Graham, the late senator’s sister who was appointed to fill his seat in South Carolina and is running for election this November to keep it, said at a campaign stop on Saturday that the decision was Trump’s to make; however, she voiced disapproval, saying that she would prefer to “keep the pressure on Russia.”
“I don’t trust Putin and I don’t trust Russia,” she said.
