War on Iran has cost EU more than $112 billion, Spanish PM Sánchez says
TEHRAN- Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has warned that the war against Iran has cost Europeans more than €100 billion ($112 billion), arguing that ordinary citizens are paying the price for a conflict they opposed.
In a post on X on Friday, Sánchez said those who had spoken out against the war had been right to warn of its consequences.
“Those of us who raised our voices against the war were right when we said NO to war,” he wrote. “We knew ordinary people would end up paying the bill.”
“Now, it's time to put an end to this disaster,” Sánchez said.
His remarks underscore mounting concerns in Europe over the economic fallout of the war, particularly its effects on energy costs, household budgets and business competitiveness.
European citizens face the economic fallout
The €100 billion figure cited by Sánchez highlights the scale of the economic burden that the conflict has placed on Europe. Higher energy costs can feed through to transport, manufacturing, food prices and household expenditure, placing additional pressure on governments already grappling with economic challenges.
The economic repercussions raise a broader question for European governments: how can they protect their populations from the consequences of a conflict while addressing the extent to which their own military infrastructure has supported US operations?
British base used by US bombers in strikes on Iran
The debate has gained a further dimension following reports by major Western media outlets that US long-range bombers operating from RAF Fairford in England were used in strikes against Iran.
The Washington Post reported on October 6 that the Pentagon abruptly moved approximately a dozen B-1 bombers out of the British base amid concerns about a possible attack on the aircraft and personnel. The newspaper noted that the aircraft had recently been used in bombing missions against Iran.
Reuters also reported on October 5 that US President Donald Trump had linked the bombers' withdrawal to a security threat. The aircraft were subsequently returned to their home bases in the United States.
The episode highlights the strategic importance of European military facilities to Washington's ability to deploy and sustain long-range air operations. It also brings into focus the role of host countries in determining whether their territory and infrastructure can be used in military action against another state.
Britain had authorized the United States to use RAF Fairford for what its government described as specific and limited defensive strikes against Iranian missile sites, according to reporting by The Washington Post. Iran's Foreign Ministry condemned the decision.
The distinction between the stated scope of the authorization and the broader military consequences of providing a launch platform for attacks on Iran is central to the debate over European responsibility.
A divide between opposition to war and military cooperation
Sánchez's remarks reflect the position of a European leader who has publicly opposed the war and emphasized its cost to ordinary people. The use of British territory for US bombing operations, meanwhile, illustrates that European responses to the conflict have not been uniform.
This distinction matters because opposition to a war's economic consequences is not the same as withholding military assistance that could facilitate it. Where governments permit foreign forces to use their territory for attacks, their decisions become part of the wider strategic context of the conflict.
For Iran, the issue also raises questions about the obligations of states not to allow their territory to be used in ways that facilitate unlawful uses of force.
The financial consequences identified by Sánchez and the military role of facilities such as RAF Fairford therefore point to two interconnected dimensions of the war: the costs borne by European societies and the contribution that some European infrastructure has made to US operations.
As European households and businesses contend with the economic fallout, Sánchez's call to end the conflict places renewed emphasis on the need for a political settlement that prevents further destruction and limits the war's wider regional and international consequences.

The Climate Story Hiding in Plain Sight in the Global Economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
17:36:00 UTC
02:36:00 KST

The war in Iran, AI, and countries’ growing debt burden all sat at the top of the agenda as leaders of the world’s international financial institutions gathered in Bangkok this week for the fall meetings of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund (IMF).
Even with some bright spots, the picture is challenging. The war has driven up fuel prices, leading to inflation. Meanwhile, public debt is soaring, a development the IMF warns is unsustainable. And the enormous investment in AI is a positive development keeping the bottom from falling out—though only in certain economies.
At a first glance, climate change, once touted as a key priority by the two most influential international financial institutions, has fallen off the agenda. But take a closer look and it’s hard to miss how climate change—and the related deployment of clean energy—will play an important role in economic performance. Climate events have worsened the debt challenge in developing countries. Clean energy, on the other hand, has served as a critical defense mechanism that has kept the energy price crisis from getting worse in places where it has been deployed at scale.
Future Proof
Weekly
Making sense of the climate and energy economy.
A report from the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) released this week alongside the fall meetings gets at the heart of this challenge while barely mentioning climate change at all—at least in those words. The report points to what it describes as a “triple shock”: high borrowing costs, the energy price spike, and extreme weather events driven by this year’s El Niño, which is on course to set records.
The policy responses aren’t coded climate policy—and in many cases they’re actively bad for climate efforts. The most common response cited by the report is fuel price support, think of subsidies or fuel tax reductions. An IEA survey cited by the report identified 95 countries with such policies. Explicit fuel subsidies could surpass $1 trillion this year globally, according to the UNDP. But, as the report notes, such an approach isn’t sustainable. Backlash to higher prices persists even as governments spend to keep citizens happy. In a smaller group of countries, mostly those most dependent on imports, longer-term, structural changes are emerging: investments in renewable energy, energy efficiency, and electrification. Think of subsidies for electric buses or cutting tariffs on solar panels.
But not every country can afford to remake its energy system with structural changes. Heavy indebtedness and high interest rates are key factors. So too is El Niño and broader climate shocks, which make it harder for countries to pay for new infrastructure that reduces exposure to fossil fuel volatility.
The IMF’s World Economic Outlook is similarly light on climate talk. But follow it to its logical conclusion, and it takes the UNDP argument even further. Indebtedness makes it more difficult to invest in AI infrastructure necessary to compete in the emerging economy. It plots countries’ AI preparedness alongside the non-fossil share of their energy supply, suggesting that energy security and the capacity to adopt AI may increasingly intersect. After all, dependence on volatile imported fossil fuels only compounds this challenge given AI’s energy needs.
This emergent growth dynamic comes with important implications. For one, it adds yet another layer to the argument for non-fossil energy in emerging markets. But it also shows how complicated achieving that end will be. Cheap clean tech hardware isn’t enough.

Nexus of Russia, Iran relationship on display amid US sanctions controversy - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
17:31:15 UTC
02:31:15 KST

Recent news about the United States reducing or waiving sanctions on Russia, at a time of record-high oil prices, and rumors of a return to fighting with Iran illustrate how Moscow and Tehran are connected in terms of the conflicts in Ukraine and the Gulf.
This matters because sanctions relief for Russia does not happen in isolation, as if it occurs in a vacuum.
Iran has backed Russia, and Russia has backed Iran. Therefore, if Russia is empowered on one front to weaken Iran on another, it’s worth seeing it as part of the same global conflict.
It’s also important to understand how we got here.
Russia and Iran have a relationship and ties that go back many decades, and Russia has been involved in supporting the Iranian regime during that time. For instance, Russia was involved with a nuclear power plant in Iran.
During Barack Obama’s administration, it’s worth noting a similar interplay between Russia and Iran.
The US reduced pressure on Russia and was perceived as reducing support for European allies regarding a missile shield, which apparently led to Russia getting on board with support for the Iran deal.
At the time, the Obama administration prioritized the Iran deal.
One theory was that the US could reset relations and get along with Moscow, perhaps by reducing the perception of support for European allies, and that appeasement would somehow lead Russia to pressure Iran on its nuclear program.
We must understand that Russia is very adept at playing this card and this game. It understands that the US has priorities, but it doesn’t always seem able to keep focus on multiple priorities at once.
Russia likes to play a game where Moscow waits until the US is tied up with another conflict, such as with Iran now, and then moves in to try to get things for itself.
Russia-Iran ties predate war on Ukraine
The Russia-Iran connection also predates the war in Ukraine. Iran supplied Russia with its Shahed-136 drones, and Russia used them from early in the 2022 invasion of Ukraine to terrorize the Ukrainian population.
These drones do not win wars by themselves, but they do spread terror.
Iran supplied Russia with hundreds or thousands of them, and Russia then began manufacturing them domestically, illustrating the close relationship between the two nations.
Tehran exported the same type of drones to the Houthis in Yemen, probably in 2020 or 2021. It was clear then that Iran was using the Houthis as a testbed to threaten Israel and other countries.
Iran and Russia tend to see most of these conflicts as interconnected. For instance, Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022 after watching the chaotic US withdrawal from Afghanistan.
Later, when Hamas attacked Israel on October 7, 2023, Russia took advantage of that chaos: Moscow was pleased to see Israel, a close US ally, tied up in a massive war, shifting the international spotlight to the Middle East and away from Ukraine.
Russia continues benefiting from Middle East strategy
Russia continues to benefit from what happens in the Middle East: whenever America is tied up in conflicts there, Moscow benefits, and it continues to pursue this strategy.
Russia is keenly aware of some skepticism within US President Donald Trump’s administration regarding Ukraine. Therefore, it has always been happy to use the Ukraine conflict to its advantage and has tried to exploit tensions between Washington and Kyiv.
After the US war began against Iran in February, Russia has clearly seen this as an opportunity to gain sanctions relief or energy sales, and it is part of the overall Russian grand global strategy.
Moscow views itself as confronting the American-led world order. It wants to revive Russian influence and power, work with Iran and China, and believes the 2026 conflict in Iran is another way the world order will accelerate toward becoming a more multipolar world.
As such, when Moscow looks at possible sanctions relief, it sees how this nexus between Russia and Iran can continue to bedevil the Americans, and it will continue to exploit it in order to achieve its goals and interests.
The question then for the US is whether it thinks it can achieve its goals and interests regarding Ukraine and a peace deal, or Iran and a deal with Iran.
As long as Iran and Russia are able to play US policy off against itself, it will be difficult for the United States to achieve its goals.

Ceasefire must cover all fronts to end regional war, says diplomat

Ceasefire must cover all fronts to end regional war, says diplomat
TEHRAN— Iran has stressed that ending hostilities on all fronts is essential to achieving lasting peace in West Asia, warning that continued fighting in any part of the region would mean the war remains unresolved.
Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh made the remarks in an interview with Lebanon’s Al Mayadeen television network on Friday, emphasizing that an end to Israel’s war on Lebanon was integral to broader efforts to bring the regional conflict to a close.
Khatibzadeh, who arrived in Beirut on Wednesday for talks with Lebanese officials, said Iran remained committed to ending Israeli military aggression against Lebanon and had pursued that objective within the framework of the memorandum of understanding reached between Iran and the United States in Islamabad in mid-June.
He described Lebanon as one of the key issues discussed in Iran’s engagements with Washington, adding that his visit was intended, in part, to help bring the two sides closer together.
During his stay in Beirut, Khatibzadeh held what he described as positive talks with senior Lebanese officials, including Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, and representatives of the Foreign Ministry.
Iran calls for an end to hostilities across the region
The Iranian deputy foreign minister stressed that Israel must end its military campaign in Lebanon and across the Levant, arguing that developments on the different regional fronts are closely interconnected.
“One of Iran’s conditions is an end to all wars,” he said, explaining that continued hostilities on any single front would effectively mean the continuation of the broader regional war.
Khatibzadeh said Iran had therefore remained committed to ending the conflict in Lebanon, describing the effort as part of a wider approach to stopping the war throughout the region.
His remarks underscored Tehran’s position that a ceasefire limited to one theater of conflict would not be sufficient to establish lasting regional stability if military operations continued elsewhere.
The Iranian diplomat accused Washington and Tel Aviv of violating the Islamabad understanding through their attacks on Iran and Lebanon. He also said US efforts to secure a ceasefire and end Israel’s war on Lebanon had reached an impasse.
Khatibzadeh questioned Israel’s willingness to honor its commitments, arguing that Washington bore responsibility for restraining its regional ally and ensuring that any agreed arrangements were respected.
Tehran rejects US war aims
Addressing the war against Iran, Khatibzadeh described the US military campaign as illegal under international law and said Washington had failed to eliminate Iran’s air-defense systems and deterrence capabilities.
He said Iran had resisted an existential war and would continue to defend its sovereignty and territorial integrity.
He also reiterated Iran’s readiness to address concerns raised by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and the United States regarding its peaceful nuclear activities.
Khatibzadeh pointed to more than 15 IAEA reports that, according to him, confirmed Iran’s compliance with its commitments. He presented this record as evidence that concerns over Iran’s nuclear program could be addressed through engagement rather than military confrontation.
Khatibzadeh also said Iran had proposed reopening the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, signaling Tehran’s readiness to pursue a diplomatic solution to tensions surrounding one of the world’s most strategically important maritime routes.
The Iranian deputy foreign minister stressed that Tehran did not seek war but would resist any conflict imposed on the country.
Hezbollah as a Lebanese political movement
Commenting on Hezbollah, Khatibzadeh described the movement as a Lebanese political party established in response to Israeli attacks and occupation.
He said Iran’s relations with its regional allies were rooted in shared beliefs, values, and principles, presenting these ties as part of Tehran’s broader regional outlook.
The remarks came as Iran continued diplomatic engagement with Lebanon, where the consequences of Israel’s military campaign remain central to regional security discussions.
Khatibzadeh’s statements placed the need for a comprehensive cessation of hostilities at the center of Iran’s approach to ending the conflict, arguing that peace cannot be secured through isolated ceasefires while fighting continues elsewhere.
For Tehran, the central requirement is an end to the war across all fronts, accompanied by respect for national sovereignty and the fulfillment of commitments made through diplomatic agreements.

Israeli settlers attack European diplomats, French mayor in West Bank

Can Denmark teach Britain how to raise royals?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
17:30:00 UTC
02:30:00 KST

The Danish secret to raising royals who are (almost) like us
As Denmark's Crown Prince Christian prepares for a life of public service, his parents have given him something many royal heirs often lack: Time to grow up.
Crown Prince Christian of Denmark turned 21 this week and marked his birthday with a gift to the Danish taxpayer: foregoing the government-funded stipend he's entitled to claim with his coming of age.
Instead, just as he did at 18, the crown prince is not taking on a regular place in the working royal roster, nor the annuity. Christian's position as heir to the throne demands he fill in for his father, King Frederik X, as regent. He has already done so on multiple occasions and will continue as needed. But rather than becoming a full-time working royal he has chosen to pursue a military career.
At a time when Harry and Meghan are struggling to integrate back into some parts of the British royal life they quit so acrimoniously in 2020 to set up their own brand of "service", they would do well to take a few pointers from King Frederik's kids who seem to be managing the "half in, half out" compromise these two so desperately crave.
On the surface Britain's House of Windsor and Denmark's Glücksburg face similar issues — both ancient institutions that place royals at the top of an increasingly less forelock-tugging food chain trying to hang on to relevance in the 21st century. At the same time they must navigate a voracious public and media that gorges on all aspects of royal life, public and private. Pound of flesh hardly covers it.
But how these two monarchies operate in the modern world may explain why King Frederik X and Australia-born Queen Mary's four offspring seem so happy and sorted as the Sussex family lurches from one drama to the next and Prince William prefers to send his heir to school at the elitist of elite, Eton.
Over in Denmark, as youngsters, the royal children cycled to their regular state-run primary school with their parents and now integrate into public life with an apparent ease. But in the UK Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet are driven to an unnamed private school by limo with a convoy of security and paparazzi recently spotted outside the gates.
How have the Danes managed to give the new generation of royals an inner sense of adolescent freedom and agency over their lives and outer glow of duty? It's all in the detail.
'I've always wanted to do it'
Crown Prince Christian, Denmark's next king, began his four months of military service in February 2025, compulsory for every fit Dane over the age of 18. Then, in August that year, he started lieutenant school. Officer training followed and in June, the crown prince was promoted to second lieutenant.
It's not a constitutional requirement for royals to join the military but certainly the crown prince was following in the footsteps of his forebears. The royal family and the military are intrinsically entwined, and generations have served the nation. But he didn't have to. What's more, unlike many British royals — including Princes William and Harry — he's also chosen to refuse a military salary as well as the royal stipend. Christian's living expenses will be funded by his family.
In his first-ever major newspaper interview, given in the lead-up to his 21st birthday, Christian told Politiken that he faced no pressure from his parents nor the royal court to sign up.
"I've always wanted to do it and thought it sounded exciting," he explained, admitting he was shaking on his first day, wondering if he'd made the right choice and whether he would fit in with the other recruits. He needn't have worried.
No-one in Denmark was surprised by the move, after all Christian's father King Frederik had famously served with the Danish Frogman Corps following a rigorous selection process. As an amusing aside the monarch earned the nickname "Pingo" in the corps — something to do with his wetsuit filling with water causing him to waddle like a penguin.
Back in 1958 Christian's grandmother, Queen Margrethe II, shattered glass ceilings when she chose to volunteer with the Women's Flying Corps at a time when women weren't allowed to do national service and were rare in the military.
The pertinent decision is the lack of payment for this future king. Money talks and where royals are concerned that talk is rarely complimentary. British royals were paid regular military salaries when they served, many also receiving income from other public and private sources.
And let's not forget Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor who served in the Royal Navy for 22 years when he was a prince, currently draws a modest naval pension of about $40,000 a year.
"I think it was a very wise decision," Marie Rønde, royal correspondent for Denmark's TV 2 News told me. "The thought in the Danish royal court is taxpayers pay a lot of money to the royal family already, why should we also pay more for Christian to serve?"
Following King Frederik's ascension to the throne on January 14, 2024, the royal house received an additional 17 million kroner ($3.65 million) per year.
"And no-one questioned it. There was literally no debate in Denmark," Rønde says. "So, I think for the palace the thought was, we don't want to push it."
That decision would have been a discussion between the king, the queen and court advisers, as well as Christian himself. This was all about public connection.
Navigating royal privilege
The Danish monarchy is one of the most popular in the world, with 72 per cent of Danes supporting the ancient institution in a recent national poll. While optics are everything, keeping in step with the public mood is important too.
Jakob Steen Olsen, royal affairs commentator at Berlingske, Denmark's oldest national daily newspaper, says in this case the palace messaging was spot on and so was the intent.
"This was saying we are here to serve and we are aware that we have a privileged position in society," Olsen says.
While Crown Prince Christian cannot avoid military service altogether, his undergoing military training is the ultimate sacrifice in many ways, Olsen believes: "He shows that he's willing to give his life for the country."
Also serving is Princess Isabella, Denmark's 19-year-old spare to the heir who made history as the first Danish female royal to take part in military service when she joined up in August for the required 11 months of training.
Like her brother, Isabella has turned down a military wage.
"We just recently decided that girls are obliged to go into the army. She's actually the first part of the first generation of those girls," Olsen says. "So of course that's an important sign also that the royal family supports that decision by government."
Denmark's recent deployment of troops to Latvia may mean that either or both royals are posted to the Baltic nation, considered NATO's eastern front line against Russian invasion, so their military service is far from academic.
For Christian declining his birth right payment from the public purse as well was, Rønde says, a smart move by the royal court.
"He could have had it at 18, like his father and grandmother did," he says. "But he didn't. It's all part of the signals the king and queen are giving."
Just like other Danes
Money and military service aside, the royal couple is eager to allow Christian and Isabella space to enjoy their youth, away from the royal spotlight.
"It's sort of a trade-off," Olsen says. "They won't be carrying out official royal duties for quite a while, so let's make this deal. The public doesn't pay for them, but they don't show up so much for official work."
Carefully choreographed photo ops of the siblings in army fatigues fill the official royal social media. The pair are clearly enjoying their duty and have become royal role models for young Danes.
Also filling social media, though not from the official royal account, have been photos of Christian and Isabella at music festivals and these are equally popular with the public.
"People like them being able to live lives that are quite close to how all other Danish teenagers live. They drink a lot of beer, they dance around, they hug different girls and boys, and Danes like that. It's not a problem," Olsen says.
Venture onto TikTok and there are videos of Princess Isabella and her younger sister Princess Josephine doing cute dance routines, just like other teens.
Princess Isabella, particularly, has a reputation as a "spirited" young lady, Rønde says.
"She's bubbly and open and quite vivacious," Olsen adds.
"She's funny and you can see the energy in her eyes … she definitely likes to party," Rønde agrees.
Things don't always go to plan but so far those misdemeanours seem to make them popular too.
In 2021 cameras picked up Isabella answering her mother back at Crown Prince Christian's confirmation and "she became an overnight royal star", Olsen says. "Danes liked the idea of this bratty teenager in the royal house speaking the way that most teenagers speak to their mums in this this day and age."
Isabella's credibility rose further in 2025 when she was photographed at a music festival in a Danish rap band T-shirt with words that translate to "I f**ked him yesterday" and an arrow pointing to the person standing next to her.
"That did cause a sensation," Olsen says. "Some people thought it was a bit too much and I'm sure she was scolded for it at home, because if some people don't like it, of course, it's not good for the royal family. But she also got some points. A lot of Danes are quite liberal, and they liked it."
When asked by a journalist about her daughter's choice of clothing her mother Queen Mary said: "Let's put it this way, some decisions are better than others."
Such pranks are a long way from Prince Harry wearing a Nazi uniform to a private "colonials and natives" themed costume party in 2005 or playing strip billiards in a VIP suite in a Las Vegas hotel in 2012.
Rønde says that while Danes really do want their royal kids to live a little and enjoy their youth like everyone else, what is important is "that they are not using their royal status to be privileged or to get something that other people can't get".
Dance festival v the crown
Evidently there was debate last summer when the king was out of the country and Christian had to step in as regent.
"He was at a festival and there was a question about whether he should be there when he actually had the responsibility for the country at that time," Rønde says. Public opinion was divided and it was another lesson learned.
Olsen says this idea of give and take only works if there's also a visible healthy respect from the youngsters for their royal duties.
"So, as long as they show that they understand what the job is about and they're willing to sacrifice themselves on that altar, Danes actually allow them I think to live quite normal lives," he says. "And certainly, if you ask young people from the future taxpayers, who are the same generation as Christian and Isabella, what they think of them, generally it's, 'We like them because they're so much like us.'"
Rønde, who reports on all the European royals, regularly travels to the UK to attend engagements and is surprised by the differences between what British people expect from their royals and what Danes expect from theirs.
"We like [Danish royals] to be down-to-earth and [in Britain] they expect them to be on a pedestal and dressed in a certain way. But King Frederik and Queen Mary have given their kids an upbringing that is as much like a normal family when your family is not normal and that shows," she says.
It started from the moment they were born. Prince Christian was the first heir apparent to go to a regular kindergarten and his siblings followed suit.
"When they are travelling with their parents they just wear jeans and sneakers, and they were also allowed to decide for themselves which schools they go to. It's just a modern way of being parents," she says.
Rønde says Mary and Frederick "listen" to their children: "They give them responsibility and they let them make up their own minds."
Crown Prince Christian did briefly attend a prestigious private school but left after a scandal involving other students and completed his education at Ordrup Gymnasium, a state high school.
One wonders if Prince George was the one who chose to go to Eton, where his uniform is from another era — pinstripe trousers, waistcoat and tails!
The contrast is stark
Rønde landed the first TV interview with Prince Christian a few months ago when the heir crossed the finish line at the annual Royal Run through the streets of Denmark. She says he was relaxed, polite and certainly not daunted by the role ahead.
Growing up royal is not easy and Prince Christian and Princess Isabella along with their younger siblings, twins Prince Vincent and Princess Josephine, now 15, have been raised in a very different manner to their father and to young royals in other countries, and it's paying off.
"King Frederik was sort of thrown to the wolves at the age of 18 taking up official duties almost immediately," Olsen says. "He represented Denmark on a trip to Japan and a host of other duties and that was a terrible thing. He wasn't ready for it. He felt let down by the people surrounding him. He felt insecure and hated it."
As a child Frederik barely saw his parents and rarely ate meals with them. Queen Margrethe has confessed that she doesn't really like young kids and was distant and disconnected from her sons. Frederik has said that he doesn't blame his parents, it was a different time.
"But he has been very clear all the way that he wanted a different childhood for his own kids. He wanted to be closer to them," Rønde says.
Add in Mary Donaldson, Tasmanian born, close to her family, and you have a radically different approach to parenting.
"I remember when they took Christian home from the hospital after the birth and they explained to media that he would always be only an arm's length away from them," Rønde says.
The contrast is stark, Olsen says. "They've been trying with the unusual circumstances that they have, to give their four as grounded an upbringing as possible and allowing them as part of the strategy to make their own mistakes. And then gradually they've been exposing them to their life in the public eye. They've been brought along to various events and they are now more and more exposed to being in the limelight. And it seems like it's worked," he explains.
"If you look at Princess Isabella and Prince Christian out with the public, they don't mind and they're used to being the centre of attention. They're not paralysed by it like their father was. He was terrified and irritated."
A new approach
It's quite obvious that all four royal kids have been prepared in a totally new way.
Olsen tells a story about the royal family attending a concert.
"They came in this van, and out came Mary and she looked like the duck mum with her ducklings, and they instantly knew how to line up in which order," he says.
Compare this to the British royal kids suited and booted and riding in carriages at say Trooping the Colour and it's clear to see how Denmark is leading the charge for a new approach to monarchy.
"Queen Margrethe has always described that process of learning as a kind of osmosis that you don't really sit down and talk about it. But I think there have been more discussions around the breakfast table for these young royals than Queen Margrethe ever had with her sons," Olsen says.
Prince Harry's obsession with the VIP security he now doesn't have in the UK, constantly feeling paranoid about potential assailants or paparazzi snapping sneaky photos of his kids, is barely an issue in Denmark.
Yes the Danish royal kids all have personal protection officers who are publicly funded, but the presence is discreet and is much less for the children of non-working royals. What's more the Danish public is very used to seeing the royal family out and about in the streets all over the country.
Even now as queen, Mary rides in the woods and goes for morning walks with the dog.
"When they are at Fredensborg [the royal family's castle in the countryside, used in spring and autumn] the public often meet the queen or the king jogging or just taking a walk," Rønde says.
"It's a really relaxed relationship that we have with them and people really like it. Of course there's an understanding that you can't just run towards them and you have to give them some space."
Similarly, although there are no privacy laws in Denmark, there's a clear line between public and private that domestic media observes.
"We don't photograph the kids when they go to school, when they play soccer in a regular club. And when the family goes to the beach in Skagen every year, we don't photograph them in bikinis with their kids. This is their space. It's really a matter of courtesy," Rønde continues.
Hazards ahead
For the moment it is just Christian whose future career path as a working royal is unavoidable, but many feel Princess Isabella would also be a useful sidekick to her brother.
"We have the same problem of a slimmed down monarchy that they're facing in other royal households in Norway and Great Britain. If somebody is ill, who will actually do the job?" Olsen says.
When Danes were asked in a poll, "Would you support paying for Isabella as well, if she decides she wants to and parliament agrees?" a majority liked the idea and supported that, he says.
While the concept of a republic is rarely raised in Denmark, that sense of entitlement that has caused scandals and damage for other royal families is of course a watching brief.
"Danes were quite satisfied with the 52-year reign of Queen Margrethe. I mean, there's money in the bank that has been transferred to the next generation," Olsen says. "But apart from being likeable and people that we can identify with, it's all about carrying on and doing a good job, being industrious. We're a country of small-time tradespeople. We like a good bargain. We want our money's worth."
The other vital piece of the puzzle, he notes, is "about knowing what's right and what's wrong".
"If you look at the problems that some European royal households have run into, it's always about sex and greed, dangerous pits that you can fall into."
Whether Prince Christian will make a good king is yet to be seen. There are so many unforeseen hazards ahead and public opinion can be cruel and fickle.
"If you look at the popularity polls that these poor people are subjected to, he's not as popular as his parents or the old Queen Margrethe," Olsen says.
"But we don't really know him yet" he says, adding that with every handshake or soundbite "we get there's a development".
"Already he has to shake a lot of hands and one little thing that I have noticed is that he looks people straight in the eye, even though it's just for five seconds, and I like that. It shows that [Christian is] aware he has a role to play in the lives of real people."

‘They call her a traitor?’ Son of beaten photographer blasts treatment of his mother
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
17:28:31 UTC
02:28:31 KST

Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, who was brutally beaten by Jewish rioters near Ramallah on Friday, remains hospitalized at Beilinson Hospital in central Israel. The hospital said Saturday that her condition was moderate, that she had sustained injuries to her limbs and that she had undergone surgery earlier in the day. One of her fingers was nearly severed in the assault.
President Isaac Herzog said he had spoken with Levine and personally apologized for the attack. "As president of the State of Israel, I strongly condemn this outrageous and shocking phenomenon of violence, both the horrific attack you suffered and other serious incidents, such as what happened today in Taybeh," Herzog said. "I was morally tormented throughout Shabbat thinking about it, and I express deep sorrow and apologize for what you endured. The despicable conduct of these criminals does not represent the citizens or values of the State of Israel."
"Israel is a democratic state governed by the rule of law, and it must act with an iron fist against every form of violence," Herzog continued. "I know the circumstances of each incident are being thoroughly investigated, and we expect to see the findings. Every government, security and law enforcement agency must use all available means to investigate, identify the lawbreakers and bring them to justice. We all embrace you and your family, and on behalf of the entire nation, I wish you good health and a speedy recovery."
Levine's son, Michael Milner, told Ynet that his mother was suffering considerable pain following the assault. "She's in terrible pain because she was beaten so badly. Even though she was wearing a bulletproof vest and helmet, she still suffered injuries all over her body, and she's hurting," he said.
Milner said his mother underwent surgery on her hand after one of her fingers was severely injured. "They practically scraped away a significant part of her finger. The finger was cut, the skin was torn off and its function was affected. Fortunately, it was her left hand and she's right-handed, but she obviously won't be able to work for the next few weeks. She flew here from Ukraine, where she had been covering the war, to cover the elections, and now she won't be able to."
The family is still struggling to come to terms with what happened. "I'm simply shocked that something like this can happen in the State of Israel and that people who riot and behave with such horrific violence aren't held accountable," Milner said. "Even if we don't agree with the presence of the Palestinian people, it's still not acceptable to burn trees, shoot at civilians or throw stones at people, including elderly people."
Milner also sharply criticized Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's response to the assault. Netanyahu's office described the attack as alleged and said the circumstances remained unclear and under investigation, while condemning violence against civilians and journalists.
"I'm shocked by the prime minister's statement describing the attack as 'alleged' when there are all these videos and photographs showing the horrific assault on my mother," Milner said. "I can find plenty of evidence on Instagram for the prime minister if he doubts that the attack really happened."
Milner said he was particularly offended by Netanyahu's reference to footage showing a young man lifting Levine from the ground. "I asked her about it, and she told me he lifted her up so he could steal more things from her. Then he threw her back onto the ground and they kicked her," he said. "My mother has puncture wounds on her back. They stitched up wounds all over her body today, and she's covered in bruises. The only reason her face doesn't look terrible is that she instinctively protected it by keeping it toward the ground."
According to Milner, his mother clearly saw that some of the attackers were wearing tzitzit, the ritual fringes worn by observant Jewish men. "She says she clearly saw who they were. She screamed and begged them to stop, but they wouldn't," he said. "Even after someone managed to run toward her, one of her colleagues who helped her off the ground, you can still see in the video how they continued throwing stones and attacking my mother."
Milner, who has lived in Poland in recent years, had already planned to visit Israel next week to vote in the upcoming election, but brought forward his arrival after the attack. "I'll stay and make sure my vote is among those cast here in the election," he said. He is now at his mother's bedside in the hospital. "Now I'll have to take care of her. She can't even move."
He said no one from the government had contacted his mother following the assault. "My father, Moshe Milner, was once a prime minister's photographer, going back to the days of Golda Meir, including for Bibi," he said. "I'm personally offended. After four decades of my mother working as a pool photographer for the foreign press, I know Bibi recognizes her face. She's not some photographer who just landed here to cover a single event. She's been photographing Israel for 43 years, documenting the major events in this country's history."
The family is also distressed by attacks against Levine on social media. "I'm deeply offended that people are portraying her as a leftist traitor when my mother has repeatedly risked her life to show what was happening during the wars between Israel and Lebanon, what was happening to wounded soldiers," Milner said. "She risked her life again and again to cover the truth and show the Israeli side."
"Throughout the war with Iran, from north to south, she went months without sleeping properly, sending photographs that appeared on front pages around the world to show what was happening to Israel," he continued. "And this is how they treat my mother, as a traitor."
Milner argued that Israel must urgently change its approach to violence in the West Bank. "I think it's essential to restore the Shin Bet's Jewish terrorism unit," he said. "It makes no sense that I'm hearing the police can't enter Areas A and B, and that's why they aren't making arrests. It's a complete failure."
He said his mother had repeatedly warned him about escalating violence in Palestinian communities. "For more than a year, she's been telling me again and again, 'You won't believe what they did yesterday. They burned people while we were inside the house.' She sent me videos of people attacking her while she was filming from inside Palestinian homes."
"There's simply no order and no governance," he said. "I also don't believe the army can stop them, because my mother has photographed soldiers praying alongside the rioters. Not during this particular incident, but we have photographs like that. Nobody is dealing with them, and I'm not surprised there was another report today and there will be more tomorrow."
"Beyond the fact that it's morally wrong, it's causing enormous strategic damage to us as a people around the world," Milner added. "Our situation is unbelievable. We are the most hated people on the face of the Earth."
Attacked for 10 minutes
Levine was attacked Friday near the Palestinian village of Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah, while covering the annual olive harvest. According to Palestinian accounts, approximately 80 masked Jewish rioters descended from a hillside overlooking terraced olive groves where villagers had gathered to pick ripe olives.
"I was attacked and thrown to the ground," Levine said after the assault. "Luckily, I had my protective vest and helmet. If I hadn't been wearing them, I probably wouldn't be here right now. They just kept kicking me, probably 50 times."
Speaking to The Associated Press, Levine said the attackers kicked her for approximately 10 minutes as she tried to protect her cameras and bag. She said her protective vest was clearly marked "PRESS."
"As a mother, I can't understand how a parent can raise monsters like these," Levine said. She described her attackers as "Jewish terrorists" and expressed doubt that any of them would be brought to justice.
As Levine recovers in the hospital, members of Commanders for Israel's Security, an organization comprising hundreds of former senior Israeli defense and security officials, sent her a letter of apology. The signatories protested what they described as encouragement of violence by senior government officials and lawmakers and called for a fundamental change in government policy.

Romania shoots down two drones over Black Sea
Unknown

02:27:04 KST

Romania has said it shot down two drones that entered its airspace over the Black Sea, the latest in a series of incidents believed to be spillover from Russia’s war in Ukraine.
Defence Minister Radu Miruta said on Facebook on Saturday that Romanian F-16 fighter jets intercepted and shot down both drones about 20 kilometres southeast of Sulina.
“Two drones were engaged and shot down a few minutes ago by Romanian military pilots over the Black Sea, moments after they had illegally entered our country,” he wrote.
The first drone entered Romanian airspace at 17:59 local time (14:59 GMT) and was shot down within two minutes, Miruta said.
The second was downed at 18:05, five minutes after crossing into the country’s airspace.
Two F-16 fighter jets of the Romanian Air Force engaged the drones, according to a press release of the defence ministry.
NATO has previously shot down four drones in Romania's airspace, all of them this year.
Russian drone incursions
Romania, a NATO member bordering Ukraine, has repeatedly reported Russian drone incursions since the Russia-Ukraine war began in February 2022. Much of the border follows the Danube, close to Ukrainian ports targeted by Russian forces.
The latest incident follows drone strikes on two tankers near Romania’s Black Sea coast earlier this week.
Romanian authorities resumed searches on Friday for seven missing sailors from one of the vessels, raising further concerns about the war’s impact on commercial shipping.
Neighbouring Bulgaria has also requested NATO combat aircraft and anti-drone systems following attacks on ships in the Black Sea. Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Friday that Sofia had formally sought additional support to strengthen its defences.

Pezeshkian: Iran’s missile, defense capabilities built on foundations laid by schools, universities
TEHRAN — President Masoud Pezeshkian has underscored the contribution of Iran’s schools and universities to the country’s defense and missile capabilities, saying investment in education and younger generations is essential to strengthening national security and safeguarding the country against external threats.
Speaking on Saturday at a ceremony inaugurating a series of educational projects, Pezeshkian described education as a foundation of Iran’s scientific and technological progress.
“If we are capable of defending our country today, building missiles and standing against threats, it is because our education system and universities have played a role in this path and laid the groundwork for such capabilities,” he said.
The president stressed that strengthening Iran’s ability to deter potential aggression requires continued efforts to develop the country’s scientific, educational and technological capacities.
Although positive steps have been taken to protect Iran’s territory from threats, he said, more work remains to ensure that adversaries cannot threaten the country’s security.
Pezeshkian emphasized that young people are central to achieving this objective, adding that their potential can be realized only if adequate investment provides them with opportunities to learn, innovate and contribute to national development.
During the ceremony, the president also paid tribute to those who lost their lives in the Islamic Revolution, particularly student martyrs and the victims of the Shajareh Tayyebeh elementary school attack in Minab, southern Iran.
The school was struck on February 28, the first day of the US-Israeli war against Iran, killing at least 168 people, including 157 schoolchildren, as well as teachers, parents, and other members of the school community, according to Iranian authorities.
The attack on the school has become a symbol of the civilian toll of the war and the vulnerability of children and educational institutions during armed conflict.
Pezeshkian’s tribute placed the loss of the Minab students alongside the broader sacrifices made by generations of Iranians, while reinforcing the importance of protecting education and ensuring that young people have the opportunity to shape the country’s future.
The president’s remarks highlighted the connection between education, scientific advancement and national defense, presenting investment in young people not merely as a social priority but also as a long-term contribution to Iran’s security and technological independence.
His message was that the scientific and technical capabilities required to defend the country are built over years through schools, universities, and the development of skilled generations.
By calling for greater opportunities for young people, Pezeshkian stressed that sustaining these capabilities requires continued investment in education and the people who drive scientific progress.

Trump faces bipartisan backlash over Russia sanctions waiver

Unknown Publisher

Trump faces bipartisan backlash over Russia sanctions waiver
Republicans and Democrats condemn Trump’s decision to suspend sanctions, saying it undermines support for Ukraine.
United States President Donald Trump has drawn criticism from Democrats and Republicans after waiving sanctions targeting Russia and countries that buy its oil and gas, days before the restrictions were due to take effect under a law he signed last month.
In an executive order signed on Friday, Trump said the waiver was in the US national interest. He did not specify when the restrictions might be introduced, saying they would remain suspended until he or senior officials determined further action was appropriate.
The move has been condemned by both Democrats and Republicans.
Republican Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina called the decision “beyond irresponsible”, accusing the administration of capitulating to Russian President Vladimir Putin, who launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
“What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisers not understand?” Tillis wrote on social media on Saturday.
Republican Senator John Cornyn of Texas also criticised the move, saying the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, who championed the legislation, “would be appalled”.
Representative Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat, said Trump’s move betrayed Ukraine and disregarded Congress’s intent to punish Russia for its invasion.
Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts accused Trump of “thumbing his nose” at Congress and enabling Putin to continue his war against Ukraine, urging colleagues to take action to reverse the decision.
The legislation, named after the deceased Senator Graham, was passed with overwhelming bipartisan support. It would have allowed tariffs of up to 100 percent on goods from countries that continued buying Russian oil and gas or helped Moscow evade sanctions. The bill was then signed into law by Trump last month. Before he unexpectedly died earlier this year, Graham had worked for about a year to get the legislation passed.
The decision came shortly after Trump agreed to a deal to buy Russian diesel in an effort to lower fuel prices, which have risen amid the US-Israeli war on Iran. Politicians from both parties have questioned whether the deal would meaningfully reduce energy costs while providing Moscow with revenue to support its war effort.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also criticised the sanctions waiver on Saturday, saying easing pressure on Russia would encourage further attacks.
“Financial rewards for Putin – all of this only encourages him to keep attacking,” Zelenskyy posted on X, urging the US to maintain pressure on Moscow.
Congress is in recess until after the November 3 midterm elections, limiting immediate opportunities to challenge Trump’s decision. Representative Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has introduced legislation to block the separate diesel deal with Russia.

Bernard Baudoux, mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France, told AFP that the attack took place on Saturday during a goodwill visit to the Palestinian town of Taybeh, where he had planned to sign a cooperation agreement.
“I think that if settlers are behaving like this, there is a tolerance on the part of the Israeli government,” Baudoux said.
“The whole world needs to know what’s happening there. For me, I’ll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here,” he added.
Baudoux, a left-wing politician, was accompanied by the French consul general in Jerusalem and a priest from his home parish.
The visit aimed to establish closer ties between his town, which has an olive emblem, and Taybeh, a predominantly Christian Palestinian community.
Mayor describes attack by men carrying iron bars
Baudoux said two or three cars suddenly arrived and men emerged, shouting insults about France that he could not understand.
Wearing a sash in the colours of the French flag, he said he was kicked and struck with iron bars before being knocked to the ground.
“It’s the gratuitous nature of the violence that stuns me,” he told AFP. “They arrived completely enraged.”
The mayor said his parish priest helped him to his feet before they fled by car. He did not suffer serious injuries and was able to continue his visit to Taybeh.
Baudoux expressed doubt that those responsible would face consequences, despite Israeli promises of a swift investigation.
France vows not to be intimidated by violence
The attack came as French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu condemned the use of violence to advance political agendas.
In a post on X on Saturday, Lecornu said France would not be intimidated by violence following protests over rising living costs and declining public services, held months ahead of a presidential election.
“To those who clearly want to use this violence as a ‘warm-up’ before the presidential election, I say clearly: We will not let ourselves be intimidated. No one will impose their political agenda through violence,” he wrote.
Baudoux’s account has drawn attention to concerns over the safety of Palestinians and international visitors in the occupied West Bank, where the olive harvest is under way and Palestinian communities have reported increased attacks by illegal Israeli settlers.

Iran calls on UNSC to hold Israel accountable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
17:16:58 UTC
02:16:58 KST

Iran calls on UNSC to hold Israel accountable
TEHRAN— Iran has called on the United Nations Security Council to take decisive action to compel Israel to fulfill its obligations under international law, end its military aggression across West Asia, and face accountability for serious violations of international law.
Gholamhossein Darzi, Iran’s ambassador and chargé d’affaires to the United Nations in New York, made the appeal on Friday during the Security Council’s open debate on the situation in the Middle East, warning that Israel’s continued aggression, occupation, and destabilizing activities pose a grave threat to regional and international peace and security.
Darzi said the Israeli regime had repeatedly demonstrated disregard for international law and the principles enshrined in the UN Charter, while continuing its military operations and violations despite the announcement of a ceasefire in Gaza.
He pointed to Israel’s actions in the Gaza Strip, the occupied West Bank, Lebanon, and Syria, as well as the two wars launched against Iran by Israel and the United States over the past year, as evidence of the urgent need for international accountability.
“The Security Council must act decisively to address the root causes of this tragedy, end impunity, compel Israel to fully comply with its obligations under international law and relevant UN resolutions, and bring an end to the decades-long injustice inflicted upon the Palestinian people,” Darzi said.
Gaza and Palestine at the center of the crisis
Addressing the humanitarian and political situation in Palestine, Darzi said Gaza remained devastated and subject to continued military attacks, leaving its population to endure immense suffering despite the announced ceasefire.
He also condemned Israel’s continued settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank, escalating settler violence, and measures aimed at annexing Palestinian land and displacing its inhabitants.
Darzi stressed that an immediate and permanent end to Israeli aggression was essential, alongside the complete and unconditional withdrawal of Israeli occupying forces from Gaza, the safe and unhindered delivery of sustained humanitarian assistance, and full protection for civilians and humanitarian personnel.
He further emphasized that any political or administrative arrangements for Gaza must respect the inherent rights of Palestinians rather than subordinate them to security conditions imposed from outside.
The Iranian envoy reaffirmed the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination and the establishment of an independent, sovereign, and viable Palestinian state, with Al-Quds Al-Sharif as its capital and full membership in the United Nations.
He argued that no sustainable solution could be achieved while occupation, settlement expansion, forced displacement, and violations of Palestinian rights continued.
Iran urges an end to Israeli aggression across West Asia
Darzi called on Israel to halt its continued violations of Lebanon’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, withdraw fully from Lebanese territory, and comply with UN Security Council Resolution 1701.
He also urged Israel to end its military incursions and attacks on Syrian territory, withdraw from the occupied Syrian Golan and other occupied areas, and respect Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.
The Iranian envoy framed these issues as part of a broader pattern of military aggression and violations of international law, arguing that the Security Council must address the underlying causes of regional instability rather than rely on selective condemnation.
Accountability for international crimes
Darzi described accountability for serious violations of international law, particularly international humanitarian law, as both an indispensable requirement and a legal imperative.
He said that over the past three years, Israel had committed grave international crimes against the peoples of Palestine, Lebanon, Syria, and Iran, including genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity, and the crime of aggression.
He also accused Israel and the United States of waging two unjustified wars of aggression against Iran in violation of the UN Charter and fundamental principles of international law.
According to Darzi, the two countries had deliberately targeted civilians and critical infrastructure, crossing fundamental legal and humanitarian boundaries.
He stressed that those responsible for such acts, as well as those who enable, support, or facilitate them, must be held fully accountable under international law.
Darzi warned that politically motivated conditions and selective condemnation must not be allowed to undermine the consistent, impartial, and unequivocal enforcement of international law.
Iran rejects allegations over the Strait of Hormuz
In the closing section of his address, Darzi rejected 'baseless and politically motivated allegations' directed against Iran by some speakers, including certain members of the Security Council.
He said such accusations distorted the facts, overlooked the root causes of the current crisis, and sought to reverse the roles of aggressor and victim.
Turning to the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf, Darzi said the current tensions were a direct consequence of the US-Israeli war against Iran, which began on February 28, 2026, and subsequent US actions, including 'an unlawful maritime blockade.'
He reiterated that Iran remained committed to safe and secure navigation and had exercised its inherent right of self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter to protect its sovereignty, territorial integrity, population, and vital interests.
Concluding his remarks, Darzi said the restoration of normal and safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz required an immediate and permanent end to US aggression, credible guarantees against its recurrence, respect for Iran’s sovereign rights, and the complete lifting of the maritime blockade and all other unlawful coercive measures.

Tens of thousands march in Lisbon over housing and living costs
LISBON – Tens of thousands of people marched through central Lisbon on Oct 17 to protest against soaring living costs and a deepening housing crisis in Portugal, increasing pressure on the centre-right government.
Portugal’s biggest union, CGTP, which called the rally, said “tens of thousands” packed one of the capital’s main avenues. Police gave no crowd estimate.
Protesters say low wages are failing to keep pace with housing costs and the rising cost of living, leaving many people struggling to make ends meet in the European Union and NATO member state.
The demonstration followed days of growing unrest, including a tent camp set up by housing activists in the northern city of Porto that police cleared in a pre-dawn operation on Oct 12.
It coincides with protests in France against rising costs and declining public services, and smaller protests in Belgium. There are also mass protests in Albania, where protesters are demanding the prime minister’s resignation.
Portugal’s inflation hit 3.6% in September, driven by rising food and fuel prices, the latter up 15% year-on-year following an increase in tensions in the Middle East.
House prices have more than doubled since 2017, while rents for new leases have nearly doubled, fuelling one of Europe’s worst housing affordability crises.
The squeeze is most acute in major cities.
Protesters’ concerns
Carolina Cruz, 26, a PhD student and biology researcher earning about €1,300 (S$1,870) a month on a scholarship, may lose her home as her rental contract nears expiry.
She and her partner pay €716 monthly for a flat in the Lisbon area, but renewal could push the rent above €1,200 – far beyond their means.
“I’m the first person in my family to enter a doctoral programme and even with all the studying I’ve done, I still can’t make it... Right now, housing in Lisbon is the problem,” Cruz said.
Pedro Penilo, 62, a teacher, said Portugal’s leaders were “out of touch with reality”.
“Life is incredibly expensive… it’s going up brutally. I need to see how my mortgage is going to turn out in the coming months when it’s adjusted. I’m very worried,” he said.
Parliamentary Affairs Minister Carlos Abreu Amorim said on Oct 16 that the “government will not yield to shouts from the street” and that concrete measures to address the concerns were already being rolled out. REUTERS

The sacred fire was then kindled in the Aazhi, located below the 18 holy steps leading to the shrine.According to news agency ANI, Devaswom Minister K Muraleedharan, Travancore Devaswom Board President K Jayakumar, Keralam State Police Chief Ravada Chandrasekhar, and MLAs Pazhakulam Madhu and C V Shanthakumar were among those, who arrived at the Sannidhanam to seek the blessings of Lord Ayyappa.Despite persistent heavy rainfall, thousands of devotees gathered at the hill shrine to offer prayers.
Temple to open for devotees at 5 am on Sunday
The temple will open to devotees at 5 am on Sunday, marking the first day of the Thulam month. The selection of the new Melsanthies, or chief priests, for the Sabarimala and Malikappuram temples is also scheduled for the day through a draw of lots.
The selection process for the Sabarimala Melsanthi will take place at the Sopanam at 7.30 am, following the Usha Pooja. Sabarimala Special Commissioner R Jayakrishnan and Devaswom commissioner B Sunilkumar will supervise the proceedings.
The draw of lots to select the Malikappuram Melsanthi will subsequently be held at the Malikappuram temple.
Thulam rituals coincide with Mahanavami and Vijayadashami
According to officials, this year's Thulam month rituals are particularly significant as the temple has opened during Mahanavami and Vijayadashami after several decades.The temple will close at 10 pm on October 22, following the conclusion of the Thulam month rituals.

Either Security Together or Insecurity Together

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
17:04:04 UTC

Either Security Together or Insecurity Together
Iran's FM tells OIC US has deepened distrust after two years of good-faith talks, making new talks impossible without credible guarantees.
TEHRAN – Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi told the 52nd Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation in Baghdad that lasting security in the region is indivisible: either states build security together, or they will endure insecurity together.
Speaking on Saturday at the OIC ministerial meeting hosted by Iraq under the theme "Dialogue and solidarity, two fundamental pillars for promoting peace and sustainable development," Araghchi laid out Iran's position on the ongoing war in the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, Palestine and Yemen.
Araghchi arrived in Baghdad to attend the 52nd session, and was welcomed at the airport by Iraq's Deputy Foreign Minister. Upon arrival at Baghdad International Airport, he paid tribute at the memorial of resistance commanders Lieutenant General Qassem Soleimani and Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis.
He opened his address by thanking the Government and people of Iraq, "our neighbor and brother," for hosting the meeting, congratulating Secretary-General Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed on his appointment, and thanking Türkiye for its successful chairmanship of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers.
The OIC was founded to give the Islamic Ummah a common voice, he said, recalling that its Charter, like the UN Charter, rests on sovereign equality, territorial integrity, non-interference, peaceful settlement of disputes and refraining from threat or use of force. Those principles, he stressed, "belong to no single country or group of countries. They protect all of us, and when they are applied selectively, they lose their value."
Aggression instead of diplomacy
Araghchi said Iran has remained steadfast in its commitment to international law, the UN Charter and diplomacy over the past two years, while "the United States chose the opposite path: aggression, threats, assassination and economic warfare, with a blatant disregard for international law."
About 5,000 Iranians have been martyred, including hundreds of women and children, he said. He accused the United States and the Israeli regime of assassinating Iran's Supreme Leader and other senior political and military officials, calling it a grave violation of international law.
Citing documented cases, he listed the killing of more than 160 students and teachers in Minab, the cluster-munition attack on Lamerd stadium, the bombing of a desalination unit in Qeshm and the attack on a wedding ceremony in Kuhestak in Sirik. The U.S. and Israel, he said, "cannot whitewash these crimes by reversing the roles of victim and aggressor."
He thanked those member states that expressed solidarity with the Iranian people and called on the Organization as a whole "to stand firmly against attacks on the sovereignty and territorial integrity of its founding member."
Iran, he added, defended its people, sovereignty and legitimate interests and will continue to do so by any means. "We never attacked our neighbors, but we did attack and destroyed the U.S. military bases and military installations, which are unfortunately located in our neighborhood."
There is no contradiction between defending rights and pursuing peace, he said: "We know the cost of war, and that is precisely why we value peace. Iran asks for no special treatment, only the equal application of rights and responsibilities to all."
"This issue will not be resolved on the battlefield. Peace cannot be built through threats of annihilation," he added.
Hormuz open until Feb. 28, reopenable in seven days
On the Strait of Hormuz, Araghchi reaffirmed Iran's commitment to safe and secure navigation in the waterway vital to the energy and trade of many OIC members.
"Until 28 February 2026, the Strait was open. The insecurity and disruption of maritime navigation since then are the direct result of the aggressive actions of the United States and the Israeli regime, and of the blockade and coercive measures imposed by the United States," he said.
"Security cannot be restored by more of the same. One cannot bomb a country, threaten its annihilation and impose a blockade, and then expect the security of navigation return to normal."
He revealed that diplomacy was in fact working. Through the good offices of Pakistan, with the support of Qatar, Iran and the United States signed the Islamabad MoU on June 17. Under paragraph 5, Iran undertook to facilitate safe movement of vessels and immediately began technical discussions with the Sultanate of Oman. Within two weeks, he said, maritime traffic had recovered to approximately 60 percent of its pre-war level.
Subsequent unilateral U.S. measures and military action blocked implementation and bypassed the dispute-resolution mechanisms it envisaged, Araghchi said.
Over two years, Iran negotiated in good faith and repeatedly was met with military action rather than diplomacy, creating deep distrust about renewed talks without credible assurances, he said.
"Even so, Iran has kept the door open. Through Qatar, we have conveyed a concrete seven-day plan: if the necessary conditions are met, the Strait can be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days. The choice now rests with the United States," Araghchi told the ministers.
Palestine and Yemen
Araghchi called Palestine the central cause of the Islamic world. "We cannot speak of peace while ignoring it," he said, describing Gaza as a victim of genocide and a symbol of the failure of international mechanisms to protect civilians.
Dozens of resolutions have not ended occupation and violence, he said, urging the OIC to make ending the killing and blockade and protecting civilians a shared priority backed by practical and coordinated action. He endorsed the proposal by Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan to designate a Gaza Genocide Memorial Day.
On Yemen, he said the people have endured almost a decade of devastating conflict, prolonged blockade and restrictions on civilian infrastructure, with undeniable U.S. and Israeli roles. Iran supports the sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity of both Yemen and Saudi
Arabia, he said, and backs a peaceful, inclusive and comprehensive political process as the only sustainable solution.
"There is no military solution," he said. "Sustainable peace cannot be achieved through military escalation or coercion."
Iran, he added, is deeply concerned by developments in the Arabian Peninsula and remains ready to assist dialogue between the parties on the basis of the peace roadmap they previously agreed. The people of Yemen have the right to live with dignity, free from pressure, sanctions and blockade.
Build security together
Closing his speech, Araghchi delivered his central message to the Islamic world in a direct appeal:
"No state can build lasting security at the expense of the security of others. We believe the problems of our region are best resolved within the region, by its own states, before they become a pretext for the wars of distant powers. In that spirit, we believe the territory, airspace and infrastructure of every regional state should be used only to serve regional security and never become a platform for staging attacks on a neighbor. We say this in a spirit of brotherhood and good-neighborliness. Our peoples share one region and one future, and the choice before us is a simple one: either we build security together, or we will endure insecurity together. Iran stands ready to work with all its brothers and neighbors toward the former."
"Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation, and will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure. But we remain ready for dialogue based on mutual respect and credible guarantees," he concluded.
On the margins of the Baghdad session, Araghchi held a series of bilateral meetings to explain Tehran's positions on Hormuz, Palestine and the Arabian Peninsula.
U.S. broke its word two weeks after Islamabad MoU
In his meeting on Saturday morning with Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty, the two sides discussed bilateral relations and regional and international developments.
Araghchi, recalling the founding philosophy of the OIC, described Palestine as still the most important issue of the Islamic world, and stressing the genocide and crimes in occupied Palestine, underlined the need for urgent and joint action by the Islamic Ummah to end occupation and genocide and end the impunity of the Zionist regime.
On the region, he said the insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz is the direct result of the aggressive actions of the United States and the Israeli regime that began on Feb. 28 and have continued in various forms.
Emphasizing Iran's commitment to diplomacy and peace, he noted that the Islamic Republic has always responsibly adhered to diplomacy to reduce tensions, but the American side has repeatedly broken its promises, and in the latest case violated its commitment only two weeks after signing the agreement on ending the war.
He also briefed his Egyptian counterpart on the latest diplomatic consultations through mediators.
On the Arabian Peninsula, Araghchi announced Iran's readiness to provide any assistance to stop clashes between Saudi Arabia and Yemen, stressing that the experience of 12 years of tension and conflict showed there is no military solution or military approach to Yemen.
Hormuz developments reviewed with Fidan
In his meeting with Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, the two sides discussed bilateral ties and the latest regional developments, particularly Palestine and the continued genocide.
Referring to the summit theme of dialogue and solidarity, Araghchi stressed the need for Islamic states to focus on Palestine and take practical measures to stop Israeli crimes and help realize the Palestinian right to self-determination.
Both sides, emphasizing stronger cooperation among Islamic countries, also consulted on using OIC capacities to confront challenges facing the Islamic world, including Islamophobia.
The latest developments in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz were also reviewed, with Araghchi briefing his Turkish counterpart on ongoing trends.
Stability in Libya is prerequisite for North Africa
In a meeting with Taher al-Baour, acting Foreign Minister of Libya, both sides reviewed Tehran-Tripoli ties and stressed strengthening consultations.
Araghchi repeated Iran's principled position in support of national sovereignty and territorial integrity and unity, and the need to stop any foreign interference, and stressed that security and stability in Libya is a prerequisite for peace and stability in North Africa.
Both sides also consulted on developments in the region and the Islamic world. Araghchi, pointing to continued occupation and genocide by Israel in Palestine, called Palestine the greatest priority of the Islamic Ummah and the international community and called for urgent and serious OIC action to end the genocide in Gaza and end Israeli impunity.
Araghchi also met his Lebanese counterpart Youssef Raji on the sidelines in Baghdad for talks on bilateral ties and regional developments.

Meta denies favouring Bolsonaro as Brazil court orders equal treatment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
17:02:58 UTC
02:02:58 KST

Meta has denied favouring Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro after a court ordered the company to treat him and incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva equally ahead of their October 25 runoff.
The company said on Friday that problems affecting Lula’s accounts stemmed from global technical glitches, anti-fraud measures and regulatory compliance, rather than political interference.
“Any suggestion that Meta favors one side is false,” it said.
Brazilian newspaper Folha de S.Paulo reported, citing internal messages it reviewed, that Meta employees acknowledged restrictions had hindered Lula’s Instagram accounts while the platform recommended Bolsonaro’s profile and WhatsApp channel.
Lula’s campaign alleged that some of his posts lacked sharing options, had reduced reach and suffered technical problems affecting audio and user interactions.
The campaign also said it would file a complaint with the Organization of American States, accusing Meta of manipulating social media during the election.
Meta said the technical issues were already public and that the internal discussions concerned their severity, not political interference.
The company cited two global disruptions earlier in October: one froze Instagram Reels view counts across more than 100 countries without affecting content distribution, while another temporarily prevented users from creating advertisements from existing Instagram posts through one of its tools.
Its response did not address why Bolsonaro’s Instagram profile and WhatsApp channel had received algorithmic recommendations.
Court orders equal treatment
On Thursday, a justice at Brazil’s top electoral court ordered Meta not to unjustifiably restrict the reach of political content related to either candidate during the runoff campaign.
The ruling also required the company’s chatbot, Meta AI, to avoid favouring either candidate in election-related content.
Meta said it would continue to defend itself in the case.
The dispute follows Bolsonaro’s stronger-than-expected first-round performance, which secured him a place in the runoff against Lula.
Lula’s administration has pursued tighter regulation of technology platforms, including measures targeting illegal content and misinformation.
Irregular political ads
Separately, a study by researchers at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro found Meta allowed at least 1,613 irregular political advertisements between July and September.
The ads, funded primarily from the United States, generated 171 million views and approximately two million reais ($400,000) in revenue, AFP reported, citing the study.
Marie Santini, a communication professor involved in the study, said only political parties, candidates and coalitions were permitted to purchase electoral advertisements in Brazil.
“It is not the first time that Meta is negligent with the electoral law, not the first country. It is a systematic behavior of the company,” she said.

Diana Kellogg updates her Tribeca home using salvaged materials
