Israeli firm exploited online ads to spy on Al Jazeera and Palestinian sites, researchers say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:33:10 UTC
19:33:10 KST

Israeli digital advertising agency Discover-Tech spied on internet users through a sprawling network of online ads that it used to track targets and help hack their devices, two research groups said on Thursday.
Its services gave Israel's Candiru – a spyware company blacklisted by the U.S. government – as well as other Israeli surveillance firms access to advertising platforms run by Google, Comcast, Russia's Yandex and others, according to separate reports from Canadian cyber watchdog group Citizen Lab and New York advertising security firm Confiant.
The reports show how the online advertising business, long a subject of privacy concerns, can also serve as a channel for sweeping espionage campaigns.
Citizen Lab said a powerful form of Candiru spyware delivered through Discover-Tech's ads had been used to compromise 45 Windows devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera between 2024 and 2025, something it said it was able to confirm because the media group had shared its network logs with the group.
In a statement, Al Jazeera said it "condemns the spyware attacks targeting a number of its staff" and that it was taking steps to protect its employees and its systems. "Those responsible must be held accountable," it said.
"The way online advertising works today is a systemic security threat," Wolfie Christl, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab, told Reuters. "For states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike."
Discover-Tech's online ads – often for ordinary products such as phones or earbuds – reached more than 120,000 websites and 75,000 apps through its various partnerships, Citizen Lab said.
Users who visited sites or used apps with the malicious ads could be identified and tracked by Discover-Tech, which would sometimes also try to extract phone numbers from some smartphone users, the researchers said. Ads only needed to load on a website for the spying to occur.
Some ads would be used to help plant spyware from Candiru on users' devices, both research groups said, though Confiant said that ads it tied to Candiru were a tiny fraction of Discover-Tech's overall volume.
Malicious ads shown in hundreds of sensitive networks
Confiant cofounder Jerome Dangu said Discover-Tech was pumping out at least 10 million ads per day all around the world and that data-sharing arrangements – called cookie matching – allowed it to track people even beyond the reach of its advertisements.
"Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech," Dangu said.
Discover-Tech, which was founded in 2020, did not return messages left via its contact form. A LinkedIn message and emails sent to its chief executive, Dekel Boni, were not returned.
Reuters' attempts to reach Candiru's owners were similarly unsuccessful. The U.S. Commerce Department blacklisted Candiru in 2021 for allegedly supplying spyware that was used to maliciously target government officials, journalists, activists and academics.
Dangu of Confiant said that the malicious ads had been shown to users in "hundreds of networks in sensitive categories," including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court. He also said that some regions, like the Palestinian territories, were particularly saturated by the Israeli firm's ads.
"You go to almost any site in Palestine – any site – you find a Discover-Tech ad. It gives them a very complete visibility on the digital activities of an entire country," he said.
Citizen Lab also said it had similar evidence showing the malicious ads were shown to people in the United Nations, NATO, the European Commission, and more than a dozen national governments. Other networks the ads appeared in included chip-related firms such as Nvidia, Sandisk, Broadcom and Micron, as well as several media organizations in Mexico, Israel, and Europe that were not identified.
In addition to identifying Candiru and a couple of other surveillance vendors, Citizen Lab said it was able to glean some details about where Discover-Tech's users might be based because the firm inadvertently exposed its authentication logs to the internet, showing people logging in from internet protocol addresses in Israel, Europe, and the Gulf.
Measures against Discover-Tech
Discover-Tech is now being frozen out of parts of the online ad market.
Google said in a statement that it had collaborated with Citizen Lab and Confiant's investigation and kicked Discover-Tech off its ad platforms "for systematically violating our policies."
IAB Europe, the European-level association for the digital marketing and advertising ecosystem, said in an email that Discover-Tech had been suspended from its list of globally approved vendors last week after an audit identified policy violations.
Comcast ad tech subsidiary Beeswax removed Discover-Tech from its platform "following recent activity," Comcast said in a statement. Yandex did not return Reuters messages seeking comment.
Advertising-driven surveillance is increasingly being seen as a national security threat. Earlier this year, the Pentagon said it had received reports that U.S. forces deployed to war zones had been targeted using location data harvested by ad tech firms and data brokers. Branches of the military have since disabled ad tracking on some devices.

HTC Made Smart Glasses That Are Way More Private
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

You can’t really talk about smart glasses without bringing up Meta. HTC, the company behind 2010-era virtual reality headsets and a failed smartphone business, seems quite eager to tackle that comparison directly.
In September, HTC started selling its $499 Vive Eagle smart glasses in the US. The Eagles have lots of the same features as other glasses on the market—cameras for capturing photos and video, speakers in the frames for music playback and calls, an embedded AI agent you can ask questions of and even get recipes from by taking pictures of stuff in your fridge.
But HTC also wants to steer clear of the ongoing debate about privacy in camera-equipped smart glasses. Meta has been dogged by controversy for its smart glasses, with people worried about the company’s interest in enabling face-recognition features, and calling the people who wear them creepy. HTC is aware of that discourse and thinks it is completely possible to make smart glasses that aren’t a privacy nightmare.
“It's not just about protecting the consumer, but it's also about protecting people around the consumer,” Dan McDowell, HTC Vive’s head of enterprise sales, tells WIRED. “People can usher in, I think, what are really tremendous experiences with a new layer of confidence and protection.”
I’ve been wandering around with the glasses for a couple of weeks, and so far they meet my expectations for what smart glasses have become. They protect my eyes from the sun. They snap good photos and videos. You can record and transcribe voice notes. The music playback has decent sound quality. (I’ll always prefer a solid pair of headphones if I’m actually trying to listen to music, but the speakers work just fine.) They come in two styles—one with square Wayfarer-esque lenses and the other more rounded.
The Vive Eagle glasses can get 4.5 hours of battery life on continuous music playback. They can last 36 hours on standby. HTC also sells a companion clip-on battery pack called Power Boost that costs $49. It clips right onto the frame and is noticeable but not as obnoxious as you might think.
Don’t forget the AI assistant, Vive AI, which can utilize OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Google’s Gemini. It doesn’t require a login, so users are “de-identified” in a way that keeps the services from retaining personal information. (That also means, by default, you won’t be able to enjoy many of the personalization features these chatbots offer by gleaning information from your emails and messages.) The glasses come with Vive’s AI Plus, free for the first two years. After that, users must pay a monthly $2.50 subscription fee.
Right by the cameras is a bright indicator light. If you cover the light, it won’t record. If someone around you says stop recording, that will stop the recording. Video footage you capture is encrypted and stored on the glasses—it’s not automatically sent to the phone or cloud. If you want to import photos or videos, you have to do it manually in the app.
Meta has faced scrutiny over the indicator light before, as some users have blocked the LED with stickers or broken into the hardware to turn it off. Meta has responded with software updates that disable the camera if someone tampers with the indicator light, along with other privacy-focused measures.
I ask McDowell how HTC, and really any smart glasses maker, can get past the “trust me, bro”–style privacy promises companies tend to make.
“We're not a social media company,” McDowell says. “There's no benefit to me to have any of your info. We don't train our AI model or any third-party AI models with any of the information that is used on the glasses.”
The real problem may be that with cameras on the frames, smart glasses are hard to distinguish between brands. The Vive Eagles look a lot like Meta glasses, and people worried about those privacy issues may not know that the Eagles are different and not tied to Mark Zuckerberg’s company. I’ve had friends see me wearing them and ask if they’re smart glasses. Yeah, I replied, but not the ones they’re thinking of. That didn’t seem to dispel any of their suspicions.
The hope, at least how HTC frames it, is that more players with better privacy practices will help shift cultural disdain for smart glasses. A bunch of other companies are going cameraless, like Even Realities, Viture, and Halliday. Others are building theirs with privacy shields or focusing on virtual displays instead of capturing the world around you. That said, no one has captured the market quite like Meta.
“We'd like to make sure that our technology adapts to society's expectations, not the other way around,” McDowell says. “I hope that everybody that's making products like these takes steps in the right direction.”

Don’t Let a Crypto Inheritance Get Stuck on the Blockchain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

If someone you know has cryptocurrency that you might inherit, let me just say ahoy matey! I hope your pirate spirit is alive and your treasure-hunting skills sharp, because that's what it might take to get those assets. And if you're the one holding crypto, know that if you do nothing, it's very possible those funds will die with you.
In the US, cryptocurrency is considered a digital asset rather than money in terms of probate and estate law. With money and physical assets, you can sign a beneficiary form and create an estate plan or write a last will and testament naming who should get what when you die. With digital assets, however, the law says we should not assume that a deceased person wanted their private materials—everything from emails to photos—given to another person unless they explicitly said so. This puts cryptocurrency, as a digital asset, in an awkward position.
The options for arranging a transfer of cryptocurrency upon one's death or incapacitation breaks down by one big division: whether the crypto is held by a custodian or in a noncustodial crypto wallet.
Two Types of Wallets
A custodian or custodial wallet means a third party, such as a bank or a cryptocurrency marketplace, holds and manages the assets for you. Typically, transferring assets after death is much easier with a custodian, especially if it's a bank.
Noncustodial wallets eliminate the middleman and let a person hold their assets directly. For crypto enthusiasts whose interest in digital currency is driven by a distaste for the traditional banking system, then using a noncustodial wallet is kind of the whole point.
Noncustodial wallets can be software or hardware-based. It can even be a piece of paper with the instructions and passwords for accessing the cryptocurrency on it. (I use "password" here and throughout to refer to any string of letters, numbers, and characters needed to gain access to someone’s cryptocurrency.) Whatever kind of noncustodial wallet you choose, passing on your assets will require a DIY solution.
Pros and Cons of a Custodial Wallet
When you use a third-party custodian to hold your cryptocurrency, you can choose one that has a beneficiary process in place.
Charles Schwab and Chase are just two examples of large, well-known financial institutions that offer crypto services and have experience transferring assets after death. Schwab, for example, houses its cryptocurrency services within brokerage accounts. Signing a beneficiary form for a brokerage account applies to the crypto account as well. One and done.
Another benefit of using a bank is that at least three entities know you have an account: the bank, the government, and the credit reporting bureaus. Avenues exist for finding the banked money of deceased people. With a noncustodial wallet, this is not at all the case.
Similarly, if you get locked out of your online bank account, you can go to a bank branch with ID (I've had to do it) and get back in. More important to your heirs, it doesn't matter if you were locked out of the online portal when you died—that has no bearing on the account or a beneficiary's ability to receive the funds. This is not the case with noncustodial wallets.
Note that cryptocurrency accounts, even when held through a bank, are not FDIC-insured.
Other custodians include crypto marketplaces, such as Coinbase, and peer-to-peer payment services, like PayPal. Neither Coinbase nor PayPal have beneficiary forms as of this writing, though they do have a clear process for proving a person is entitled to a decedent's account. In both cases, you must have legal documents saying you are the executor of the estate (for PayPal) or are entitled to inherit the account (Coinbase), as well as a death certificate and other documentation. So the process is clunky and takes some advance planning, but it's still straightforward.
How many disadvantages there are to using a custodian depends on your outlook. As mentioned, crypto enthusiasts who eschew traditional banking may not see any value in using a custodian. Banks require ID, so you cannot hold the crypto anonymously. Banks and many other custodians report your transactions to the federal government, holding you accountable to an honest tax filing. Custodial wallets also cost money. They typically charge transaction fees, usually a small percentage of each trade.
Pros and Cons of a Noncustodial Wallet
The primary benefit of a noncustodial wallet is that everything is in your control. You hold the assets directly. You're responsible for knowing and keeping safe the information you need to access your assets. You also have to come up with a plan for informing your beneficiaries that a crypto account exists and making sure they can access it.
The first and biggest problem is that if you get locked out while you're alive, it's game over. "If you lose your cryptographic key, there's no company that you can appeal to," says Benjamin Orzeske, chief counsel for Uniform Law Commission and a staff attorney for the Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act, the law that guides how digital inheritance is handled in most states.
In the case of a hardware key, a corrupted device or one lost to fire or theft may also cut off a person and their heirs from their crypto, permanently and irreversibly.
The other major hurdle is that your fiduciary needs to know the crypto exists. No government or credit reporting bureau has a record of you holding the account. The only people who know are the ones you tell.
Now let's get procedural. Because of how the blockchain works, you must figure out a secure way to give your heirs instructions for obtaining the assets. Your system has to be safe. It doesn't come with any backups or failsafes unless you create them. And whether you can test your system to make sure it works before you die will require a huge amount of trust.
Ideas from Reddit users for how to build a system for passing on cryptocurrency include email dead-man switches, printed instructions given to a trusted person, and splitting instructions across two people who will need to come together to obtain access. All these solutions could work but have obvious flaws: the failure of an email system, a trusted person dying alongside you, someone forgetting you gave them instructions, and so forth.
The best option may be to put the bulk of the instructions into your estate plan, including your named fiduciary, but crucially omitting any passwords. As Catherine Hodder, a senior attorney editor at FindLaw, explained to me, “The will is a public document,” and you should never put any usernames or passwords in your will.
An excellent place to put your password is inside a safe-deposit box at a bank. The existence of the deposit box should also be listed in your will. Some crypto owners have suggested stamping the password into a metal plate, which I suppose is a fine idea if you don't trust ink and paper to last longer than you.
One potential flaw is still that you can't do a dry run to make sure your system works unless you trust your fiduciary completely. Something as simple as needing your fingerprint to unlock a device could spell the end of your plan.
An objection that some staunchly anti-capitalistic investors may have is that by including your cryptocurrency in your estate plan, you've returned it to the realm of traditional law and governance.
Then again, you'll be dead.

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi announced Saturday that he intends to leave office in 2030, in accordance with Egypt's amended constitution, ruling out the possibility of further constitutional changes. He said his departure was "settled and not open for discussion."
Amendments to Egypt's constitution were approved in 2019, allowing el-Sisi to remain president until 2030. At the time, critics argued that the changes marked another step toward consolidating authoritarian rule in Egypt, potentially creating a regime even more repressive than that of President Hosni Mubarak, who was ousted in a popular uprising in 2011. Mubarak's overthrow, after 29 years in power, had raised hopes of establishing a genuine democracy.
In recent days, el-Sisi has also addressed the question of when he will leave office in several other speeches. Speaking Saturday at a ceremony at Egypt's military academy, he added: "My duty is to protect the country and hand over its flag while it is still flying high. We are committed to preparing people capable of assuming the responsibility of leading the country. We will not allow people who are incapable of taking on that responsibility to lead."
He also expressed unequivocal support for the Gulf states and Saudi Arabia, which is currently facing attacks by the Houthis in Yemen.
"We stand firmly with our brothers in the Gulf and fully support the defense of their territories. We will take any measure Saudi Arabia requests to protect its security and sovereignty," he said.
El-Sisi came to power more than a decade ago after ousting Muslim Brotherhood leader Mohamed Morsi in a military coup in 2013. Morsi had been elected president following the revolution that toppled Mubarak.
Since the military takeover, el-Sisi has ruled Egypt virtually unchecked. During his decade in power, he has overseen a sweeping crackdown on liberals, left-wing activists and Islamists alike, with human rights organizations alleging that tens of thousands of people have been imprisoned. El-Sisi and his supporters maintain that the arrests were necessary to stabilize Egypt and curb radical Islamism.
After winning the 2014 presidential election with 97% of the vote and securing a similar result in 2018, el-Sisi won 89% of the vote in 2023, in yet another election whose outcome was widely seen as a foregone conclusion.

BANGKOK – The global economy is showing remarkable resilience but there is no room for complacency, the head of the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) steering committee said on Oct 17, while divisions over Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine sparked a walkout of delegates.
Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, who heads the IMF’s steering committee, acknowledged the walkout by nearly half of the delegates during remarks by Russia’s finance minister at a meeting on Oct 17, but said the important thing was that members ultimately agreed to the chair’s statement.
“We came here for a reason, and we achieved it. Look at this chair statement; it clearly says that all members agreed to the statement, so that’s what matters,” the chairman of the International Monetary and Financial Committee (IMFC) told Reuters.
Al-Jadaan told a news conference that the global economy was demonstrating “remarkable resilience” in the face of profound ongoing challenges, including wars, threats to energy and food security, high public debt levels, and risks linked to the rapid development of artificial intelligence, while warning finance officials against letting down their guard.
“The message from the IMFC members is clear: There is no room for complacency,” Al-Jadaan said in the final news conference of a week of IMF and World Bank annual meetings that brought more than 18,000 people to Bangkok.
“Escalating conflicts and trade tensions could further disrupt critical trade routes, exacerbate commodity price pressures, including in refined energy products, and worsen energy and food security,” the chairman's statement said.
Fiscal authorities should work to rebuild buffers while protecting vulnerable populations and growth-enhancing investments, Al-Jadaan told reporters, underscoring the need for continued central bank independence and policies that supported private sector-led growth and investment.
“International cooperation remains critical to addressing excessive global imbalances and trade tensions,” he said.
IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva called the meetings productive but said there was clearly heightened anxiety among members about increasing divergence.
Many lower-income countries that were not part of the AI value chain feared they were falling behind, she said.
“These meetings also have shown that in a world of repetitive shocks and geopolitical fragmentation, still there is desire for multilateral dialogue and cooperation,” she said. “It is there.”
Walkout amid tensions
Those comments came shortly after many IMFC delegates left the room when Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov addressed the group in Russian.
Bundesbank president Joachim Nagel told a bank event on the sidelines of the meetings that nearly 50% of the delegates took part in the walkout, sending a clear message to Russia.
“This is a very strong signal about solidarity and values. It would be the best for the world economy if this unprovoked war of aggression against Ukraine would end,” Nagel said.
“I was really proud so many left this plenary.”
The Bank of England confirmed that Governor Andrew Bailey was among the delegates who joined the walkout, which comes ahead of Britain hosting the Group of 20 in 2027.
Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 has roiled the IMFC, preventing it from reaching consensus statements in the years since. There were deep divisions again at this week’s meetings as fresh tensions flared between the US and Ukraine.
Sources said those who left while Siluanov spoke included delegates from Britain, Germany, France, Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Norway, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, among others.
“The Ukraine war is existential for us in Europe,” one European diplomat said. “We cannot normalise relations with Russia.”
Germany on Oct 15 warned against efforts to bring Russia back on to the international stage after Siluanov attended a meeting of G-20 finance ministers and central bankers, just over a month after the US hosted his first in-person G-20 appearance since Russia invaded Ukraine, at a meeting in Asheville, North Carolina.
US Treasury Undersecretary Erin Browne told Reuters the same day that Washington, the current leader of the G-20 nations, supported Russia’s presence despite European concerns.

Egypt's Sisi says he will step down in 2030, rules out another term
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:17:00 UTC
19:17:00 KST

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sissi said Saturday that he would leave office when his current term ends in 2030, ruling out any further constitutional amendments to extend his rule as he also pledged to defend Saudi Arabia’s security and sovereignty if requested.
“The year 2030 will mark the end of my presidential term. This matter is completely settled,” el-Sissi said during a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy in the New Administrative Capital, according to state-run Al-Ahram newspaper.
“I said that the Egyptian constitution would not be touched,” he added. “This is an entirely settled matter and will not be discussed.”
The 71-year-old president, a former army general who has led Egypt since 2014, is serving a six-year term after winning re-election in December 2023. Constitutional amendments approved in a 2019 referendum extended presidential terms from four years to six and allowed Sisi to seek an additional term, enabling him to remain in office until 2030.
The amendments reshaped Egypt’s presidential limits and drew criticism from opponents who warned they would consolidate power in the hands of the president.
El-Sissi came to power in 2013 after the military ousted Mohamed Morsi, Egypt’s first democratically elected president, following mass protests against his rule. El-Sissi subsequently won the presidency in 2014 and has maintained a tight grip on the country’s political system.
His latest remarks appeared aimed at ending speculation about whether he might seek another constitutional change to remain in power beyond his current mandate.
El-Sissi also spoke about the role of the military and the need to prepare a new generation of leaders, linking the armed forces to the protection of Egypt’s constitutional order and state institutions.
He said the constitution defines the military’s responsibility to safeguard democracy, the constitutional framework and the fundamental pillars of the state.
“I will not leave the Egyptian state until it is brimming with its own people capable of shouldering responsibility,” el-Sissi said, referring to efforts to prepare younger generations to take on leadership roles through the Egyptian Military Academy.
The comments did not provide further details about how the transition to new leadership would be managed or what role el-Sissi might play after leaving office.
El-Sissi also declared that Egypt was prepared to take any measures requested by Saudi Arabia to protect the kingdom’s security and sovereignty, underscoring Cairo’s stated commitment to the defense of its Gulf partners.
“We will take any measure to protect Saudi Arabia,” he said, adding that he would call on parliament to convene an emergency session to authorize such action if Riyadh requested it.
“We stand firmly to protect and defend the territories of our brothers in the Gulf,” he added.
El-Sissi did not specify what measures Egypt might take or identify a particular threat that would prompt such a response.

Pope Leo discharged from hospital 4 days after surgery for lung cancer
Pope Leo XIV was released from Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Saturday, four days after undergoing surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his right lung.
The pope exited via the hospital's main entrance. A large crowd waiting outside the hospital cheered for him.
He shook hands with several people, then stopped to talk with a young woman who appeared to be wearing a bandage on her right arm and was holding a doll in the image of Pope Leo.
The Pope was smiling. Once in the car, he waved to the crowd. His motorcade returned to Vatican City at 3:43 p.m. local time.
The 71-year-old pope had a portion of his right lung removed and received a diagnosis of lung cancer earlier this week. No information about his prognosis has been publicly shared.
Leo was initially expected to remain hospitalized until Oct. 20 but on Thursday he resumed some work activity, and doctors said Friday that tests confirmed "steady improvement in his recovery." On Saturday morning, the Vatican announced he would leave later in the afternoon.
His personal physician and surgeon said in a separate statement that Leo was "deemed fit for discharge from the hospital" based on blood test results and a chest X-ray performed Saturday morning along with an assessment of his clinical condition.
The Vatican also confirmed that Leo will recite the Angelus prayer from the window of the papal apartment on Sunday.
The pontiff's surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, said in an interview with Vatican News that there is no clinical reason the Pope should skip an upcoming trip to South America. The visit, planned for early November, has been in question since Leo's hospitalization. On Friday, the Vatican published the names of journalists accredited to fly on the papal plane to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, signalling that the trip appeared to be going ahead.
Leo also conducted some work from the hospital. The Vatican released pictures of the American-born pope standing at an altar in green vestments, celebrating Mass at a small chapel in Gemelli Hospital on Friday.
The Vatican also said Leo spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin over the phone on Friday, during which he "expressed his deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation in the city of Oleshky" in Ukraine.
The pope also held separate meetings with Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, the dean of the College of Cardinals, and Cardinal Baldassare Reina, the vicar general of the Diocese of Rome.
In the interview with Vatican News, Margaritora said the discovery of the pope's lung tumor was "entirely accidental," and that he had no symptoms. The tumor was found at the base of the lung, Margaritora said, but if it had been "a little higher up, it certainly would not have been seen."
"The Holy Father falls into the category of people who discover they have lung cancer entirely by chance – not because they are undergoing preventive screening, but because they undergo examinations for other reasons," Margaritora said.

Solar power booms in Philippines as war on Iran spikes energy costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:12:01 UTC
19:12:01 KST

Solar power booms in Philippines as war on Iran spikes energy costs
With Southeast Asia’s largest electricity bills rising even higher, Filipinos invest in rooftop panels.
Manila, Philippines – Keith Cantera and his family have been thinking about having their own solar power grid at home for years. But spending up to $5,000 for solar panels was nothing to scoff at, so they put the idea on the back burner.
It all changed this year when the United States-Israel war on Iran rattled global energy markets and sent electricity prices soaring. From paying a monthly bill of about $150 before the war began in late February, Cantera said his family went to forking out as much as $220.
Eight months later, they are having solar panels installed on their rooftop.
“The cost is about the same as paying our electric bills for three or four years based on the current rate,” Cantera said. “But in the fifth year, we’ll have recovered our investment, and electricity will essentially be free.”
Cantera is one of a growing number of Filipino homeowners turning to solar power in a country that had Southeast Asia’s highest electricity costs even before the war. They were comparable only to Singapore, where the average income is more than 10 times higher.
A report by the energy think tank Ember estimated that rooftop panels had nearly doubled in the Philippines since early 2025.
And in the first months of the war from March to May, the rush for solar power led to $407m in panel imports, according to government trade data from China, where most panels are manufactured. The Philippines became the biggest single overseas market for that period. Only the Netherlands bought more, but it redistributes them to the rest of Europe.
Lexus Grepo, CEO of the solar power supplier Solarmaxx, can attest to the boom.
“There is a 30-day wait because solar panel shipments can’t keep up,” Grepo said. “In March, we had 40 projects, which was almost triple our monthly clientele. Since then, we have been setting up 25 to 30 systems a month.”
Grepo does not expect demand to slow down even if tensions in the Middle East ease and shipping routes for energy supplies reopen.
“I think people now realise that the world is an unpredictable place, so they have to be ready for any eventuality. Filipinos now see that they don’t necessarily have to be at the mercy of the global energy market.”
The Philippines, one of the few countries in the region where electricity is not subsidised, relies on imported coal and gas for more than 70 percent of its power mix. The value of its currency, the peso, which has slid to a record low of more than 63 to the US dollar, is making these imports even costlier.
In late March, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr declared a national energy emergency in response to the war and what he described as the “imminent danger” posed to the national energy supply. Still, electricity rates have continued to increase.
The shift to solar is also partly driven by anger at electric companies that have come under scrutiny for charging customers for so-called system losses, which include illegal connections.
Cantera said learning about having to pay for someone else’s electricity consumption was the last straw.
“Who would agree to paying for something that you did not use? It’s not like the money we spend for electricity just fell from heaven,” he added.
But while the soaring demand is real, the upfront cost of a solar power system is still too high for most Filipinos. The government in March launched a new initiative offering loans for residential rooftop installations, but these are available only to public sector workers.
What officials hope can bring power rates down for the majority of people are the dozens of renewable energy projects in the pipeline, including a 3,500-hectare (8,650-acre) solar farm north of the capital, Manila, that is projected to be the largest in the world. When fully operational, the project is expected to generate 850 megawatts of electricity for 2.4 million households.
But some consumers said such projects could take years to complete, leaving them with ballooning electricity bills unless they take action themselves.
“It’s just so unpredictable nowadays. You have the impending El Nino weather pattern. There’s still war, the continuing fuel price hikes and so much more,” Cantera said. “So why not utilise a natural resource?”

Trump faults aides as Republican midterm prospects dim

WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump is blaming senior aides and political operatives for a faltering midterm strategy, questioning campaign spending, faulting redistricting and second-guessing candidate choices as Republicans fight to retain control of Congress, said three people familiar with internal discussions.
Trump is not on the Nov 3 ballot but repeatedly tells supporters to pretend that he is, hoping to mobilise voters who might otherwise skip the election.
He has embarked on a frenetic campaign schedule while largely avoiding acknowledging his own role in shaping the strategy and how his unpopularity is weighing on Republican candidates in competitive races.
Much of the friction has centred on James Blair, the long-time aide who runs Trump’s super PAC MAGA, and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who until now had largely escaped criticism.
Trump has faulted Blair’s handling of campaign funds, while some White House officials and allies have questioned Wiles’ oversight of the political operation.
As Trump questions why campaign spending has failed to improve Republican polling numbers, his advisers are also blaming one another.
Wiles has pointed to Blair, while Blair has faulted the White House legislative affairs team, one of the people said.
“What’s really happening is a circular firing squad,” the person said.
Opinion polls suggest Democrats will win the House of Representatives, while the Senate remains too close to call.

Trump has long distanced himself from political setbacks

Erdogan hails new chapter in Türkiye's energy history as floating production platform heads to Black Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:10:22 UTC
19:10:22 KST

Gizem Nisa Demir
17 October 2026•Update: 17 October 2026
Türkiye is opening a new chapter in its energy history with the deployment of the Osman Gazi floating production platform to the Black Sea, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Saturday in a video message.
"Today, we are opening a brand-new page in our energy history. We are sending Osman Gazi, essentially a floating industrial facility, off to its duty station in the Black Sea," Erdogan said in a video message sent to a ceremony marking the platform's departure from Filyos Port in Zonguldak province.
Erdogan said he had announced in July 2024 that Türkiye would acquire its first floating production platform. In May 2025, the platform, named Osman Gazi, was sent from Dolmabahce Palace in Istanbul to Filyos.
He described the platform as the first production facility of the Blue Homeland, Türkiye's maritime vision under its Century of Türkiye initiative.
"Osman Gazi is the first factory of the Blue Homeland, the maritime counterpart of our Century of Türkiye vision," he said.
Erdogan expressed his hope that the platform would provide beneficial services to the country and its people, thanked everyone who contributed to the project, and wished success to the personnel who will work aboard it.
Production capacity and technical specifications
Equipped with 21 different units, the platform will process natural gas extracted from wells in the Sakarya Gas Field and transport it to Filyos through subsea pipelines, Erdogan said.
"Natural gas production in the Black Sea will double to 20 million cubic meters per day, and starting in 2027, one in every three households will use our domestic natural gas," he added.
Measuring 298.5 meters (980 feet) in length, 56 meters (approximately 184 feet) in width and 29.5 meters (approximately 97 feet) in depth, Osman Gazi will accommodate 140 personnel, Erdogan said, describing it as a floating fortress of energy.
According to information shared by the Communications Directorate on Turkish social media platform NSosyal, the platform will operate around the clock at its designated location in the Black Sea for 20 years. It will deliver processed natural gas to the national grid in a form ready for use.
The platform is expected to contribute $3.5 billion annually to the economy. With its commissioning, the Sakarya Gas Field's total production target will reach 20 million cubic meters per day, enough to meet the natural gas needs of 8 million households, according to the directorate.
Platform's departure and operational targets
Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar spoke at a ceremony at Filyos Port marking the departure of the Osman Gazi floating production platform for its operational destination in the Sakarya Gas Field.
Bayraktar also stressed that the platform would increase daily gas production at the field to 20 million cubic meters in 2027, describing it as Türkiye's first floating natural gas processing facility.
The Communications Directorate also announced that the platform would begin operations following the ceremony.
An accompanying graphic said the platform would be dispatched from Filyos, Zonguldak, to its designated location in the Black Sea, where it is expected to remain in service for two decades.

The veteran photographer was wearing a press vest clearly distinguishing her as a media worker, but was knocked to the ground and her camera and phone seized.

Video footage circulating of the attack showed the cars completely engulfed in flames, with emergency services grappling to put out the fire between plumes of dark smoke.

Pope Leo XIV to leave hospital after lung cancer surgery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:07:16 UTC
19:07:16 KST

Pope Leo XIV is being released from the hospital on Saturday, four days after lung cancer surgery, and will deliver the traditional noon blessing Sunday from a window overlooking St. Peter's Square, the Vatican announced.
The 71-year-old Leo had the lower lobe of his right lung removed after doctors identified a suspected cancerous nodule. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.
His personal physician and surgeon said in a separate statement that Leo was “deemed fit for discharge from the hospital” based on blood test results and a chest X-ray performed Saturday morning along with an assessment of his clinical condition.
He is set to leave the hospital in the early afternoon and return to the Vatican, the Vatican said in a brief statement.
During his recovery, Leo continued some of his official duties, including a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin and meetings with senior Vatican aides. Medical bulletins indicated that his condition was steadily improving and that he could carry out normal daily activities independently.
On Friday, the Vatican released the first images of the pontiff since his surgery, showing him celebrating Mass in a hospital chapel while wearing green vestments. Leo distributed Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes and thanked hospital staff for their care.
Leo underwent surgery Tuesday at Rome's Gemelli Hospital after doctors discovered a small, localized nodule in his right lung during routine medical examinations. The 71-year-old pontiff had publicly disclosed the finding during his Sunday noon prayer, explaining that doctors recommended removing the growth because it had been detected at an early stage.
The operation, led by Gemelli's chief thoracic surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, lasted approximately 90 minutes, although Leo spent about three hours in the operating room. Surgeons removed the entire lower lobe of his right lung in an effort to eliminate the suspected cancerous tissue. Tests conducted during surgery confirmed lung adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer, a diagnosis doctors had suspected based on preliminary examinations.
The Vatican said the procedure was completed successfully, on schedule and without complications. Leo regained consciousness after the operation and returned to his hospital room, where he spent a peaceful night, according to a Vatican statement issued Wednesday.
Doctors have not disclosed the tumor's precise size or whether cancer cells were found in nearby lymph nodes, factors that could influence the pope's prognosis and determine whether additional treatment is necessary. Before the operation, oncologists said his outlook could be excellent because the growth was detected early and appeared to be localized.
The pope's next major scheduled engagement is a November 6-17 trip to Latin America, involving about a dozen flights and two helicopter journeys. The Vatican has continued preparations for the visit, although Leo's ability to travel will depend on his recovery.
Meanwhile, doctors are awaiting further test results to establish the cancer's molecular and genetic characteristics, determine whether it has spread beyond the removed lung lobe and assess whether additional treatment will be necessary.
The American pontiff arrived at Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday morning, walking through the main entrance and waving to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered outside. His decision to publicly disclose the diagnosis and planned surgery marked an unusual degree of transparency surrounding the first major health problem reported during his papacy.
Elected in May 2025, Leo has generally maintained an active lifestyle, including playing tennis, and is not known to smoke. He had no previously disclosed major health problems since becoming pope.
The Vatican initially expected Leo to remain hospitalized for approximately one week and canceled all his public engagements through October 20. Unlike previous popes who stayed in the hospital's dedicated papal apartment, Leo was accommodated in a nearby room because the apartment was undergoing renovations.

Trump-Zelenskiy rift threatens vital support for Kyiv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17

19:05:35 KST

Trump-Zelenskiy rift threatens vital support for Kyiv
WASHINGTON/KYIV, Oct 17 - From US threats to cut off intelligence support for Ukraine to a waiver of tariffs on Russian exports and a diesel deal that could help Russia fund its war, it has been a damaging week for ties between Kyiv and its most important ally, Washington.
US President Donald Trump, frustrated by high energy costs he blames partly on Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, has repeatedly criticized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy. A disruption of US-provided satellite internet services raised fears that Ukraine could be vulnerable as it prepares for another winter of Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure.
Zelenskiy responded to Trump's barbs with an unusually sharp series of public criticisms of Trump, suggesting the US was now favoring Russia. He said Ukraine would defy Trump's demand to stop striking Russian energy targets, citing Russia's continued attacks.
Intensifying the discord, Trump waived key US Russia-related sanctions and tariffs on Friday, shortly before they were scheduled to take effect. That prompted Zelenskiy to say in social media posts that Trump's action would encourage Russia to continue attacks on Ukraine.
The widening rift has sparked concerns that Trump and Zelenskiy's tumultuous relationship could lead to even worse outcomes for Kyiv. Trump could yet restrict the supply of weapons to Ukraine, follow through on threats to stop sharing battlefield intelligence, or strike more economic deals with Moscow.
Despite Zelenskiy's remarks, Kyiv wants to continue dialogue with Trump's envoys, his friend Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, two Ukrainian officials familiar with the talks said, speaking on the condition of anonymity.
Denys Sienik, chargé d'affaires at Ukraine's embassy in Washington, told Newsmax on Friday that Ukraine was grateful to Trump and his team for their efforts to end the war and said Ukraine was willing to engage in talks with Russia.
Trump told reporters on Friday he would continue to deal with both Zelenskiy and Russian President Vladimir Putin. “I want that war to end,” he said.
'MISSED OPPORTUNITY': FORMER US OFFICIAL
Daniel Fried, the senior State Department official on Europe from 2005 to 2009, said it was unclear whether Washington was making a lasting shift away from Ukraine, but the fallout was damaging prospects for an end to the war that began with Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion.
"It's not only a missed opportunity, it causes genuine suffering in Ukraine and encourages Putin to continue the war, so it's not cost-free," said Fried, now at the Washington-based Atlantic Council think tank.
Trump's relationship with Zelenskiy has long been uneasy. Trump and US Vice President JD Vance publicly upbraided Zelenskiy during an Oval Office meeting in February 2025. Washington has paused or slowed military assistance to Ukraine under Trump, while allowing European allies to purchase US weapons for Kyiv.
The relationship had steadied until Ukraine's strikes this year on energy sites in Russia began contributing to rising fuel prices. High gasoline and diesel prices are a political headache for Trump ahead of November's midterm elections, in which his Republican Party could lose its majorities in the US Congress, according to analysts.
Experts say that surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the US-Israeli war with Iran, which brought Iranian attacks on energy facilities and has largely shut the vital Strait of Hormuz.
Frustrated by Zelenskiy, however, Trump turned to Russia to increase fuel supply and contain prices, according to a person familiar with the internal debate, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.
Trump said on October 9 he had reached a deal with Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian fuel and import Russian diesel.
In an executive order released by the White House on Friday, Trump also waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs shortly before they were supposed to take effect under the Graham Act, which Trump signed last month.
Although the law, named for the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, called for new penalties on Russia starting next week, it also allows the president to waive them if it is in the US national interest to do so.
Zelenskiy said Trump's latest action undercuts the Graham Act's main goal and will fuel Russia's "desire to keep killing people."
The US diesel deal with Russia and the waiver are the latest steps in what Zelenskiy said he expects to be continued sanctions relief on Moscow.
The prospect of the US continuing to pressure Russia to end the war has dimmed since Graham's death in July, Zelenskiy said. Graham, a South Carolina Republican and a confidant of Trump, strongly supported Ukraine.
"It’s difficult without him, I’ll be honest," the Ukrainian president wrote.
HIGH STAKES FOR UKRAINE
For Kyiv, the stakes are high and immediate. Zelenskiy said on Tuesday that Ukraine had received no warning from Western partners before a deadly Russian attack on the capital.
Without US intelligence, Ukraine could face greater difficulty detecting and countering Russian missile and drone attacks, particularly against energy infrastructure that Moscow has repeatedly targeted during previous winters.
Trump has said the US is still sharing intelligence with Ukraine. But Zelenskiy told NPR that US officials had warned Ukrainian commanders intelligence could be reduced or cut off.
Ukraine's Starshield system, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink service, was disrupted after what two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter said was an order originating from the White House, Reuters reported on Thursday.
The service has been partially restored, but the episode highlighted the vulnerability created by Ukraine's dependence on technology controlled by US companies and subject to decisions by the Trump administration.
Trump may face resistance if congressional Republicans see his approach as weakening Ukraine while benefiting Russia. Ukraine retains support among Trump's fellow Republicans, some of whom argue that Washington should not pressure Kyiv into accepting a settlement on terms favorable to Moscow.
Zelenskiy's tough responses to Trump were risky, but he may be counting on a power shift on Capitol Hill after the midterm elections to make it harder for Trump to ease sanctions on Russia and further reduce military assistance to Kyiv, said Brett Bruen, a former foreign policy adviser in the Obama administration and head of the Global Situation Room consultancy.
“Zelenskiy knows who he’s dealing with,” he said. “Trump’s threats don’t have the same kind of effect as they did when JD Vance tried to shame him in the Oval Office.” REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Nostalgia for a party’s past cuts both ways when it comes to support for political violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:00:57 UTC
19:00:57 KST

A recent study suggests that longing for a political party’s past is tied to support for political violence in opposite ways, depending on how people relate to their party. Among partisans whose commitment is obsessive, stronger collective nostalgia went along with a stronger link to support for violence, while among those whose commitment is harmonious, it went along with less support. The findings, published in Journal of Applied Social Psychology, suggest that nostalgia for “the good old days” does not carry the same meaning for everyone who feels it.
The way people commit to a political cause can take two distinct forms. Harmonious passion describes a freely chosen involvement that coexists easily with a person’s other life commitments, such as family or hobbies. Obsessive passion describes a more compulsive attachment where the political cause becomes deeply tied to a person’s sense of self-worth. In this state, people often feel inner pressure to defend their beliefs and struggle to step away from politics when they need to.
This distinction helps researchers understand the psychological roots of radicalization. For instance, a 2019 study by Bélanger and colleagues found that obsessive passion for a cause was linked to moral disengagement, a way of justifying harmful actions as acceptable, and to support for political violence, whereas harmonious passion was linked to peaceful activism.
Separately, psychologists have examined collective nostalgia, which is a sentimental longing for the past of a group that a person belongs to. For example, a 2015 study found that a collective longing for a nation’s past can unite people around their own group while also being linked to hostility toward outside groups. In addition, a 2020 study found that the effect of collective nostalgia on attitudes toward outsiders depends on what kind of past people long for, such as whether they yearn for an open society or a more uniform one. Relatedly, a study covered by PsyPost in 2022 showed that collective nostalgia is associated with populist attitudes.
These two lines of inquiry left an open question about why only a small fraction of people who feel longing for a past era come to view violence as acceptable. The research, led by Jocelyn J. Bélanger, an associate teaching professor at Carnegie Mellon University in Qatar and co-author of The Three Pillars of Radicalization, sought to connect these ideas. The authors proposed that collective nostalgia might widen the gap between the two forms of passion, going along with more support for violence among the obsessively passionate and less among the harmoniously passionate.
“Politicians on every side sell voters a golden age to reclaim, yet research on collective nostalgia had left a puzzle: longing for the group’s past sometimes breeds hostility and sometimes breeds belonging,” Bélanger told PsyPost. “We suspected the answer lay not in the nostalgia itself but in the kind of passion a person brings to their cause.”
To test this idea, the researchers surveyed 417 adult political partisans in the United States, recruited online in March 2022. The sample was split into two groups, consisting of 263 Democrats and 154 Republicans. Participants answered questions about their political party, rating how much their involvement felt harmonious and how much it felt obsessive.
The survey also measured participants’ feelings of collective nostalgia, asking how often they longed for the “good old days” of their party or past presidents from their side of the aisle. In addition, the authors assessed willingness to support or engage in hostile actions against the rival party, from physically attacking opponents to cutting off friendships with rival supporters. The researchers accounted for participants’ overall ideological commitment, so that the results would reflect how people internalized their beliefs rather than simply how much they cared about their party.
The initial results were consistent across both the Democratic and Republican groups. Obsessive passion was linked to greater support for political violence against the opposing party, while harmonious passion was not. Support for political violence was low overall, averaging about 1.7 to 1.8 on a 7-point scale.
When the researchers looked at collective nostalgia, they observed that the two forms of passion diverged. For participants with high levels of obsessive passion, increased feelings of nostalgia went along with even stronger support for political violence. The authors describe this as an amplification pattern, while stressing that the term describes the shape of a statistical relationship, not cause and effect.
But among participants high in harmonious passion, the pattern ran the other way. When nostalgia was low, harmonious passion was unrelated to support for violence, but when nostalgia was high, people with more harmonious passion reported less support for violence.
“We predicted it, but I was still struck by how cleanly nostalgia cut both ways: the same longing tracked greater openness to violence among obsessive partisans and less among harmonious ones,” Bélanger noted. “That crossover appeared among Democrats and Republicans alike, which tells me we are looking at the psychology of devotion rather than the psychology of one party.”
The researchers interpret this divergence through nostalgia’s bittersweet nature, though they did not measure these feelings directly. For the obsessively passionate, a longed-for past might feel like something stolen that must be forcefully reclaimed. For the harmoniously passionate, reflecting on a shared past might evoke connection and belonging, which could encourage restraint.
“How you care about a cause matters more than how much you care,” Bélanger explained. “Among people whose politics is a freely chosen part of life they can set aside at the dinner table, longing for the group’s glory days went with less support for political violence; among people whose politics has swallowed their identity, the same longing went with more.”
“In statistical terms the effects are modest (the interplay between nostalgia and passion explains an extra 1 to 2 percent of the variation in support for violence), yet the link between obsessive passion and support for violence was roughly twice as strong among highly nostalgic partisans as among less nostalgic ones,” Bélanger said. “Support for violence was low on average, so picture nostalgia as a force that pulls the most zealous toward the dangerous end of the scale, not as a nation primed for conflict.”
The findings align with earlier research covered by PsyPost in 2024 by members of the same research team. That study also examined American political partisans and found that obsessive passion was linked to support for political violence, whereas harmonious passion was not.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. “The misreading I’d most like to head off is ‘nostalgia breeds violence,’ because its main role was to magnify whichever kind of passion a person already had, for better or worse,” Bélanger pointed out. “We can show that these things travel together but not that nostalgia causes them, and agreeing with violence on a questionnaire is a long way from committing it.”
It is also possible that an underlying factor drives both, or that a person’s willingness to support violence colors how they remember the past. Collective nostalgia also tends to accompany feelings of threat, anxiety about the group’s future, and grievance, none of which were measured, so these related feelings could account for the pattern. Additionally, the researchers did not directly measure whether participants felt their party had fallen into decline, a perception that often travels alongside nostalgia and might help explain the pattern among the obsessively passionate.
The study also measured how people felt about political violence rather than observing actual behavior. The leap from endorsing aggressive tactics on a survey to carrying out physical harm in the real world is a large one, and future studies would need to track actions over time to see if these patterns hold.
“Next, we want to induce nostalgia in the lab to see whether it causes these shifts, and to test our hunch about why: obsessive partisans may dwell on the bitter half of nostalgia, what was taken from the group, while harmonious partisans savor the sweet half, what the group shared,” Bélanger said. “The long-term goal is practical: if we can help people hold their convictions more harmoniously, we may blunt the political appeals that turn longing into rage.”
“Nostalgia is among the oldest tools of political persuasion, and our findings suggest its effect depends less on the message than on who hears it,” the researcher added. “The same appeal to a golden age that steadies a calm partisan may embolden a zealous one.”
The study, “Collective Nostalgia Widens the Gap Between Obsessive and Harmonious Passion in Support for Political Violence,” was authored by Jocelyn J. Bélanger, Daniel Snook, Danaiym Talantbekova, and Jais Adam-Troian.

Zest is a Key Ingredient to Good Living
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

Approaching life with positive expectations, a get-up-and-go attitude, and eagerness is related to many good things in life. This individual asset is often referred to as zest, and it can be purposefully developed to assist us in managing daily stressors as well as creating meaningful lives.
True zest is not due to hyperarousal or too much caffeine. It is a cultivated cheerfulness and joy. When we are stressed or not feeling well, it’s hard to avoid doing things halfway or halfheartedly. But there are ways we can increase zest even when it seems like the deck is stacked against us, the world is filled with conflict, and our social media feeds are thick with chaos and gloom.
Psychologists Christopher Peterson and Martin Seligman pioneered the field of positive psychology, the scientific study of human flourishing. One of the highlights of their initiatives was published in 2004, Character Strengths and Virtues, a groundbreaking text on the 24 universal character strengths. Zest is one of the 24 strengths.
When you cultivate zest, you’ll want to fully engage in life and not just view it from the sidelines, look forward to each day, and wake to anticipation over the day’s possibilities. Zest has also been referred to as vitality, exuberance, and joie de vivre, the French phrase for the joy of living.
In an analysis of data from 130 studies involving more than 275,000 people around the globe, most character strengths were associated with greater mental health. But zest was one of just two strengths (the other is hope) that had the strongest relationship to mental well-being across countries and age groups. Zest contributes to life satisfaction among children, adolescents, and adults. In addition, in a study of nearly 10,000 employed adults, those who scored high on zest had higher work satisfaction and were more likely to view work as a calling. People who score high on measures of zest are also more likely to view their lives as meaningful.
I reached out to Ryan Niemiec, a psychologist and author of several books, including The Power of Character Strengths and Character Strengths Interventions: A Field Guide for Practitioners. Niemiec is the chief science and education officer at the VIA Institute on Character, a non-profit focused on the science and practice of character strengths. I asked him about the most effective ways people can increase zest in their own lives.
“In terms of boosting zest, I turn straight to behavioral activation, one of the most proven strategies for depression,” Niemiec said. “In practical terms, this means to take action in some way to boost oneself—to take that one step forward in lifting one’s energy.” He encouraged people to engage every day in one healthy pleasure, one form of physical activity, and one action that makes you feel like you accomplished something.
Some of us seem to naturally have this irresistible aliveness, often invigorating those around us. Others work hard to cultivate zest. Research supports the idea that we are never too old to change. And we can learn how to cultivate zest.
We can learn to savor pleasures, set good intentions, and try to view life as an adventure. Other intentional ways to potentially lift our spirits include taking a brisk 10-minute walk every morning, doing cardiovascular or strength-building challenges, practicing Reiki or yoga, laughing with friends, and engaging in stimulating tasks and work. The VIA Institute on Character has activities, workbooks, videos, webinars, and courses—some of them free—on improving all the character strengths, including zest.
To be sure, practicing a zest for life can be harder for those who have physical illness and pain and those who engage in unhealthy lifestyle behaviors. And those striving for zest under these circumstances may benefit from assistance from a mental health professional like a psychologist, a physical health provider like a physician, or a personal trainer or fitness instructor.
For some of us, being hard on ourselves is second nature. We expect our mental health to stretch under strain. Rather than exclusively focusing on what’s wrong with our mental health, one approach is to develop skills, traits, and perspectives that can help us. Acquiring zest is a worthwhile investment and may help us not only through challenging times, but also help us to see beauty and soar in our lives and workplaces.

ROME – Pope Leo left hospital in Rome on the afternoon of Oct 17 and returned to the Vatican four days after surgery for lung cancer, an illness that has prompted speculation about how it might affect his 17-month papacy.
The 71-year-old walked unaided to his waiting car, stopping to speak to well-wishers outside Rome’s Gemelli Hospital. He stopped to speak to a 13-year-old girl named Varvara from Ukraine who has been in Italy for cancer treatment.
He was pictured smiling broadly and waving through an open window when his black SUV left the hospital. He waved again to crowds as he was driven back into the Vatican but did not speak to anyone there before re-entering the world’s smallest country.
His doctors had earlier said he was well enough to return home after they carried out the latest blood tests and chest imaging.
The Pope, who had an operation on Oct 13 to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, will hold his first public engagement since surgery on Oct 18 when he leads weekly prayers with pilgrims in St Peter’s Square at noon.
Leo has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.
The diagnosis for a pope known to be relatively young and energetic and who was elected only in May 2025 caused shock and raised questions about the future shape of his papacy as he deals with the illness.
The Pope’s doctors have said his surgery was completed successfully, without complications.
They have not yet disclosed the size of the tumour or whether the disease had spread to nearby lymph nodes, key factors in determining prognosis.
Pope pursues packed agenda
The Vatican signalled on Oct 16 that Leo, known for following a busy schedule, intended to keep up his commitments, as some cardinals began to publicly express concern about the Pope’s health.
In a sign the Pope was back to work, Leo held a phone call on Oct 16 with Russian President Vladimir Putin, urging a ceasefire to help get vital supplies into the Russian-controlled Ukrainian town of Oleshky.
The Vatican said work on his Nov 6 to 17 visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, one of the most intense arranged for a pope in decades, was “going forward”.
It released a list of journalists accredited to travel with Leo and cover the trip.
Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican Secretary of State, said on Oct 16 that Leo may need to adjust the pace of his schedule going forward “according to the condition of his health”. It is unusual for a cardinal to say openly that a pope might need to modify his routine.
The Vatican on Oct 16 released the first images of the Pope since his surgery, showing him celebrating mass and standing unaided.

====================================================================================================

Gaza shelters deteriorate after repeated displacement as winter approaches: IOM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:54:15 UTC
18:54:15 KST

Repeated displacement during three years of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has left shelters across the enclave increasingly deteriorated, while restrictions and funding shortages are hampering preparations for winter, a senior UN migration official said late on Friday.
Karl Baker, regional crisis coordinator for the Gaza response at the International Organisation for Migration (IOM), said some Palestinians have been displaced as many as eight times, damaging or destroying tents and other temporary shelters each time families are forced to move.
“When they move, all those goods that they currently have or did have either get destroyed, or they have to seek new shelter,” Baker told UN News.
Even basic materials such as tarpaulins need to be replaced roughly every six months, but humanitarian agencies have been unable to bring replacements into Gaza at the required scale, he said.
Baker said agencies now need to move beyond temporary solutions toward more durable transitional shelters.
Materials needed for stronger roofing, concrete floors, and more substantial walls, however, are affected by Israel’s “dual-use” restrictions over security concerns.
“After three years of war, we do need to improve the level of shelter which is inside, and move further away from temporary and more toward transitional type of shelter,” he said.
Baker said IOM remains in constant contact with Israeli authorities, but some durable materials continue to be denied entry over security concerns.
He also cited funding shortages and disruptions to international shipping as obstacles, saying IOM relies on suppliers in countries including China, India, and Pakistan.
Although funding has begun to arrive, it remains insufficient to meet the needs of an estimated 1.8 million to 1.9 million people requiring shelter assistance, he added.
Baker said only around 30 percent of Gaza is currently accessible to most of the population, forcing displaced Palestinians into increasingly crowded and often flood-prone areas.
“The 30 percent in which they currently live is a very large displacement camp,” he said.
With winter rains already beginning, humanitarian organisations are working to address flood-prone areas and deploy water pumps, but Baker warned that getting displaced Palestinians through the winter would be the biggest challenge.
Earlier this month, IOM said available and incoming shelter supplies covered only 17 percent of Gaza’s winter needs, while more than half of tents and makeshift shelters were in poor condition.
A ceasefire has been in effect since October 10 2025, but Israeli attacks and restrictions on the entry of humanitarian and shelter supplies have continued.
