====================================================================================================

As Israel blocks PA funding, the West Bank’s healthcare system is failing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:47:55 UTC
18:47:55 KST

As Israel blocks PA funding, the West Bank’s healthcare system is failing
Hospitals across the occupied West Bank have been hit by a funding shortage.
Beit Jala, occupied West Bank – Khaldoun Atwan starts each day in the oncology ward at Beit Jala Government Hospital, not knowing what barriers will come his way.
The Nabi Yunis checkpoint in Halhul seems to be “always closed”, so the head of the daytime oncology unit at the hospital leaves his car and finishes the commute from Hebron by taxi.
“More than once, by God, I found the mirror broken. I found the wiper broken,” he said about his journey through an area where settlers are now active.
Traversing a dizzying array of gates and checkpoints opening or closing at will, he does not know whether he will reach the hospital, whether his patients will, or whether the drugs they need will be on the shelf when they do.
Beit Jala is the only government hospital in Bethlehem governorate, home to some 320,000 people. Inside his tiny, spartan office, Atwan is struggling to keep up with his cancer patients who have regressed because they missed crucial appointments or essential drugs needed for their chemotherapy treatment.
Not even during the second Intifada, he recalls, was drug supply an issue. Now, it’s inescapable.
“Everything’s short … whatever’s available we give,” he said. “It’s a disaster.”
The Palestinian Authority (PA)’s finances have collapsed over the last three years due to a reduction in international aid and disruptions in Israel’s transfers of tax receipts. Israel’s actions in the occupied West Bank since October 2023, including widespread road closures, checkpoints and a series of settler pogroms against Palestinian communities, have also impacted the economy.
As a result, the occupied West Bank’s healthcare system is rapidly deteriorating, with staff receiving just half their salaries, while the PA can’t pay for essential medications.
‘Emergency cases only’
Alongside others nervously pacing in the courtyard, an older cancer patient from a village in Bethlehem governorate stood at the entrance of the hospital, weighing with his son what to do. “Every month they do their best, the doctors and the cleaning staff, but they aren’t provided with anything,” he said.
Ministry clinics are now operating part-time, with doctors seeing well more than 100 patients a day when they are. Now, even a doctor’s visit is rushed and unaffordable: “If we want to go to the doctor for a checkup, we need 200 shekels [$65],” said an older cancer patient.
“It’s not a story of there being no staff,” said Iyad Dari, the attending physician at the dialysis unit at Beit Jala. Getting paid only half their salaries, “the government employee is working just two or three days a week, because he hasn’t got enough to come in for his full hours,” he added. As a result, the hospital ends up covering emergency cases only.
“At first, [patients] were [angry]. But now everyone understands: Everyone’s suffering,” Dari said.
The medical supplies crisis in Beit Jala and across the West Bank is the result of Israel’s withholding of tax revenues earmarked for the PA, an action spearheaded by Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.
“This crisis is very predictable, and we saw it coming 100 percent,” said Milena Ansari of Physicians for Human Rights Israel. Even before the genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023, Israel was periodically withholding tax revenues, endangering the Ministry of Health’s coffers, Milena said.
According to Yosef Ojra, an internal medicine specialist at Beit Jala, the withheld revenues have depleted the Health Ministry’s funds to pay medical suppliers, who are now withholding their services. The ongoing borrowing of supplies between the public and private arms of healthcare has greatly strained private clinics, pharmacies and hospitals.
Hisham Amle, an oncologist at the hospital, said shortages are “an old problem, not a new one”, but that about 90 percent of important items – for chemotherapy, above all – used to be there. Now, even immunotherapies and biologics are missing, and cancer treatment runs on an unbroken chain. “If the patient misses a session or two, he’s lost all the treatment before it,” he said.
“When I first took over the department, the drugs were available,” said Atwan, the lead oncology nurse. He then began to list all the crucial drugs he was now missing for his patients. “There’s not one single complete protocol I’ve got.”
Khuloud Dweib, the hospital’s director of pharmacy, said the ministry recently managed to obtain eight previously missing oncology drugs and four biologics. This should be enough for between a month and a half and two months. But many other drugs are still out of stock, she said.
Unlike in Gaza, Israel is not blocking medicines from entering the West Bank, Ansari noted. The problem is “strictly” that the PA has no money to buy them. But “Israel has the primary legal obligation as an occupying power,” she notes, to ensure adequate medical care and access to occupied populations.
Denied movement, denied care
For all of the southern West Bank, Beit Jala’s hospital is the only public option available for cancer and dialysis treatment, with patients coming from Bethlehem and Hebron governorates, parts of occupied East Jerusalem and sometimes Jericho.
But as Israeli checkpoints and gates multiply, reaching the hospital has become a nightmare. Dari described a dialysis patient from Nahalin, with an appointment at seven or eight in the morning, whose village was sealed. “He sat about four, five hours at the checkpoint,” Dari said. Then he took the long way round, through Jaba, Surif, Halhul and Hebron, and reached the unit at four in the afternoon. A normal journey costs about 10 shekels. “A detour like this costs more than 100 shekels,” Dari said, and some patients need dialysis four times a week.
The ministry’s central supply warehouse, meanwhile, is in Nablus, Dweib said – and an hour-and-a-half drive can now take six to 10 hours when closures hit.
Often, Atwan’s patients require treatments split between his unit and the Augusta Victoria Hospital in occupied East Jerusalem. Before the war, cancer patients from the West Bank routinely received medical permits to enter Jerusalem. Some treatments are in Beit Jala, while others are only available in East Jerusalem. But there are no guarantees any more that patients can reach Jerusalem. “I’ve got a cancer patient … He waited on a referral, and there’s no treatment, and after all the running around it comes back he’s security-rejected, too,” Atwan said. “I mean, he doesn’t get a permit to go to [Augusta Victoria]? Where’s he supposed to go?”
Atwan recalled patients who became neutropenic due to missed treatment sessions, and one was lucky not to end up with sepsis. “These are disasters.”
He’s not sure exactly how many cancer patients he’s lost due to missed and incomplete treatments; many of the poorer patients, he said, simply go home and die there.
‘I’ve started cutting back, not taking much’
As crowds swell at front desks and people wait at the hospital’s entrance, a nervous exhaustion percolates through the hospital’s aged halls. “People are really tense. Everyone’s scared,” Dari said.
Atwan, who receives half his salary, struggles to cover his commute from Hebron and help support his daughters at university.
“Let’s not talk about our state of mind – we’ll start crying, for God’s sake,” said Atwan. “Our morale is at rock bottom … We smile in spite of ourselves.”
Amid mass unemployment with labour permits systematically revoked, more sick Palestinians are pushed towards public hospitals just as those hospitals have less to give. Hospitals “will prioritise someone who will actually pay them”, Ansari added.
Ahmed, a Palestinian from Bethlehem with a medical degree, would check every couple of days with the pharmacist to see if they had Humira, an injection every two weeks that his sister with Crohn’s disease needs. For three months, the pharmacists were out of stock. Buying directly from the pharmaceutical company would cost about 2,000 shekels ($650) for one or two injections. “We couldn’t afford that,” he said. “So we just struggled until it became available again.”
The elderly cancer patient from a village facing settler pogroms has cut back on his own medication. “It’s not supplied regularly,” he said. A course of it costs 20,000 shekels ($6,500). “I’ve started cutting back, not taking much,” he added.
Amid supply and staffing shortages, surgery backlogs have piled up. Sayed Ayyad, 22, from al-Eizariya, fell during an accident, fracturing his ankle badly last month. With serious operations taking priority, he waited three weeks for a slot.
“They told me there’s 60 people waiting for an operation,” he said. “One day we couldn’t do the surgery because there were no medicines, no painkillers, no anaesthetic, nothing.”
Fates left to chance
Khuloud Dweib, who heads the pharmacy department at Beit Jala, has to manage the worsening crisis as patients struggle with their health and finances. “There’s no security. We don’t have political, or health, or even financial security,” she said.
She’s left thinking of cases like a young man with multiple sclerosis studying medicine in Egypt. The Health Ministry used to provide his medicine through private purchase until the company stopped supplying without payment. His mother came to see her. “I want to sell my house so I can get the injection for my son,” the mother told her. “Because he’s in Egypt, away from home, studying, and … he’s stopped seeing, stopped walking.”
“So, what can I tell you,” Dweib said, fighting back the tears. “God help people.”
The medical staff fear that with their supplies being hollowed out, they could face a similar fate to their colleagues in Gaza who have been kidnapped or killed.
“We know that at any moment we could be targeted as medical staff, just because we’re medical personnel providing services to people,” Dweib said. “We’re a father and a mother in this society.”
Nobody in the ageing hospital wards sees an end in sight. “The longer we stay, the worse the situation gets,” said Dari.
At three o’clock each afternoon, Atwan has to leave in the hope that he can reach Bab az-Zawiya in Hebron, where he waits for a shared taxi.
“Maybe there’ll be a checkpoint for me, maybe there won’t be,” he said. It’s not so different from the conundrums his patients face. “When a patient gets sick, it’s his luck if the medicine’s there,” he said. “We’ve got no future. I swear: We’ve got no future.”

Sudan’s army claims dozens of RSF fighters killed in Nyala attack
Rapid Support Forces accuse army of killing 30 civilians in attack on Nyala’s busy livestock market.
The Sudanese army says it has killed dozens of fighters from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in a series of air attacks on the southwestern city of Nyala, but the paramilitary group says the military has killed civilians.
The targets of Friday’s attack were RSF positions and command centres in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur state and the seat of the paramilitary group’s self-declared administration, the army said in a statement.
However, the RSF said the army carried out a drone attack on a busy livestock market, killing 30 civilians, including 17 women and five children.
The group has not confirmed or denied whether separate attacks by the army killed some of its fighters and destroyed its command centres.
Separately, the human rights group Emergency Lawyers said in a post on X that a market was hit on Friday in Nyala and the drone used was “affiliated” with the Sudanese army.
Reporting from the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, Al Jazeera’s Almigdad Alruhaid said on Saturday that the fighting between the army and RSF has “intensified”.
“In South Kordofan, a source in the Sudanese government told Al Jazeera that the RSF carried out drone attacks on mining sites with the exchange in fire intensifying in many parts of Sudan in the past 24 hours.”
The army has repeatedly targeted the Darfur region in western Sudan with drones to try to retake territory controlled by the RSF, which holds most of the area.
This month, Sudanese military chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan promised to seize “every inch” of territory under RSF control.
The Sudanese civil war began in 2023 and has killed tens of thousands of people. The United Nations has described the situation in Sudan as the world’s worst humanitarian crisis.

Student activist Neha Bora, a prominent face of the protests, was also detained Friday as she tried to reach central Delhi with dozens of supporters. She was released Saturday.

Dipke was detained Friday as he left a house in central Delhi. Police forced him into a police car and drove away after a brief argument.
Dipke had called Friday's protest in support of two CJP leaders who were detained and sent to jail for five days this week for demonstrating at a protest site in violation of a ban.
Earlier Friday, police had met with Dipke and warned him against proceeding with the protest.
The Cockroach movement has emerged as a significant source of political pressure on Modi and the BJP during the prime minister's 12 years in power.
A weeks-long sit-in by the movement's supporters earlier this year forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign over exam paper leaks.

Pope Leo cleared for discharge 4 days after lung cancer surgery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:42:00 UTC
18:42:00 KST

Pope Leo XIV will be discharged from the hospital Saturday, four days after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, and is expected to deliver his traditional noon blessing Sunday from a window overlooking St. Peter’s Square, the Vatican said.
The 71-year-old pope had the lower lobe of his right lung removed Tuesday after doctors identified a nodule suspected of being cancerous. The operation confirmed a diagnosis of adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.
His personal physician, Luigi Carbone, and surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, said in a statement released by the Vatican that blood tests, a chest X-ray performed Saturday morning and an assessment of his clinical condition showed he was fit to leave the hospital.
Leo is expected to return to the Vatican in the early afternoon, according to the statement.
The discharge comes earlier than the Vatican’s initial estimate of a weeklong hospital stay and follows several indications that the pope has been recovering well. His audiences had been canceled through Tuesday, but Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni said the timing of his release would depend on his medical team.
Leo disclosed his condition last Sunday during his traditional appearance before the faithful gathered in St. Peter’s Square, telling them that doctors had found a nodule in his lung that would need to be removed.
Since undergoing surgery, he has continued several official and religious activities from Rome’s Gemelli Hospital, including a telephone conversation with Russian President Vladimir Putin, meetings with senior aides and the celebration of Mass in the hospital chapel.
Medical updates from his physician and surgeon have described a positive postoperative recovery, saying Leo has been able to carry out his normal daily activities independently.
The Vatican released the first images of the pope since his surgery Friday, showing him standing at an altar in a hospital chapel wearing green liturgical vestments. Doctors said the latest tests confirmed his continued improvement.
Leo presided over the liturgy himself and distributed Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes attending the service, Bruni said.
During his homily, the pope thanked hospital staff for their daily work caring for sick people and for the attention they had given him during his treatment, Bruni said.
His recovery will be closely watched ahead of a planned trip to Latin America from Nov. 6-17. The journey, scheduled to begin about three weeks after his discharge, includes 12 flights and two helicopter trips.
The Vatican has signaled that preparations for the visit are continuing. On Friday, it published the names of journalists accredited to travel aboard the papal plane.
Oncology surgeons say patients can generally be cleared to fly about three weeks after surgery, provided their recovery allows it. Whether Leo will be fit for the demanding trip will depend on his continued progress and his doctors’ assessment.
Medical teams are still awaiting test results that will establish the cancer’s precise molecular and genetic characteristics, determine whether it has spread beyond the removed lung lobe and clarify whether further treatment will be necessary.

Repeated displacement leaves Gaza shelters deteriorating ahead of winter: IOM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:41:48 UTC
18:41:48 KST

Repeated displacement during three years of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has left shelters across the enclave increasingly deteriorated, while restrictions and funding shortages are hampering preparations for winter, a senior UN migration official said late Friday.
Karl Baker, regional crisis coordinator for the Gaza response at the International Organization for Migration (IOM), said some Palestinians have been displaced as many as eight times, damaging or destroying tents and other temporary shelters each time families are forced to move.
“When they move, all those goods that they currently have or did have either get destroyed, or they have to seek new shelter,” Baker told UN News.
Even basic materials such as tarpaulins need to be replaced roughly every six months, but humanitarian agencies have been unable to bring replacements into Gaza at the required scale, he said.
Baker said agencies now need to move beyond temporary solutions toward more durable transitional shelters.
Materials needed for stronger roofing, concrete floors, and more substantial walls, however, are affected by Israel’s “dual-use” restrictions over security concerns.
“After three years of war, we do need to improve the level of shelter which is inside, and move further away from temporary and more toward transitional type of shelter,” he said.
READ: Gaza residents face another winter amid shelter shortages, dwindling aid
Baker said IOM remains in constant contact with Israeli authorities, but some durable materials continue to be denied entry over security concerns.
He also cited funding shortages and disruptions to international shipping as obstacles, saying IOM relies on suppliers in countries including China, India, and Pakistan.
Although funding has begun to arrive, it remains insufficient to meet the needs of an estimated 1.8 million to 1.9 million people requiring shelter assistance, he added.
Baker said only around 30% of Gaza is currently accessible to most of the population, forcing displaced Palestinians into increasingly crowded and often flood-prone areas.
“The 30% in which they currently live is a very large displacement camp,” he said.
With winter rains already beginning, humanitarian organizations are working to address flood-prone areas and deploy water pumps, but Baker warned that getting displaced Palestinians through the winter would be the biggest challenge.
Earlier this month, IOM said available and incoming shelter supplies covered only 17% of Gaza’s winter needs, while more than half of tents and makeshift shelters were in poor condition.
A ceasefire has been in effect since Oct. 10, 2025, but Israeli attacks and restrictions on the entry of humanitarian and shelter supplies have continued.

IMF urges support for poorer nations facing high inflation, war spillovers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:31:47 UTC
18:31:47 KST

IMF urges support for poorer nations facing high inflation, war spillovers
Low-income countries spend up to 14 percent of their revenue on debt repayments, IMF chief says.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has a responsibility to help poorer nations struggling with rising debt, high inflation and price shocks caused by war spillovers, the head of the global lender says.
Speaking as the IMF’s annual meetings in Bangkok wrapped up on Saturday, Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said discussions with global policymakers showed both “optimism and worry”.
“Optimism from the resilience of the global economy, the promise of AI, the dynamism of Asia,” Georgieva told reporters. “But AI is also recognised to be a source of worry and so are inflation, high levels of debt, wars, climate risks.”
Georgieva said vulnerable nations are missing out on the AI investment boom that is driving growth in richer countries while at the same time dealing with higher borrowing costs.
Higher global interest rates mean low-income countries now spend 8 to 14 percent of their revenue on debt repayments, up from previous years, she said.
“I can tell you that people everywhere, but especially in poorer countries, don’t like inflation. Inflation is like a tax on the poor,” Georgieva said.
The warnings came as low-income, oil-importing countries take the strongest hit from rising global energy costs. Prices have soared since February when the United States and Israel launched a war on Iran, leading to retaliatory strikes in the Middle East and disrupted oil and gas flows.
“Escalating conflicts and trade tensions could further disrupt critical trade routes, exacerbate commodity price pressures, including in refined energy products, and worsen energy and food security,” said a statement issued by Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, the chairman of the International Monetary and Financial Committee (IMFC).
The IMFC is the main steering committee for the 191-member crisis lender.
Debt relief and regional support
Georgieva said her organisation has a responsibility to help countries restructure debt if needed to assist with domestic resource mobilisation, bring in international finance and create conditions for private investment.
Such countries need to set spending targets that prioritise growth and protect the most vulnerable people, she said, adding that the IMF has a “relentless pursuit of more resources for low-income countries”.
“When we do our best, it translates into better lives for people,” she said.
Georgieva also said the IMF plans to back Iraq “very firmly” with a requested loan programme while talks with Lebanese authorities are making progress.
“We will get to Iraq both money and policy support,” she said. “In the case of Lebanon, we are in very intense discussions with Lebanese authorities. We have made significant progress towards the programme. We have still a bit more work to do together, and I’m confident we will be successful.”

India's 'cockroach' movement founder arrested after detention

Dipke was arrested to prevent a breach of the peace and will be called before a Special Executive Magistrate on Saturday, broadcasters NDTV and India Today said.
Delhi police did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment.
The youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), opposition groups and student organisations have held near-daily protests this month demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation over a revision of voter lists that they say favours Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
More than 130 million voters were deleted during the revision. The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol.
The BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Student activist Neha Bora, a prominent face of the protests, was detained on Friday as she tried to reach central Delhi with dozens of supporters and released on Saturday.
"Please, spare the people of India. Impeach Gyanesh Kumar and halt SIR (special intensive revision), so that the ordinary citizens of this country can breathe a sigh of relief, feel at ease, and have their voting rights ensured," Bora told ANI news agency after she was released.
Dipke was detained on Friday as he stepped out of a house in central Delhi, with police hauling him into a police car and driving away after a brief argument.
Dipke had called Friday's protest in support of two CJP leaders detained and sent to jail this week for five days for demonstrating at a protest site in violation of a ban.
Earlier on Friday, police met Dipke and warned him against proceeding with the protest.
The cockroach movement has emerged as one of the biggest political challenges Modi and the BJP have faced in the prime minister's 12 years in power.
A weeks-long sit-in by supporters of the movement earlier this year forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign over exam paper leaks.

Iran-backed Houthis strike Yemen’s Aden: What that means
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:16:48 UTC
18:16:48 KST

Houthis strike Yemen’s Aden: What that means
Armed group has hit the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the city’s airport as war spreads across the region.
The Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), have fired missiles at the presidential palace in the southern Yemeni city of Aden, killing five people and wounding 16, on Thursday.
On Friday, two missiles landed on the grounds of Aden International Airport as a passenger plane prepared to take off for Cairo.
After the Houthis seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, in 2014, the internationally recognised government of Yemen decamped to Aden with the backing of a Saudi-led coalition of Arab countries.
The latest attacks come as Yemen’s war, largely frozen under a 2022 truce, has reignited and become another front in the wider regional conflict involving Iran.
So what has happened in Aden, and why does it matter?
Here’s what you need to know:
What happened at Maashiq Palace?
The Houthis hit the Al-Maashiq Presidential Palace with five missiles, according to Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani.
Health Minister Qasem Buhaibeh said the dead and wounded included guards and civilian employees.
The government said Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani and other officials were safe, but two of his bodyguards had been killed.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had struck what he called the “Saudi military operations headquarters” in Aden.
What happened at the airport?
On Friday, two missiles landed on the airport’s grounds, according to the Aden Security Department, which blamed the Houthis. It said it was the second attack on the facility in less than a week.
Yemenia Flight 612 to Cairo was preparing for takeoff. Al-Eryani said the missiles landed about 500 metres (1,600ft) from the aircraft. No casualties were reported.
Al-Eryani called the strike “a direct threat to the lives of passengers and aviation crews”.
The Houthi-run Saba agency claimed the group was targeting a military headquarters and weapons depots inside Badr Camp, a military site next to the airport.
Why are attacks on Aden significant?
Aden is the interim capital of Yemen.
The government moved there after the Houthis took control of the capital, Sanaa, by force in 2014 and later imposed their own government.
The al-Maashiq Palace is the internationally recognised government’s headquarters and its seat of power.
The Houthis currently control much of the country’s north and west. Fighting between the Houthis and a Saudi coalition supporting the government had largely ended following a 2022 ceasefire.
But in September, the Houthis launched a lightning offensive along the Red Sea coast, seizing territory overlooking the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea. Nearly two weeks ago, government forces launched a counteroffensive dubbed “Operation Dawn of Yemen” with Saudi air support, but have so far failed to reverse those gains.
Saree said the Houthi attacks on Aden were part of the group’s declared policy of targeting “Saudi reinforcements wherever they were located”.
The city has been hit before.
In December 2020, an attack on Aden airport as a new cabinet arrived from Saudi Arabia killed at least 22 people.
A second attack hit the palace where ministers had been taken to safety. The coalition blamed the Houthis, who denied responsibility.
What reaction has there been?
On Thursday, Rayed Krimly, Saudi Arabia’s deputy minister for public diplomacy, blamed Iran for having “encouraged” the escalation.
He said the Iran-backed Houthis had rejected an offer to meet for talks in Oman when the latest round of hostilities began.
Tehran denied the claim on Friday. “The Islamic Republic of Iran rejects any claim that Iran has played a role in Yemeni (Houthi) operations,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said.
Baghaei said Iran “has always been ready to use its good offices to help end the hostilities”, offering again to mediate.
Canada’s embassy in Saudi Arabia condemned the palace attack and called for “an immediate de-escalation of hostilities”.
“We stand in solidarity with the internationally recognised Government of Yemen and the Yemeni people,” the Canadian embassy in Saudi Arabia said in a post on X.
On Thursday, the United Nations Security Council condemned escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including those affecting civil aviation and energy infrastructure.
The governing council of the UN’s International Civil Aviation Organization also condemned recent attacks on civilian airports and aircraft in Saudi Arabia.
On October 9, Hans Grundberg, the UN special envoy for Yemen, told the UNSC the country had slid back into “full-scale war”.
What is happening in the wider conflict?
Fighting resumed in July, ending a 2022 truce.
Last month, the Houthis took control of the Bab al-Mandeb strait, one of the world’s most important waterways. Since the Strait of Hormuz was closed by Iran in March amid US strikes, Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on sending oil exports to the Red Sea via its East-West pipeline instead. The Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi ships there earlier in the year.
On October 4, Rashad al-Alimi, president of the Presidential Leadership Council, announced Operation Dawn of Yemen to retake Houthi-held territory, including Sanaa.
The Saudi-led coalition said 100 fighter jets took part, its first acknowledgement since 2022 that it had resumed air attacks on the Houthis.
The Houthis, in turn, have repeatedly fired missiles and drones at Saudi airports, oil facilities and other infrastructure.
On Friday, the coalition said it intercepted a ballistic missile headed for Yanbu, a Red Sea oil hub which Saudi Arabia has been using to export crude.
On the ground, fighting has intensified in Taiz governorate, where the Houthis have been holding the city of Taiz under siege, and which borders the Red Sea. State-run Saba media outlet, citing the Taiz Axis military command, reported that 168 Houthi fighters had been killed and 210 wounded there.
In Houthi-held areas, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said 124 civilians had been killed and 327 wounded in what it called “Saudi aggression” since September 3.
Early on Saturday, Houthi-affiliated media reported attacks east of Saada, with the coalition saying it had destroyed two ballistic missile launchers there.

Former Haitian President Joseph Michel Martelly registered online Friday as a presidential candidate for the upcoming election, bringing the total number of registered contenders to 16, The Haitian Times reported.
Martelly registered under Debloke, a political coalition that includes former members of the Haitian Tet Kale Party (PHTK), which he once led. His registration remains preliminary pending document submission and approval by Haiti’s Provisional Electoral Council (CEP).
The move follows an Oct. 6 amendment to the electoral decree that removed a requirement for candidates to submit a certificate from the Bank of the Republic of Haiti. The change eased a hurdle for individuals affected by sanctions, although US sanctions remain a potential barrier for designated candidates.
Sanctions, backlash and election delays
Martelly is not on the UN sanctions list, but UN experts have accused him of helping finance armed groups and benefiting from illicit activities. He has denied the allegations. Canada sanctioned him in November 2022, the US in August 2024, and the EU in December 2025 over allegations including gang financing and drug trafficking.
Martelly returned to Haiti on July 15 after spending years abroad. His potential political comeback has drawn criticism from Haitians at home and overseas, with concerns about his record and the strength of the opposition.
“As I always say, the most important thing was not to let him register, but everyone stayed silent,” Ronmdy Francois, a young auto mechanic, told The Haitian Times.
“However, from what I’m hearing, if it’s true that he has registered, then he is already president because I don’t see which candidate could stop him.”
No major political leaders had publicly supported or condemned his candidacy as of publication, according to The Haitian Times.
The election process faces persistent insecurity fueled by gang violence and technical challenges. The campaign, initially scheduled to begin on Thursday, has been postponed, while candidate registration has been extended through Oct. 31. The CEP has pledged to issue a revised electoral calendar.
As of Friday, the CEP had recorded 16 presidential candidates, 302 Senate candidates, and 1,050 candidates for the Chamber of Deputies. Registration and document submissions began Aug. 20.

All affected children received hospital treatment or home-based nutritional intervention, and by July 20, 2025, most had completed their first course of treatment and been discharged from the hospital.

Israeli settlers burn olive trees, attack 8 farmers in West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:12:00 UTC
18:12:00 KST

Masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian farmers in the occupied West Bank on Friday, burning olive trees, throwing stones and injuring residents and an American photojournalist as violence escalated during the annual harvest season.
About 80 settlers dressed in black descended on a terraced olive grove above the village of Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah, where Palestinian residents had gathered to pick olives, according to Reuters witnesses. Some carried gas canisters, while others used slingshots to hurl stones at the farmers.
The villagers retreated down the hillside before some threw stones back at the attackers. Olive harvesting is an important annual tradition for Palestinian families and a vital source of income for many farming communities.
“The settlers want to attack us and force us from our homes,” said Moutaz Abdelhadi, 42, a farmer who witnessed the assault.
At least two Israeli military jeeps later sped through the area as villagers moved out of their path. Soldiers fired tear gas toward Palestinians, while the sound of live gunfire echoed across the area. A Reuters photographer saw at least one armed settler fire a gun.
The Israeli military said soldiers and border police officers deployed to the scene fired warning shots. It also acknowledged that troops fired toward a person they believed posed a threat.
“Attacks and violence against innocent civilians are grave and unacceptable,” the military said, adding that attempts to provoke tensions between communities undermined security.
The office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the incident was under investigation.
Heidi Levine, an American photojournalist working for The Washington Post, was among those injured in Abu Falah. Palestinian medics said at least two people were taken to hospitals in the Ramallah area.
Video of the attack showed Levine lying on a dirt path with her hands covering her face as at least three settlers stood around her.
Speaking from a hospital bed, Levine said the attackers pushed her to the ground and repeatedly kicked her.
“I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn't even be here, because they just kept kicking me and kicking me,” she said.
Levine said her Palestinian colleagues intervened before medics transported her by ambulance to a clinic in Abu Falah and then to a hospital in Ramallah.
The Washington Post later reported that she had suffered lacerations across her body and a broken rib. She also required surgery on one hand after a finger was torn open, exposing bone.
Matt Murray, the newspaper's executive editor, condemned the attack and called for a thorough investigation.
“This morning, a Washington Post photographer, Heidi Levine, was attacked by Israeli settlers while reporting in the West Bank,” Murray said.
He said Levine had been wearing visible markings identifying her as a journalist and urged authorities to investigate the assault and ensure accountability.
The U.S. State Department said it was deeply concerned about the harm suffered by an American citizen overseas and had contacted The Washington Post to offer consular assistance.
The department also condemned criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and supported holding those responsible accountable.
The assault in Abu Falah was part of a wider wave of settler violence reported across the occupied West Bank as Palestinians began their annual olive harvest.
Local officials and the Palestine Red Crescent Society reported attacks in at least eight villages in the northern West Bank, where many of the territory's olive groves are concentrated.
The Red Crescent said its medics had treated 14 injured people, while local officials reported at least four injuries.
Palestinian officials said at least four Palestinians had been killed and more than 100 injured since the harvest season began earlier in October. They also reported damage to thousands of olive trees.
In Turmus Ayya, another village near Ramallah, settlers attacked farmers harvesting olives and burned three cars, according to local accounts.
Salah Abu Niswa, who witnessed the attack, said the assailants approached the farmers before targeting someone who was alone.
“They snuck up like thieves, they caught someone by himself and began to beat him,” he said.
Yesh Din, an Israeli organization that monitors settlement activity and settler violence, reported at least 170 attacks against Palestinians since Sept. 27, around the beginning of the olive harvest.
The organization’s figures highlight the risks facing Palestinian farmers during a season that is central to their livelihoods and cultural traditions. Attacks on farmers, damage to trees and restrictions on access to groves can threaten both current harvests and future income.
Residents and rights groups have accused Israeli authorities of failing to adequately prevent the assaults or hold perpetrators accountable. Settler violence has intensified this year, with a further increase reported in the weeks leading up to Israel's Oct. 27 election.
Netanyahu has criticized settler violence, but his government has faced international criticism over its response. His right-wing coalition has overseen an expansion of Israeli settlements and smaller outposts across the West Bank.
The attacks have also drawn condemnation from some of Israel's longtime allies, including Britain, which has considered sanctions over settler violence.
About 500,000 Israeli settlers live alongside at least 3 million Palestinians in the West Bank. The United Nations and most countries consider Israeli settlements in the territory illegal under international law. Israel disputes that position and regards the territory as disputed rather than occupied.

Eight converted power stations that show the power of reuse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:00:30 UTC
18:00:30 KST

Eight converted power stations that show the power of reuse
In this roundup, we take a look at decommissioned power stations that have been given a second life, from the Tate Modern museum in London to the Dyson headquarters in Singapore.
Originally built to generate electricity, these industrial buildings typically have expansive interiors with tall ceilings, giving architects plenty of flexibility for conversion.
Battersea Power Station, UK, by WilkinsonEyre
The Grade II*-listed Battersea Power Station in London stood decommissioned for 39 years before architecture studio WilkinsonEyre's transformation reopened it as a shopping, office and residential building in 2022.
Originally built in the 1930s, a bustling shopping centre is now located in the building's restored turbine halls and glazed apartments were built atop the roof.
Find out more about Battersea Power Station ›
Ballers, USA, by Good City Studio and Hexagon Studio Architects
Local firms Good City Studio and Hexagon Studio Architects revamped the main turbine hall of Delaware Power Station in Fishtown, Philadelphia, into a sports club with indoor pickleball, soccer and squash courts.
Named Ballers, the sports club formed part of the wider plan to transform the 1920s power station into The Battery, a mixed-use complex containing apartments, offices and a hotel.
Dyson headquarters, Singapore, by M Moser Associates, W Architects and Studio Lapis
Technology company Dyson established its global company headquarters inside Singapore's St James Power Station, which was transformed by local studios W Architects and Studio Lapis, with interior fit-out by architecture studio M Moser Associates.
The turbine hall of the 1926 building was reimagined as a four-storey atrium framed by exposed black steelwork and a sculptural spiral staircase, while an area of amphitheatre-style seating provides gathering space next to a cafe.
Find out more about the Dyson headquarters ›
Tate Modern, UK, by Herzog & de Meuron
Iconic London landmark the Tate Modern was once the Bankside Power Station, originally designed by Giles Gilbert Scott, who also designed Battersea Power Station.
Swiss studio Herzog & de Meuron's pioneering transformation of the building opened in 2000, complete with a cathedral-like gallery space in the turbine hall, and ignited a global trend of converting disused power stations into hubs of art and culture.
Find out more about Tate Modern ›
Powerhouse Arts, USA, by Herzog & de Meuron
In more recent years, Herzog & de Meuron converted the remains of a 115-year-old power plant in Brooklyn into an art manufacturing hub called Powerhouse Arts.
The studio refurbished the brick-clad turbine hall, the only part of the original building left standing, and converted it into an art production centre, while the demolished Boiler House was rebuilt in red concrete.
Find out more about Powerhouse Arts ›
Shajing Village Hall, China, by ARCity Office
As part of wider plans to transform an industrial site into a public wetland, architecture studio ARCity Office restored and extended a 1980s power plant in Shenzhen, China, converting it into a community hub.
The studio left the building's concrete remnants as-found, using its structural shell to support a series of new steel and glass volumes that draw upon the spaces found in traditional ancestral halls.
Find out more about Shajing Village Hall ›
Global Leadership Centre, UK, by John McAslan + Partners
British studio John McAslan + Partners added learning space and accommodation to Oxford's first electrical power plant to form the Global Leadership Centre, designed for the University of Oxford's Saïd Business School.
John McAslan + Partners created a triple-height entrance and shared space in the turbine hall, restored the 1890s brick facades and rebuilt and extended the metal-clad upper levels.
Find out more about Global Leadership Centre ›
The former Philips power plant in Eindhoven was converted into an innovation hub housing a dozen businesses, with offices arranged along a communal street-like passage.
Rotterdam-based Atelier van Berlo worked with Eindhoven-based studios Eugelink Architectuur and De Bever Architecten on the project, aiming to celebrate the building's original features by preserving its structure and coal chutes.
Find out more about Innovation Powerhouse ›

Shisha smoking will cause 1 million new lung cancer cases globally by 2050: WHO study
Western Pacific region will bear the brunt of such cases, says Dr Mahdi Sheikh of International Agency for Research on Cancer
Water pipe smoking will contribute to about 1 million new lung cancer cases globally by 2050, with the Western Pacific region bearing the brunt, according to a study led by a World Health Organization (WHO) research agency that was recently presented in Hong Kong.
The study, which is yet to be published, was headed by Dr Mahdi Sheikh, a scientist of the early detection, prevention and infections branch at the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC). It estimated that there would be 82 million new lung cancer cases around the world between 2025 and 2050, with 944,700 or 1.1 per cent of them caused by water pipe smoking.
“One per cent does not seem a lot, but when you translate it into numbers, it’s 1 million cases – when we want to save lives, every life matters,” Sheikh told the South China Morning Post on the sidelines of the World Cancer Congress, which was held in Hong Kong for the first time in late September.
“Most of these countries have a low or medium human development index … it means that the burden is going to cluster in the countries with the least resources, which could bear the least burden of cancer.”

Microplastics React With Water, a New Study Says. That’s a Problem for Biology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

One of the reasons plastic has become so ubiquitous is that, generally, it’s very chemically stable, meaning it does not readily react with the substances around it. That’s why this material is so often used for food packaging and water bottles.
The same was thought to be true of microplastics—those tiny pieces of debris that break off from larger plastic objects and which, according to numerous studies, have spread to virtually every ecosystem on the planet. But scientists at Columbia University and UC Berkeley have just discovered that water can make the surfaces of microplastics chemically active and turn them into a potential hazard.
According to the findings of the article published in Nature, this activity can trigger the spontaneous formation of chemicals capable of altering other molecules, like those that are essential for living organisms. The phenomenon, the authors note, occurs even under normal environmental conditions, without the need for sunlight or other agents that cause plastic degradation.
So how can microplastics be so reactive when bigger plastics generally aren’t? The scientists suggest this has to do with the greater available surface area for these reactions to occur.
“As plastic fragments into smaller and smaller particles, its surface area increases enormously,” Wei Min, a professor of chemistry and biomedical engineering at Columbia University, said in a press release. “Then microplastics change the water that surrounds them, generating high-energy, reactive radicals that very likely contribute to biological damage that we see in animals and potentially in humans as a result of microplastic exposure.”
Among these potentially dangerous chemical products—called reactive oxygen species—a variety known as hydroxyl radicals stands out. They are particularly dangerous because they can snatch electrons from the proteins and fats that make up cell membranes, disrupting their structure and function. These “are textbook examples of the kinds of molecules that can damage animal and human tissue,” added Naixin Qian, a postdoctoral researcher in Min’s lab who helped lead the research.
Our body has some defenses against this kind of damage. This is the biological function of the buzzy molecules known as antioxidants. These neutralize the reactive chemicals, but if the reactive compounds greatly outnumber antioxidants, this line of defense can be overwhelmed.
This can develop into a scenario called oxidative stress, leading to the damage of cells. Previous research had already identified oxidative stress among the cellular responses associated with exposure to microplastics, although the mechanisms responsible for this damage are not yet fully understood.
The extent to which microplastics have pervaded our bodies remains an open debate, with some of the more sensational findings having been called into question. But if even a small amount of microplastics are present in our tissues, they could be reacting with the water in our bodies.
The researchers were particularly concerned with the potential effects on blood, which is largely composed of water. If contact with this fluid can chemically activate the surfaces of microplastics, their presence inside the body could pose an additional danger beyond that of the pollutants they carry or release.
When the researchers exposed red blood cells extracted from mice to different types of microplastics, the cells became deformed and ruptured—a phenomenon known as hemolysis. The effects were greater with plastics that were more reactive with water, indicating that this activity was the cause of cellular damage.
Research into the effects of microplastics has long focused on other chemicals leaching from the particles or on their physical effects, often considering the plastic itself chemically inert. The larger pieces generally are, but these findings challenge the assumption that what is true of plastic on a grand scale is also true of the microscopic pieces it breaks down into.

====================================================================================================

Why AI Isn’t Ready to Tackle Our Convoluted Genomes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.
Since its molecular structure was deduced in the 1950s, DNA has been hailed by many biologists as the secret of life. They’ve read and studied the information stored in the DNA found in the cells of living organisms, known as their genomes, and claimed that this genetic database must be some kind of blueprint, code script, or computer. But if DNA really does harbor some greater secret about how life works, biologists have yet to find it.
In fact, the human genome is less a script than a puzzle that gets harder the closer they look. Knowing the entire sequence—the order of all 3 billion or so of our DNA’s chemical building blocks, nearly fully deduced by the international Human Genome Project between 1990 and 2003—hasn’t helped much. That investigation showed that barely 2 percent of the human genome consists of actual genes, the information-coding sequences of DNA.
It’s now clear that understanding the human genome is no longer a matter of figuring out what each gene does. The deeper and much harder question is how those genes are used, or regulated, a question that seems to involve some and perhaps much of the rest of the genome. By switching suites of genes on and off, the many different cell types in our bodies can all be created from the same material. Cells also regulate their genes from moment to moment in response to a constant inflow of signals from their neighbors and surroundings. But the processes that govern gene regulation are proving so complex that some biologists wonder whether a full understanding of it—of how the genome really works—will ever be within the grasp of our puny minds.
Some are counting on outsourcing the analysis to artificial intelligence. Genomic “foundation models” such as Evo 2, Genos, and Google DeepMind’s AlphaGenome are trained on vast quantities of genomic data, which biologists use to make predictions about how differences in DNA sequence affect biological processes and ultimately the traits (including disease risk) of a whole organism. These algorithms don’t worry about the complicated regulatory stuff going on. All of that is supposedly subsumed by the algorithm’s “training,” through which it deduces correlations from cases we already know about.
This approach is likely to be useful, but for those who crave real understanding of how the genome, and ultimately life itself, works, a computational black box will never suffice. And perhaps more to the point, the genome might not submit to the kind of straightforward input-output approach that such AI models ultimately assume.
That’s because the genome is no blueprint or algorithm. It’s something else.
Given that it’s the product of around 4 billion years of evolution, perhaps it’s not surprising that our genome is complicated. The surprise has been what those complications are. “Our genome is not what we might make it if we sat down at the drawing board,” said the biologist Karen Adelman, who studies gene regulation at Harvard Medical School.
The traditional view posits that a small proportion of our DNA holds the code for making the protein molecules that orchestrate our cells’ chemistry. Each instruction for a protein is held in a corresponding gene—we have around 20,000 of these—and gene sequences can range in length from a couple of dozen to almost 3 million DNA “letters” (representing molecules called nucleotides).
Making a protein from its gene is a two-stage affair. First the DNA is read, letter by letter, by an enzyme called a polymerase, which creates a copy of that code in a related molecule called messenger RNA (mRNA). This is called transcription. The mRNA is then read by a piece of molecular machinery called the ribosome, which constructs the protein—a process called translation. The proteins made by the ribosome then go off to do their jobs in making and sustaining the organism.
This picture is still more or less correct. But it turns out that “the genes are probably not the most interesting part of the genome,” Adelman said.
What matters more is how our genes, many of which we share with simpler organisms, are regulated—turned on and off. Which proteins a cell needs changes over time and according to cell type: muscle, brain, skin, and so on. How the genes that encode those proteins are regulated depends on some of the genome that doesn’t code for proteins.
Biologists have known about gene regulation, and the involvement of “noncoding” DNA, since the 1960s. But for many years, most of what they understood about this came from studies of simple organisms like bacteria, where the principles are generally straightforward. It has gradually become clear, though, that in complex eukaryotic organisms like us, gene regulation is far more complicated, involving overlapping systems of oversight and control, each with its own intricacies.
Transcription gets started by proteins called transcription factors, which are like the operations managers of gene regulation. These proteins stick to sections of DNA (typically close to the target gene) and recruit the polymerase enzyme to make an mRNA copy. In bacteria, transcription factors are rather like keys that fit the locks of unique binding sites on DNA. But that’s not how they work in complex organisms. In us, the logic of transcription factors is more difficult to parse.
For one thing, our transcription factors don’t show strong preferences for particular DNA binding sites. What’s more, they tend to work in pairs or groups. And a given transcription factor might have different effects in different contexts, such as activating gene transcription in one cell type but suppressing it in another, depending on which other transcription factors are around.
In bacteria, regulation tends to have an “OR” logic, Adelman said, whereby a particular signal turns a gene on or off: It’s either this or that. But in the human genome the logic is more like what computer scientists designate “AND.” Many signals are integrated to reach a regulatory decision: This and that and also that other thing. In this case, regulation can be more responsive to nuances of context, and the regulatory knobs are tunable rather than being just on or off. “This is part of the beauty” of our regulatory complexity, Adelman said.
When they interact with the genome, transcription factors bind to pieces of DNA called enhancers—which present a puzzle of their own.
Enhancers are gathering points for transcription factors, and they are thought to be the decisive influence on transcription: They deliver the “go” signal for a waiting polymerase to make an mRNA version of the DNA sequence. Seems simple enough, but mapping enhancers to their respective genes is far from straightforward. Our genome has hundreds of thousands, perhaps millions, of enhancers. That means we have many more of them than we have genes. Each gene might be influenced by many enhancers, and each enhancer might influence multiple genes.
“It’s embarrassing that 25 years after the Human Genome Project, we don’t know where all the enhancers are in the genome, let alone what they do when they act and which genes they control,” said Wendy Bickmore, a genome biologist at the University of Edinburgh.
Biologists do know that most enhancers won’t respond to a single transcription factor. Their activation “requires a cocktail,” Bickmore said. “That’s what gives [an enhancer] that exquisite specificity—because it’s only in a particular cell at a particular time that you have the right combination of factors to bind and activate that enhancer.”
Some enhancers are, as you’d expect, close to the genes they regulate, or even sit on DNA inside a gene. But others sit far away from the gene—perhaps millions of nucleotides away, with more genes in between.
The existence of such so-called “distal” enhancers “seems bonkers,” Bickmore said. “How do you get that information from over there to over here, to the gene that needs to be activated? That’s a largely unanswered question.”
One of the answers comes in the form of a loop.
Distal enhancers are brought to the gene they regulate on great loops of DNA or, more strictly, of chromatin, the combination of DNA and its packaging proteins that are unraveled as if from a ball of wool. The loops are created by a protein motor called cohesin, which runs up and down the DNA strand and extrudes it as needed.
Once cohesin has formed a loop to bring elements together, what then? It was once thought that they then stick together or assemble into a molecular machine, but they don’t. Rather, the components appear to form a loose but dense blob in which they interact rather weakly, fleetingly, and indiscriminately—a sort of committee, sometimes called a condensate.
These transcription hubs are extremely fluid and differ from one cell to another. “There’ll be a bit of loop extrusion going on over here, in the next cell it might be over here, and the whole thing is turning over incredibly fast,” Bickmore said. Even if the cells are notionally identical—both skin cells, say—exactly what the gene-regulatory machinery is up to at any moment is never quite the same in any two of them.
Chromatin loops are just one reason why a gene’s transcription depends on the shape and structure of the chromatin around it.
The textbook image of a chromosome—one of the 46 units into which our genomes are divided—is of a compact, X-shaped cluster of chromatin. But any time a cell is not actively dividing, its chromatin is unwound into what looks like a tangled mess. There is order to the chaos, however. Some parts of chromatin are densely packed into a form called heterochromatin. The compacted DNA there is relatively inaccessible to transcription factors; the genes it contains are typically silenced. Meanwhile, other parts are relatively loose, open, and accessible: This is called euchromatin.
There are special enzymes involved in packaging and repackaging chromatin, thereby controlling transcription. In other words, what matters is not just the encoded information in the DNA but also how it exists physically and dynamically in space. “We’ve stopped thinking about the genome as a linear piece of DNA code,” Bickmore said. “Thinking about this incredibly dynamic three-dimensional folding as absolutely inherent to regulation is a very exciting change.”
One aspect of this 3D organization is the clustering of segments of chromatin into compartments called topologically associating domains (TADs). Within a TAD, the genes seem to be coregulated: switched on or off in groups. Such groups keep suites of genes active or silent together to form and provide function in different cell types. Cohesin is also involved in the shuffling of chromatin to construct TADs—a dynamic process in which the chromatin is constantly rearranged in our cells.
Chromatin shape can also be influenced by chemical modifications called epigenetic marks: small molecules attached to DNA packaging proteins called histones or stuck directly to DNA. Some of these epigenetic modifications can alter the electrical charges on histones, which changes how the proteins attract or repel one another and so rejigs the chromatin packing. Epigenetic modifications to chromatin are like annotations of the DNA script that change its meaning in a given context. When cells divide, the epigenetic annotations are copied, too.
How and when the marks get added and changed, and what each type of mark means for gene activity, are complex questions with no simple answers. Some researchers talk of an “epigenetic code” governing this aspect of gene regulation, but it’s far from clear if anything so systematic really exists.
All of these processes and others can determine whether a gene gets transcribed into mRNA. But there are further layers of regulation that determine whether the mRNA is then translated into a corresponding protein—and which protein arises.
This post-transcriptional regulation is often controlled by RNA molecules that are said to be noncoding. These short-lived molecules aren’t templates for proteins, as mRNA is, but have other jobs of their own. While mRNA is produced from the protein-coding areas of DNA (so-called “coding genes”), noncoding RNAs are transcribed from other DNA regions now generally described as noncoding genes. These noncoding RNAs are versatile, taking on varied roles in a cell. Researchers are learning more about what they can do every day, and many if not most of them seem to be involved in gene regulation.
Small noncoding RNAs called microRNAs, for example, can silence mRNAs before they can be translated into proteins. They do this by guiding special enzymes to a particular mRNA to degrade or chemically modify it. The microRNAs don’t do this job alone but, not unlike transcription factors, act combinatorially, in groups, and in a rather promiscuous manner: A given microRNA might regulate many mRNAs, and a given mRNA might be regulated by many microRNAs.
Why make an mRNA only to stop it getting translated in a protein? This sort of post-transcriptional regulation is like having another checkpoint: Does the cell really need this protein? MicroRNAs can be mobilized to allow cells to adjust gene expression depending on the immediate context. In this way, the workings of the genome are less like a program’s inevitable progression and more like an adaptive and responsive process.
Another post-transcriptional complication is that mRNAs get translated to protein only after they have been reorganized. Fresh from transcription, an mRNA contains sequences that encode bits of protein, called exons, as well as sequences that shouldn’t be translated and need to be snipped out, called introns. (Strictly speaking, this pre-edited RNA is called pre-mRNA.) The job of editing introns out and splicing exons together is done by a molecular assembly called the spliceosome, which is made from several proteins together with various noncoding RNAs.
The spliceosome too can be sensitive to context, so that it might splice the pre-mRNA to encode one protein in one cell type and a slightly different protein in another. Sometimes these different protein “isoforms” can have very different roles. Transcription factors, for example, are often alternatively spliced in this way, and their isoforms can take on different regulatory tasks—some might activate gene expression, for instance, while others repress it.
All told, these and other regulatory mechanisms show that the genome is far from some automated program running in the background to build us and keep us alive. Our cells are, in effect, making complex decisions about how to use their genes—both the information they contain and the structure they assume.
Thus, cells need to assemble a rather loose and fuzzy committee of components, such as transcription factors and enhancers, to get transcription underway, which also depends on how the chromatin strand is shaped and molded at that moment. Then there are further layers of decisionmaking and action-taking in between mRNA and the final, functional protein.
Remember, too, that all the players—from transcription factors to noncoding RNAs—are themselves produced from the genome in the same kind of context-dependent process. That makes the genome rather like a recursive, self-referential system that the computer scientist Douglas Hofstadter dubbed “a strange loop.” It acts on itself, mindful of its own history—which determines chromatin conformation and epigenetic markings, say—and heedful of messages from inside and outside the cell. Not, then, a blueprint.
And for that reason, not at all easy to understand. “I wouldn’t have designed it this way if I was God,” Bickmore said. “But here we are!”
Why is gene regulation in animals like us so darned complicated? One potential answer is that evolution doesn’t have the foresight to design with efficiency and transparent logic, but merely tinkers with what it has already available. Maybe so—but eukaryotic gene regulation isn’t just a messy version of what happens in bacteria. It has different principles, and there’s surely a reason for them.
Bickmore suspects that the complexity of regulation and of genome organization might have been the only means of generating complexity in the organism. For example, organisms with many tissue types and varied lifestyles required more control over which genes were on or off in a given cell. One thing this demanded was more and more noncoding regulatory sequences in DNA. But then they couldn’t all fit close to the gene itself.
“As you get more complexity, you need to add more and more enhancers,” Bickmore said. “But where are you going to put them? You start to put them farther and farther away. Once they are [far enough], you start to need TADs and three-dimensional [chromatin] folding to allow those things to work.”
We also need regulatory complexity because, over evolutionary time, the human genome has accumulated DNA from parasitic viruses in the form of jumping genetic material called transposable elements. These sequences have inserted themselves all over our chromosomes and are good at replicating themselves. To sift the good DNA from the bad, we needed additional layers of regulation to ensure that cells weren’t translating RNAs they don’t really need or that could be actively harmful.
With so many context-dependent checks and balances in the workings of our genome, it is evidently not a program or algorithm that predictably generates the same outcome in every situation. It’s an open informational system that responds to external inputs and the genome’s dynamic internal conditions. This poses a challenge if AI relies solely on the genetic sequences within genomes to predict what genomes will do.
Researchers Developing AI-based genomic foundation models, such as AlphaGenome, hope that all these layers of regulation—transcription factors, splicing, epigenetic marks, loops, chromatin packing, and so on—will be implicitly included in the correlations that the algorithms learn between genetic sequence and organismal traits. They’re content for the complexity described above to be in a black box, so long as the model generates accurate predictions. But will that work?
“I’m sure [AlphaGenome] is going to be useful, but with limitations,” Bickmore said. “To me the big gap is in the complexity of the human body—in all the cell types and how they change over time in development. And all that data is missing.”
Fundamentally, the challenge is that the genome is not a set of static, linear instructions. It is highly dynamic, and it uses its information contextually, with combinatorial and promiscuous logic. “Whether we’ll ever be able to capture that aspect” in algorithms like AlphaGenome, “I don’t know,” she said.
Yet the problem goes even deeper because the functioning of specific organisms, including each of us, doesn’t just depend on genomes. Other factors, such as diet, environment, microbiome, and, for us at least, culture, can matter hugely, too—not just in terms of how we act and how healthy we are but also in the state of our genome itself. The biologist Adrian Woolfson, cofounder of California-based biotech company Genyro, which aims to use AI systems for so-called “generative biology,” calls this information cloud the “informiome.”
“While the human genome forms the foundation of the human informiome, other layers of extra-genetic information are equally important,” Woolfson wrote in his book On the Future of Species, published in April 2026. Genomic foundation models won’t even be able to predict all the consequences of genetic mutations, he argued, because the relevant information is not in the genome sequence in the first place.
So how should we think about the genome? Maybe the only metaphors that can capture the way the genome really works must come from biology itself. In 2020, the biological historian Evelyn Fox compared the genome to “an exquisitely sensitive reactive system.” Rather than a sequence of genes leading to the formation of traits, she said, it’s more of “a device for regulating the production of specific proteins in response to constantly changing signals it receives from its environment.”
That sounds close to the picture painted by the geneticist Barbara McClintock in the address she delivered upon being awarded the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for her discovery of transposons. The genome, she declared, is “a highly sensitive organ of the cell, monitoring genomic activities and correcting common errors, sensing the unusual and unexpected events and responding to them, often by restructuring the genome.”
Research since that time has fleshed out this image, revealing how the shape of chromatin can matter as much as the information its DNA sequences encode and how an army of molecules collaborates to reorganize it and make collective decisions about how to use its genetic information in context-dependent ways. There is no human technology that works this way, so metaphors such as blueprints, programs, or computers will always fall short.
Bickmore is optimistic that the workings of the genome are understandable, despite its complexity. “We’ve got a handle on it now,” she said. “We might not know the details, but I think the whole field is coalescing now into a framework where we’re thinking along similar lines.” AI can surely help with this sense-making, but in the end, human reasoning will be needed to discern the fundamental principles.
“McClintock was far more on point than people realized at the time,” Adelman said. “What she said was that the genome isn’t static—it’s living.”
