Spinoza and Conatus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:51:26 UTC
16:51:26 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
In the cracks of paving stones, in crevices of distressed walls, a little dirt, blown in and moistened, provides enough sustenance for weeds to root.
I see climbing vines, bindweed, couch grass, bracken, and clumps of moss in the paving lines, delicate chickweed sprouting from damp cracks in the shade.
A leafy spurge sways as the breeze picks up. Oblivious of its precarious exposure, it stands defiantly erect from its concrete base. Its footing comprises minuscule and densely packed roots like rolled tobacco, snug in moist concrete burrows.
Taproots and robust networks of rhizomes worm through plastic barriers and crumbling, weathered brickwork in a multi-generational war of attrition that the weeds would always win.
None of these plants have any business to be there. They have no plan, no ambition. They simply persist to be what they are, and do so with everything they’ve got.
It’s astonishing how fast they rise from such meagre beginnings and flourish to the point that they bow under their own weight. A force of some kind is at work as if the conditions for life have a singular will. A build-up of dirt, moisture, a little sunlight and pockets safe from gusts of wind — whatever this force can get it takes.
It seems a pity to pull it all up. It would only take a matter of years if humans had been extracted from this city, that platlife would overgrow everything, like those lost cities swallowed by the Amazon.
Striving’s Purpose in Spinoza’s System
What is behind this relentless vitality? This endeavour that makes the most of what it has?
The seventeenth-century philosopher Baruch (Benedict) Spinoza conceptualised this as conatus, Latin for “striving”. For him it was the most fundamental force of all things—both living and inanimate.
In Spinoza’s philosophical system, everything is part of a oneness that he describes as “God or Nature” (Deus sive Natura). Ultimately, nothing is separate from an immanent God, who is not a divine engineer who set the cosmos in motion, but is in fact the cosmos itself — infinite and self-caused.
What we perceive to be parts of the cosmos are “modes” according to Spinoza. In his system, modes are temporary expressions of the one substance — the singular underlying reality that everything is made from — just as waves are an expression of the sea, or ripples are an expression of a river. The ripples and waves are all of the same substance — the river or the sea — they are part of a oneness.
And so people, animals, planets, and grains of sand are all modes of the same one substance.
But if all is part of a oneness, what explains change? Why isn’t everything just static? Why do trees grow, why do cells divide, why do people go about their business? We can explain these processes through science, but what, ultimately on a cosmic level, necessitates them?
Spinoza declares the answer in part three of his Ethics. “Each thing, as far as it can by its own power, strives to persevere in its being.” (Ethics III 6) Spinoza’s philosophy hinges on this notion — it serves to join together his ethics and his account of what reality is (his ontology).
Conatus isn’t a survival instinct; it isn’t something that modes do, and it’s not something added to modes — it’s not a feeling or a behaviour. His claim is that conatus is the essence of all things — everything that exists strives to maintain the integrity of what it is. This is true of rivers and meteorites as much as trees, cells, humans and tigers.
Existing isn’t a choice. Your body is automatically performing millions of tasks: your blood cells are pumped, filtered and manufactured in the marrow, your skin grows ceaselessly, thoughts fizz in your mind, melded together from memories, associations, conjectures. Your conatus is you being you; the striving integral to you.
Everything, to a greater or lesser extent, operates to preserve its being. Spinoza considers this to be a finite expression of the infinite power of God or Nature. If we to return to our metaphor, the wave has momentum but that momentum is a localised and limited power of the overall power of the sea of which it is a part.
Conatus, Ethics and Emotion
Conatus provides the basis for Spinoza’s theories of emotion and ethics. Value isn’t built into the universe itself and waiting to be discovered — it is registered only in the moment of need as something that helps or hinders conatus.
As sunlight and water nourishes a plant growing from the gap in paving stones, aspects of your life that bring you real strength will help you thrive, regardless of the conditions you find yourself in.
Because conatus is essence, everything that enables or expands your power to persist feels good, anything that limits that power feels bad.
When your power to persist increases you feel joy; when it diminishes, you feel sadness. From this simple correlation, we can extrapolate the whole complex of human emotions. Love is joy and the awareness of its external cause, hate is sadness and the awareness of its external cause.
We think of emotions as arising from our own choices. You may think that you simply want a slice of cake because it’s delicious, but your conatus sees that slice of cake as a means by which you can keep persisting.
You think you hate your colleague because they are untrustworthy and hold opinions contrary to yours, but your conatus sees your colleague as a factor in your life that diminishes your power.
But there is a problem with the concept, and we can perceive it in three interrelated aspects from obvious to not-so-obvious.
Firstly, cake isn’t particularly good for you, and your colleague isn’t deserving of hate. To desire sugary processed foods and hate people are unhealthy habits.
Secondly, conatus is committing Spinoza to egoism: it’s obvious that everything seeks advantage for itself, but what of altruism and sacrifice?
Following from this, conatus can also seem circular, that is, it answers its own question: we simply desire what we desire. As such, it may initially seem like a meaningless concept devoid of insight.
The Role of Reason
Spinoza’s response is that reason helps us discern what is truly good for us. To be virtuous is only to act in correspondence with your own nature, but we must fully understand that nature to be virtuous. Our desires do not necessarily identify what genuinely benefits us.
If we properly understand nutrition, we’d second guess the pangs of blind hunger that make us yearn for the slice of cake and instead eat something more nutritious.
While conatus is egoism to the extent that it is self-directed, reason shows the conatus that being pro-social and collaborative is good for everybody, including yourself.
Understanding ourselves and our circumstances allows us to distinguish truly beneficial desires from those that undermine our flourishing. And that understanding shows why rational self-interest needn’t conflict with the good of others.
You would want to work towards a situation where human beings can mutually thrive. What’s truly good for others, is truly good for us. As Spinoza puts it, “There is no singular thing in Nature which is more useful to man than a man who lives according to the guidance of reason.” (Ethics 4 P35)
Wisdom is what is most beneficial to conatus, because it allows us to understand and seek out what is truly good for us, not just the things that promise short-term pleasure.
It is most common for people to be imprisoned by their passions. We desire things that do us harm through greed, envy, anger, and obsession, because we don’t understand the causes of those desires. We mistake yearning for choosing.
Conatus is blind, and a poorly-guided conatus will be guided by base instincts and crude desires—it will envy, grab, and hoard what it can. A well-guided conatus is oriented towerd collaboration and compassion, because what seems like sacrifice is a wise pursuit of a shared good. We all thrive in free and compassionate societies.
In this way, Spinoza’s philosophy directly opposes the commonplace notion that people have fundamentally antisocial instincts that need to be tamed.
The very idea of conatus agrees that we are selfish inasmuch that we want to maintain the integrity of our being, but that self-interest guides us ultimately towards a pro-social existence. Ethical work isn’t about suppressing conatus, but rather enlightening it to what is truly good.
This is where conatus becomes a practical concept. The more you understand your own nature and that of the world, the more powerful your conatus becomes. You start to develop an inner coherence that’s no longer distracted by passions. Who is truly free? The magnanimous, or those who are driven by spite?
Conatus and Stoicism
For those acquainted with Stoicism, Spinoza’s conatus bears a striking resemblance to the Stoic concept of oikeiōsis — “affinity” — the sense of self-belonging all living things have.
It is thought to be the root of Stoic justice, we know intrinsically what is good for us, and we strive to maximise what increases our power. For both Spinoza and the Stoics, self-preservation is the starting point: all happiness flows from what is already good.
This is an important foundation for ethics that grounds it in nature: joy isn’t the goal of good acts, but rather the accompaniment of what is good. We feel joy in community and cooperation, when we eat well, when we celebrate and so on. This is a joy of true self-possession — it is beyond the cheap pleasures of selfish gratification which lead to ultimate pain.
Where conatus and oikeiōsis diverge is in the scope of the concepts. For Spinoza, all things, animate and inanimate are driven by conatus. A rock floating in space, a cog in an engine, and a river are all expressions of God or Nature and therefore strive to persevere in their own being.
In Stoicism, oikeiōsis applies to animals, including humans. There is a hierarchy of being in Stoicism, whereby animals have impulse and plants merely have physis.
While the Stoic cosmos is providential (guided by a divine plan) and oikeiōsis is part of a rational design, conatus is not a purpose or a function, it is rather the essence of a thing — it’s what the thing ultimately is.
You don’t have to accept Spinoza’s metaphysics entirely to feel the force of the notion of conatus. You know what it is to persist, to strive, you feel it diminish in all the travails you go through, and take delight in its growth in all your triumphs.
The weeds in the garden don’t know that they are striving. We do, and in that understanding of our nature, and our place in nature as a whole, Spinoza sees a blessedness — not a blessedness bequeathed from above, but a blessedness that grows from within.

Britain’s new Challenger 3 tank passes 2,000 km in trials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:50:21 UTC
16:50:21 KST

- Challenger 3 has driven 2,000 km, fired more than 200 main gun rounds and 100 smoke grenades in testing, according to RBSL.
- The British Army’s new tank enters a tougher trials phase in November, with initial operating capability planned for 2027.
The British Army’s new Challenger 3 tank has now driven 2,000 km (1,240 miles) and fired more than 200 main gun rounds in testing, and it is set to start a tougher phase of trials in November, according to its builder, Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land.
RBSL, the British-German joint venture building the tank, shared the figures in a LinkedIn post, which also counted 100 smoke grenades fired so far. From November, the company said, Challenger 3 will move into its next phase of trials, in which it will push the vehicle and its new systems harder and faster.
Challenger 3 is a deep rebuild of the Challenger 2 tank the British Army has used since the late 1990s. Under a roughly £800 million ($1.06 billion) contract, RBSL is converting 148 Challenger 2 hulls with a new turret, a Rheinmetall-made 120 mm L55A1 smoothbore gun that replaces the older rifled cannon, modern sights and digital systems, upgraded armor, and the Trophy active protection system, which detects incoming anti-tank missiles and rockets and fires small projectiles to destroy them before they hit.
The new gun lets Challenger 3 use the same standard NATO tank ammunition as allies such as Germany and Poland, including the latest armor-piercing rounds and programmable multipurpose shells that can be set to burst at different points along their flight.
The trials have built up over the past year. RBSL completed initial mobility trials of nearly 800 km on roads and cross-country routes across the UK in 2025, and in January 2026 it carried out the first crewed live firing of Challenger 3 at a Ministry of Defence training center, the first time a newly developed British main battle tank had fired its main gun in the UK in more than 30 years. The tanks have since gone through battlefield mission serials, with cross-country driving, gunnery drills and full crew exercises, which The Defence Blog reported in June.
The Ministry of Defence has said series conversion of the fleet will begin once the demonstration-phase trials have validated the tank’s performance. Challenger 3 is planned to reach initial operating capability in 2027 and full operating capability in 2030, and the tank is expected to stay in service until at least 2040.
When all 148 tanks are delivered, the British Army plans to field them in reorganized armored regiments, and the November trials will put the vehicles and their crews through more demanding conditions as RBSL works toward that 2027 initial capability date.

Restoration reveals architectural secrets of Istanbul’s Süleymaniye Mosque
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:48:50 UTC
16:48:50 KST

Restoration work at Istanbul’s Süleymaniye Mosque, a landmark of Ottoman design, has uncovered hidden acoustic vessels inside its dome, 16th-century decorative paintings and calligraphy preserved on a metal surface, shedding new light on the engineering techniques of architect Mimar Sinan.
Commissioned by Ottoman Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent and completed on Oct. 15, 1557, the mosque is regarded as Sinan’s “masterpiece of the journeyman period.” The wider Süleymaniye complex includes religious schools, a hospital, a public kitchen and a bathhouse, reflecting the Ottoman approach to urban planning and social welfare.
Kaya Üçer, an associate professor at Mimar Sinan Fine Arts University who participated in the restoration, said the work had helped distinguish architectural evidence from long-standing popular beliefs about the building. One discovery concerned the mosque’s renowned acoustics. During restoration, workers erected approximately 20,000 cubic meters of scaffolding, allowing specialists to examine parts of the dome inaccessible from the floor.
“By chance, during repairs to some cracks in the dome, we found pitchers at the bottom, used alongside bricks,” Üçer said. “When you look up at the dome from below, you cannot see them. But from above, you understand that the openings soften the sound coming from below and prevent echoes.” The vessels, installed vertically in a zigzag pattern with openings at their bases, were examined through acoustic tests.
The dome also contains elaborate Baroque and Rococo-style floral decorations, despite the building’s origins in the 16th century. Researchers examined its painted layers under ultraviolet light and through careful scraping to identify earlier designs. They found traces of another decorative scheme beneath the existing ornamentation, suggesting that different designs had been tested before one was selected. The restoration team preserved the surviving historic elements while repairing the visible decorations.
Another unusual feature was found in the structure supporting the dome’s calligraphic inscription. Although the writing is traditionally associated with calligrapher Ahmed Karahisari, historical records also name his student Hasan Çelebi, while later restoration work is said to have included corrections by Abdülfettah Efendi in the 18th century. Üçer said the inscription’s background included a zinc surface, fastened with large nails, beneath a gold-leaf-covered wooden frame. The writing on the metal surface appeared to have been designed for exceptional durability. The team also identified a missing letter in the inscription and, after consulting calligraphy specialists, restored it in accordance with the scientific committee’s assessment.
Elsewhere, scraping work in the mosque’s arcades and the imperial gallery revealed original decorative paintings from Sinan’s era, including rumi motifs widely used in 16th-century Ottoman art. Missing sections were reconstructed based on surviving examples. The team also located a broken piece of the fountain’s water-level measuring structure in a museum in Istanbul’s Fatih district and confirmed that it fitted the missing section.
Üçer said the restoration had taken a period comparable to the mosque’s roughly seven-year construction and had been designed to protect the historic structure from requiring another major intervention for approximately 50 years.

A special selection from Canadian photographer Edward Burtynsky’s “Shifting Topography” exhibition will be displayed in the southwestern Turkish city of Antalya from Nov. 9 to 20 as part of the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), bringing large-scale photographic works examining humanity’s impact on the planet to the international climate summit.
The selection draws on Burtynsky’s 2025-2026 exhibition at Perili Köşk, an arts venue in Istanbul, and focuses on how human activity has reshaped the natural environment. Through expansive images of industrial production sites, mines and agricultural landscapes, the photographer documents the physical traces of economic development and the lasting consequences of human intervention.
The exhibition will be presented at Akra Antalya through a collaboration with Borusan Contemporary. A key section of the exhibition is the “Erosion” series, commissioned by the Borusan Contemporary Art Collection with contributions from the Turkish Foundation for Combating Soil Erosion (TEMA). Featuring aerial photographs taken across Anatolia, the series brings together the geological history of the land and the effects of human activity, portraying changes to landscapes shaped over thousands of years.
The Antalya exhibition will also feature “In the Wake of Progress,” a 22-minute immersive multimedia work combining Burtynsky’s photographic output spanning several decades with music composed by Phil Strong.
The project, which will be presented in Türkiye for the first time, combines visual storytelling with an examination of the environmental consequences of industrialization and development. It will be accessible throughout the COP31 period.
COP31 will bring government representatives, climate negotiators and other stakeholders to Antalya to discuss global efforts to address climate change. The exhibition will offer visitors an artistic perspective on the relationship between human progress, environmental transformation and the long-term sustainability of the planet.

Some 120 police and 45 protesters have been injured, the figures show, although the protester figure is likely higher given that many injuries have gone unrecorded.

YOUTH PROTESTS THREATEN RAMA'S RULE

This week, protesters said they had resorted to violence because they had not felt heard.
The Kushner-backed project upset Koceku, who has a close relationship with the land. She is from the remote mountains of northern Albania where her family runs a small, no-frills guest house on the shore of a lake.
"Our country is the Albanian people," she said, the air around her thick with acrid tear gas. "They create the future, they create the now, and they are the ones who can bring our country forward. Not a single person, not a single government." REUTERS

- Furientis was selected as one of four vendors for a U.S. Army fly-off at the end of fiscal 2027 for a second IFPC Inc 2 interceptor.
- The year-old startup recently won its first funded Pentagon contract, raised $25 million, and unveiled a CAML launcher with Rheinmetall at AUSA.
Furientis, a missile startup founded just last year, has been picked as one of four companies to fly interceptors in a U.S. Army shoot-off at the end of fiscal 2027, competing to supply a second missile for the service’s Indirect Fire Protection Capability Increment 2 air defense system.
Co-founder and CEO Brody Franzen announced the selection, describing it as a downselect for a fly-off at the end of a fiscal year that closes on Sept. 30, 2027, without naming the other three companies chosen.
The Indirect Fire Protection Capability Increment 2, or IFPC Inc 2, is the U.S. Army’s mid-range air defense system for protecting bases and troops from cruise missiles, drones, rockets and artillery. Its truck-mounted Enduring Shield launcher, built by Leidos subsidiary Dynetics, now fires RTX’s AIM-9X Sidewinder, and the U.S. Army has spent the past few years looking for a second, more capable missile that can handle fast, low-flying cruise missiles and be built in larger numbers.
Lockheed Martin and a team of Boeing and Anduril are already competing in the formal second-interceptor program, which moved into its demonstration phase in September after Rafael’s U.S. subsidiary was not selected to continue. At the Association of the U.S. Army conference this week, Lt. Gen. Frank Lozano, the service’s portfolio acquisition executive for fires, said the U.S. Army would open a parallel path for companies that missed that first cut but kept investing in their own designs, inviting them to bring missiles to the range for a shoot-off in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, Breaking Defense reported, and Furientis’ selection appears to be part of that track.
Franzen and Aris Simsarian, both former engineers at Virgin Orbit and Castelion, founded Furientis in 2025 in the Los Angeles area to build interceptors designed for mass production from readily available parts. The company puts final assembly time at about 30 minutes and says it flight-tests prototypes roughly every two weeks instead of spending years on design before flying.
The startup came out of stealth in May with a $5 million pre-seed round, and on Oct. 6 it announced both a $25 million seed round led by Benchmark and its first funded government contract, a prototyping agreement with the U.S. Department of War for a 100-mile-range interceptor intended for homeland defense.
According to Franzen, the IFPC selection capped a busy two weeks in which Furientis flew its first horizontal flight test on a government range for the U.S. Army’s low-cost interceptor effort and, at AUSA, unveiled a containerized launcher developed with Rheinmetall for the U.S. Army’s Common Autonomous Multi-Domain Launcher program.
He credited the U.S. Army’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Fires and its defensive fires team, led by Brig. Gen. Guy Yelverton, for opening the door to nontraditional vendors and giving them the resources to speed up development, and said Furientis is now hiring as it prepares its interceptor for the shoot-off due by the end of September 2027.

Senegal-sized Antarctic glacier melting faster than thought: Why it matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:43:19 UTC
16:43:19 KST

Senegal-sized Antarctic glacier melting faster than thought: Why it matters
Thwaites glacier has been losing ice for decades. Now there are concerns of rapidly accelerating loss.
The world’s largest glacier is melting much faster and could add twice as much to global sea levels as previously expected over the next century.
New research published this week by a team of glaciologists has found that the Thwaites glacier in West Antarctica is losing mass rapidly because warm seawater is pushing underneath it and melting its core. This could add 1.2 inches (30mm) to water levels even if global warming does not accelerate as predicted.
The findings, published in the journal Nature Communications, add to a growing body of evidence that shows that the glacier, which has been receding for decades, is now losing mass even faster than scientists thought.
Researchers at the University of California in the United States collaborated with NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory for the study. Here’s what we know about the findings:
What is Thwaites and why is it important?
Nicknamed the “Doomsday Glacier”, Thwaites is the largest glacier on Earth, spanning an area of around 192,000sq km (74,130sq miles) or roughly the size of Senegal – and larger than the US state of Florida.
It is located on the Walgreen Coast of Marie Byrd Land in remote western Antarctica and forms part of the great West Antarctic ice sheet, which includes other glaciers and is 14 times the size of Thwaites.
The glacier was first mapped in 1947 and is named after the late American glaciologist Fredrik T Thwaites, although he never visited it.
In the 1980s, scientists discovered that Thwaites is melting rapidly and have closely monitored its melting process as concerns have grown ever since.
Because it is so big, the glacier’s collapse would sharply raise global sea levels by a catastrophic amount – although researchers don’t project that will happen for many decades, or even a few centuries.
Together, Thwaites and other glaciers such as the Pine Island glacier – an ice stream in West Antarctica which flows into Pine Island Bay in the Amundsen Sea – act as a barrier that holds back the vast and vulnerable West Antarctic ice sheet. If melted, the ice sheet could cause many coastal cities to be submerged around the world.
At present, ice loss from Thwaites contributes around four percent of all global sea-level rise. Studies have calculated that the glacier has lost more than 1,000 billion tonnes of ice since 2000, and continues to lose 50 billion tonnes of ice per year.
Why is the glacier melting?
The main drivers are warm ocean water which is actively melting the Thwaites glacier from underneath it, according to several studies.
Ocean warming is caused by human-induced climate change, in particular from the burning of polluting fossil fuels.
In a 2019 study, the NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory discovered a giant underwater cavity beneath the Thwaites glacier that spread across an area two-thirds the size of Manhattan, which researchers said was likely speeding up the glacier’s thinning.
Rising temperatures have caused glaciers to lose about five percent of their ice since 2000, according to the European Space Agency.
What has the latest research found?
Thwaites could add as much as 1.2 inches (30mm) – double the current estimates – to sea levels by 2100, even without any additional global warming, the study found.
The researchers said they used new computer models that paint a clearer picture of melting activity under the threatened glacier at its grounding line – the boundary where it transitions from resting entirely on bedrock to spreading out over the sea in the form of ice shelves.
Where other ice sheet models conclude a grounding line is fixed, the scientists said they developed the concept of a broader “grounding zone” instead. In this scenario, seawater lifts and lowers the ice in a “tidal pumping” process that allows warm water to reach “deep underneath the ice sheets and causing vigorous melting,” lead author Mattia Poinelli, a project scientist at UCLA, told media.
That melting process is accelerating the Thwaites’ “unpinning” from the Mouginot Ridge – an important underwater bedrock currently stabilising the glacier from below. The study concluded that there is a 60 percent chance that Thwaites could unpin from the ridge by the end of the century.
However, experts say more studies are needed to accurately predict the volume of Thwaites’ ice loss.
In separate findings, scientists from the British Antarctic Survey concluded that Thwaites will continue losing ice for at least the next 150 years, even under the most extreme ocean cooling conditions imaginable.
The study, which used computer simulation models that examined the melting effects of the ocean over the next century and a half, was published in Geophysical Research Letters in July.

Pakistan's finance minister on Saturday said the country had so far withstood the shock from skyrocketing energy prices due to the Iran war, but that attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries were "worrying" for the country's longer-term economic outlook.
In an interview on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Muhammad Aurangzeb said the South Asian country had procured enough energy supplies to last through November, and was now planning for the winter months, when household needs typically spike.
"The first-order impact has been negotiated well by Pakistan," he said.
"We've had no shortage, no queues at the gas stations, and no law and order situation, which at times we have seen in some of the countries."
He added that unless the government saw "an absolute dire need", it would not be procuring spot cargoes on the LNG front, which tend to be far more expensive than previously contracted shipments.
Since the United States and ally Israel launched the war on Iran in February, global energy prices have surged as Tehran's retaliatory action has targeted Washington's Gulf allies and curtailed oil and gas supplies.
With Yemen's civil war flaring back to life as well, the Houthis there have repeatedly attacked Saudi infrastructure, including energy facilities and airports, in recent days.
Aurangzeb expressed alarm at the escalation, saying damage to such sites would delay a return to economic normalcy.
"What is now (the) worrying part of it is when the energy infrastructure starts getting hit," he said.
"I, to be very honest, I don't know where that would go. But one thing is very clear: that if the infrastructure continues to get hit, the return to normalcy, even if things subside, will take longer."
'Pushback'
Pakistan has been a frequent customer at the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the lender of last resort to countries on the brink of default.
It is currently in the midst of its 25th programme with the Fund, at least 11 of which have been outright bailouts, since gaining independence in 1947.
The current programme totals around $7 billion over three years, with the Fund reaching an agreement this month to release a $1.2 billion tranche.
With global debt stocks running high, the Fund has called at this year's annual meetings on all economies, even those most vulnerable to the Iran war shock, to engage in fiscal consolidation to avoid a potential crisis.
"Fortunately for us, we have been on this fiscal consolidation path for a while," Aurangzeb said with a rueful smile.
The country's tax revenues have grown significantly in recent years, and the finance minister said the government was targeting the theft of taxes by private sector businesses that collected sales tax from consumers but never deposited it in government accounts.
Such theft accounted for billions of dollars, Aurangzeb said, adding that there remained "room for improvement" on increasing income tax collection as well.
He said the government's reform agenda had faced resistance from industry, lobbying groups and vested interests.
"Every reform, everything that you try to do when you try to change the status quo, there is pushback," he said.
One of the major pillars of the IMF's programme criteria is privatising state-owned assets in Pakistan, where the military runs a vast empire of businesses in sectors from real estate to fertiliser.
Asked about those companies, Aurangzeb denied that they were receiving state funding.
"As far as we are concerned, whichever commercial enterprises (the military) are running, they are running on a standalone basis and profitable on their own basis," he said.
"So, I can confirm to you, we are not providing any funds from the exchequer."
Pakistan's military has directly ruled the country for roughly two-fifths of its history, and under current army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, it has tightened its grip over key pillars of power, even as a civilian government remains nominally in charge of the state.

Somer, an apprentice once again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:42:24 UTC
16:42:24 KST

Somer Sivrioğlu has closed his award-winning restaurant Efendy and opened an ocakbaşı, a traditional Turkish grill restaurant, in its place. What might initially seem like a move towards simplicity is, in fact, driven by a much bigger ambition: To rediscover the relationship between meat, fat and fire and the mastery born of years of repetition. Sivrioğlu no longer wants simply to make excellent kebabs. He wants to elevate the knowledge of the usta — the master craftsman we call a kebapçı — to its rightful place in the world of gastronomy
Having spent years introducing Turkish cuisine to Australia before establishing a contemporary culinary language for Anatolian food at Efendy in Istanbul, Somer Sivrioğlu is now entering a new chapter in his culinary journey. This time, however, moving forward means looking back, towards one of the oldest ways culinary knowledge has been passed down: The master-apprentice tradition. Somer has closed Efendy, where he spent five years interpreting Anatolian cuisine through the lens of a contemporary chef-driven restaurant, and opened an “ocakbaşı,” a traditional Turkish grill restaurant, called Baharat in the very same space.
Efendy had earned a Michelin Bib Gourmand, four pearls from the İncili Gastronomy Guide and two toques from Gault&Millau. From the outside, then, the decision seems genuinely radical: Why close a chef-driven restaurant recognized by prestigious gastronomic guides to become a kebab chef?
When I put this question to Somer, his answer provided the key to understanding Baharat: “I believe making a truly good kebab requires more mastery than many of the dishes we prepare in fine dining.” It sounds like a bold claim at first. But consider the anatomy of a kebab and his point becomes clearer. In fine dining, a chef has considerable room for intervention: Techniques, sauces, textures, garnishes, presentation… A kebab offers nowhere to hide behind such complexity. There is meat, fat, a skewer and glowing embers. Every decision, from preparing the meat and determining the proportion of fat to threading it onto the skewer, judging the embers, adjusting its distance from the fire and choosing the precise second to remove it, is reflected directly in the final mouthful. The fewer the ingredients, the fewer places a master has to hide.
At a time when gastronomy seems perpetually obsessed with the “new”, the idea of perfecting the same thing through thousands of repetitions feels almost radical. One remark Somer made during our conversation has stayed with me: “I love the word kebapçı. Pideci, baklavacı, kebapçı…” Each of these words describes someone who has devoted years of their life to mastering a single craft. In recent years, our conversations about gastronomy have revolved around chef-driven restaurants, creativity, signature dishes, techniques and stars. Yet there is another form of knowledge that has carried the cuisine of these lands into the present: Craftsmanship. While a chef often feels compelled to create, a master craftsman strives to perfect. One pursues the new; the other finds greater depth by repeating the same movements thousands of times. And it is precisely this depth that fascinates Somer today.
In Baharat’s kitchen, the meat comes from eight- to nine-month-old male lambs of the “Thracian Kıvırcık” breed, sourced from the northwestern province of Balıkesir. Whole carcasses are butchered in-house daily; the meat is never minced in advance but ground and threaded onto skewers only when an order is placed. Butchery and kebabs are entrusted to Tuncay Usta, while the oven and “lahmacun,” a thin flatbread topped with spiced minced meat, are the domain of Müslüm Usta, a master from the southeastern province of Şanlıurfa. Leading the kitchen is Başak Daldaban, a female chef from the southern province of Adana with a fine-dining background who has worked alongside Somer since Efendy’s very first day.
In the predominantly male world of kebab restaurants, having a woman lead the kitchen is certainly noteworthy. But to my mind, what makes Başak’s story particularly interesting is not so much her gender as the role she plays. She is not there to replace the traditional masters; she brings different forms of craftsmanship together under one roof. The master’s accumulated knowledge and the chef’s ability to build systems come together in the same kitchen. Perhaps this is where Baharat’s true modernity lies.
That is also why the menu extends well beyond the familiar Adana–Urfa repertoire. Lahmacun is made with onions in winter, fresh garlic in spring, aubergines in summer and walnuts in autumn. When “keme,” a prized desert truffle, is in season, there is keme kebab; when loquats arrive, there is loquat kebab. Because Anatolia’s kebab culture is far more deeply connected to the land and the seasons than we often realize. When we present kebab to the world as little more than minced meat threaded onto a skewer, we erase much of the story we have to tell.
One of Somer’s most thought-provoking remarks was this: “I hope that one day the gastronomic elite in this country will accord Küşlemeci Halil Usta the same respect they give Arguinzoniz.”
It is a point worth dwelling on. As the international gastronomic community has rediscovered cooking over fire, it has elevated figures such as Spain’s Victor Arguinzoniz to the ranks of the world’s most respected culinary masters. Yet in Türkiye, we have largely confined the craftsmen who have spent generations working in front of the fire to the category of “good kebab makers.” We do not extend the same intellectual curiosity to our own masters. Why should knowledge accumulated over decades — of ember temperature, the structure of meat and the behavior of fat — not become a subject of serious gastronomic study? Why do we not document a kebab master’s thirty years of experience with the same rigor we apply to the knowledge of a fire-cooking master elsewhere in the world? It is for this reason that Somer plans to invite a master from a different region to Baharat every month. The first gathering will feature Ciğerci Mehmet Usta, a renowned liver specialist from Adana.
Towards the end of our conversation, Somer told me, “I want to devote the remaining years of my career to this.” That sentence makes Baharat, to me, far more interesting than simply another new restaurant. Because the most radical change in Somer Sivrioğlu’s career is not his decision to close Efendy and open an ocakbaşı. It is his willingness, after years spent championing the role of the chef, to become an apprentice once again at this stage of his career — and to devote himself to the pursuit of true mastery.

Hanged, electrocuted and poisoned: The killers who survived execution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:39:11 UTC
16:39:11 KST

"Take it off! Take it off! Let me breathe!" cried Willie Francis, a 17-year-old boy from Louisiana, after an electric current intended to kill him passed through his body. The year was 1946. Francis was strapped into the electric chair and prison officials had already thrown the switch. But instead of dying, his body convulsed, the chair shook — and he remained alive. Prison officials were forced to release him from his restraints and return him to his cell. A year later, they tried again. This time, they succeeded.
Francis' case became one of the most famous episodes in the history of capital punishment in the United States, but it was far from the only one. Throughout history, there have been documented cases of death row inmates surviving hanging, electrocution or attempts to kill them by lethal injection. Some survived because of technical malfunctions, others because of mistakes by execution teams. In exceptionally rare cases, prisoners survived even after the execution method itself had been administered.
These stories have returned to the headlines following the extraordinary case of Christa Pike, the Tennessee killer who survived two doses of execution drugs last month. But behind these remarkable stories lies a far more troubling question: What happens when a state sentences someone to death, attempts to carry out the punishment — and fails?
Hanged, declared dead — and revived before her autopsy
One of the earliest and most astonishing cases occurred in England in 1650. Anne Greene, a 22-year-old servant from the Oxford area, was convicted of infanticide after becoming pregnant by the grandson of the man who employed her and suffering a miscarriage. At a time when unmarried women who concealed pregnancies could be regarded as murderers if they could not prove the circumstances of their babies' deaths, she was sentenced to death by hanging.
In December of that year, Greene was taken to the gallows in Oxford. A rope was placed around her neck and she was hanged before a crowd of onlookers. According to historical records, she remained suspended for about half an hour, and people at the scene even pulled on her legs in an attempt to hasten her death.
She was then cut down and delivered in a coffin to doctors at the University of Oxford, who intended to dissect her body. But it emerged that Greene was still alive. The doctors detected signs of breathing and a pulse and began trying to revive her. They warmed her body, treated her and monitored her condition. Against all expectations, she gradually regained consciousness and recovered.
Her extraordinary survival caused a sensation. Some saw it as divine intervention, and the doctors who treated her helped secure a pardon. Greene was not returned to the gallows. She was released, married and had three children. According to a study published in the Journal of Medical Biography, she lived until 1659 — nine years after her supposed execution.
Her case became a local legend, and pamphlets and poems describing the woman who survived hanging circulated in England for years. Centuries later, her story continues to be examined in medical studies, including efforts to understand how she managed to survive for so long after being hanged.
'The man they could not hang'
More than 200 years later, in February 1885, another extraordinary incident occurred in England. John "Babbacombe" Lee was convicted of murdering his employer, Emma Keyse, and sentenced to death by hanging.
He was brought to the gallows at Exeter Prison, where executioner James Berry prepared to carry out the sentence. Lee was positioned on a wooden trapdoor designed to open beneath his feet, dropping him through the gallows.
But when the mechanism was activated, the trapdoor failed to open. Prison officials attempted to repair the malfunction and operate the gallows again, but the second attempt also failed. The same thing happened a third time.
Eventually, officials decided to halt the execution. The case attracted widespread attention across Britain, and Lee became known as "the man they could not hang." The British home secretary commuted his death sentence to life imprisonment.
Although Lee escaped the gallows, he was not immediately freed. He spent another 22 years in prison before being released in 1907. His subsequent fate remains uncertain, but his story is one of the best-known cases of an execution thwarted by a mechanical failure.
The teenager who survived the electric chair
The case of Willie Francis, more than 60 years after the failed attempts to hang Lee, ended very differently.
Francis, a Black teenager from Louisiana, was convicted of murdering Andrew Thomas, a white pharmacy owner who had previously employed him. He was sentenced to death in 1945, when he was 16, and on May 3, 1946, he was taken to the electric chair.
According to official testimony later presented to the U.S. Supreme Court, Francis was strapped into the chair, a hood was placed over his face and the operator threw the switch. The teenager's body convulsed violently and he jerked in his seat. One witness described how officials demanded that the electrical current be increased after it became clear that the boy was not dead, but the operator replied that he was already delivering the maximum possible power.
Francis continued breathing. He cried out for officials to remove the hood and let him breathe. After the attempt failed, prison officials released him and returned him to custody.
It later emerged that a malfunction in the chair's electrical system had prevented a sufficiently powerful current from passing through his body to kill him.
His lawyers argued that Louisiana had no right to execute him a second time. They maintained that another attempt would constitute cruel and unusual punishment, prohibited under the U.S. Constitution, and would expose him to the risk of death a second time under the same sentence.
The case reached the U.S. Supreme Court, which rejected Francis' arguments in January 1947. The majority held that the unintentional malfunction during the first attempt did not make a second attempt a violation of his constitutional rights.
On May 9 of that year, Francis was returned to the electric chair. This time, the system worked and he died at age 18.
His case became a significant legal precedent that continues to shape legal battles involving death row inmates who have survived execution attempts.
Eighteen needle punctures, two hours of pain — and a return to death row
In recent decades, most botched executions in the United States have involved the very method intended to replace the electric chair: lethal injection.
One prominent case was that of Romell Broom, who was convicted of kidnapping, rape and murder in Ohio and sentenced to death in 1985.
On September 15, 2009, Broom was taken to the execution chamber, placed on a gurney and restrained. The execution team began searching for a vein into which they could insert an IV line to administer the lethal drugs.
But the task proved exceptionally difficult. Time after time, team members inserted needles into Broom's arms and legs but were unable to find a suitable vein.
A total of 18 needle punctures were documented over approximately two hours. In one instance, a needle even struck bone. Broom cried and complained of pain as the team continued its attempts.
Eventually, officials decided to halt the execution. Broom was returned to his cell, with his death sentence still in effect.
He subsequently launched a legal battle to prevent the state from attempting to execute him again, arguing that the suffering he had already endured should rule out another attempt.
In 2016, however, the Ohio Supreme Court rejected his arguments in a 4-3 decision, allowing the state to set a new execution date.
Broom was never subjected to another execution attempt. In December 2020, more than 11 years after surviving the first attempt, he died in prison from complications of COVID-19. He was 64.
Cancer patient warned of the risks — and his execution attempt failed
In February 2018, Alabama attempted to execute Doyle Lee Hamm, a 60-year-old prisoner convicted of murder. But Hamm had advanced cancer, and his lawyers had warned before the execution that his medical condition would make it extremely difficult to find suitable veins for a lethal injection.
Despite the warnings, the state decided to proceed.
For approximately two and a half hours, members of the execution team attempted to insert needles into his body, including his legs and groin.
According to a medical report subsequently submitted to the court, at least 11 puncture marks were found on his body, along with bruising and other injuries.
Eventually, prison officials were forced to abandon the attempt. According to reports, Hamm was in such severe pain that staff had to carry him back to his cell.
Unlike Francis and other condemned prisoners, Hamm did not have to face the execution team again. A subsequent legal settlement stipulated that Alabama would not make another attempt to execute him, and he remained in prison. He died of cancer in November 2021 at age 64.
A year before the failed attempt to execute Hamm, a similar incident occurred in Ohio.
Alva Campbell, a 69-year-old prisoner suffering from lung cancer and other serious illnesses, was taken to the execution chamber in November 2017. The team made four attempts to establish an IV line but failed.
Campbell was returned to his cell and a new execution date was set for 2019. However, he died of natural causes in March 2018, before the state could try again.
They survived lethal injection — but the state found another way to kill them
Not everyone who survived an execution attempt managed to escape the death penalty indefinitely.
Kenneth Eugene Smith, convicted of involvement in a contract killing in Alabama, was taken to the execution chamber on November 17, 2022.
For hours, the execution team attempted to establish an IV line but failed to complete the procedure before the execution warrant expired at midnight.
Smith was returned to his cell alive. His lawyers later argued that the failed attempt had caused him severe psychological trauma, but Alabama remained determined to carry out his sentence.
In January 2024, Smith became the first person in the United States to be executed by nitrogen hypoxia, a method in which the oxygen a person breathes is replaced with nitrogen gas.
Alabama presented the method as an alternative to lethal injection, but the execution drew fierce criticism. Witnesses said Smith shook and writhed for several minutes, contradicting authorities' claims that he would lose consciousness quickly.
A similar case involved Alan Eugene Miller, who was convicted of murdering three people.
In September 2022, Alabama authorities attempted to execute him by lethal injection but were also unable to establish an IV line. The procedure was halted after more than an hour.
Miller's obesity, with his weight reaching 159 kilograms (350 pounds), significantly complicated efforts to locate suitable veins.
Two years later, in September 2024, Miller was executed using nitrogen gas. He became the second person in the United States to be executed by that method, after Smith.
Both condemned prisoners who survived their initial lethal injection attempts ultimately died when the state used a different execution method.
Eight needle attempts — and a prisoner still awaiting his fate
In February 2024, Thomas Eugene Creech, one of the longest-serving death row inmates in the United States, was taken to the execution chamber in Idaho.
Creech, who was convicted of multiple murders, had spent decades in prison and was set to become the first person executed by the state in 12 years.
For about an hour, the execution team attempted to insert an IV line into his arms and legs. Eight attempts were made, but each time, the vein located proved unsuitable or the team was unable to insert the needle properly.
. (Tennessee Department of Correction)
Eventually, the prison warden decided to halt the procedure. Creech was returned to his cell, and Idaho began examining changes to its execution protocol.
His subsequent legal argument that another attempt would constitute prohibited punishment was also rejected.
He remains alive under a death sentence.
In May 2026, a similar incident occurred in Tennessee.
Tony Carruthers, convicted of murdering three people, was taken to the execution chamber. The team successfully established an initial IV line but was unable to insert the additional line required under the state's procedures.
After more than an hour of attempts, the procedure was halted.
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee announced that he was granting Carruthers a reprieve of at least one year.
Four months later, the same state would find itself at the center of a far more extraordinary case.
Seven needles, two doses of lethal drugs — and Christa survived
On September 30, 2026, Christa Pike, 50, was taken to the execution chamber in Tennessee.
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.
Despite difficulties inserting the needles, the execution team administered two doses of pentobarbital, a drug intended to cause her death.
But Pike continued breathing.
She was rushed to a hospital unconscious and in critical condition, and doctors and her lawyers feared she would not survive.
Emergency call recordings released afterward revealed that efforts to save her life were also marred by failures.
After the execution attempt failed, more than half an hour passed before emergency responders were allowed into the prison, partly because dispatchers initially suspected the call was a hoax.
Witnesses continued to hear Pike breathing heavily even after the curtain in the execution chamber was closed. It remains unclear what medical treatment she received during those minutes.
On October 10, Pike was discharged from the hospital and returned to prison, where she continues to receive medical care.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, she is the first known person to survive an execution attempt after lethal drugs were administered.
Experts believe the drugs may not have properly entered her bloodstream, but the official cause of the failed execution has yet to be determined.
Following the incident, Tennessee's governor ordered a suspension of further executions pending an investigation into the failures, and the state's corrections commissioner resigned.
The question of whether the state will attempt to execute Pike again remains unresolved.
Can a person be executed twice?
Pike's case brings the American legal system back to a question considered nearly 80 years ago following Willie Francis' survival: Does a failed execution attempt effectively constitute the carrying out of a person's sentence, and would another attempt violate the constitutional prohibition against cruel and unusual punishment?
The ruling in Francis' case established that the mere failure of an execution attempt does not necessarily prevent a second attempt.
However, legal experts point to the distinction between a case in which equipment fails before the punishment is administered and one in which a lethal substance has already been injected into a person's body, causing suffering and other consequences.
The issue becomes even more pressing in light of data on botched executions.
A study by Amherst College professor Austin Sarat, which examined 8,776 executions in the United States between 1890 and 2010, found that 276 had gone wrong in some way — approximately 3.15%.
The highest failure rate was recorded in lethal injections, long considered a more advanced and humane method of execution: approximately 7.2%.
The stories of Francis, Greene, Broom, Smith and Pike differ greatly.
Some took place centuries ago, others in recent years. Some of the condemned prisoners were convicted of particularly brutal crimes, and victims' families waited years for their sentences to be carried out.
Yet all these cases point to a single reality: Even a procedure designed to end a human life is not immune to mistakes, malfunctions and unexpected failures. For some condemned prisoners, survival meant genuine salvation. For others, it was merely a temporary postponement of death.
Willie Francis survived the electric chair but died in it a year later. Kenneth Smith and Alan Miller survived lethal injection attempts but were ultimately executed using nitrogen gas. Others died in prison without the state ever succeeding in carrying out their death sentences.
Now, nearly 80 years after Francis cried out to be allowed to breathe, the United States once again faces the same question: What happens when a person the state has decided to kill refuses, against all expectations, to die?

'Israel should stay out of Trump's oil war. Netanyahu is doing the opposite'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:38:55 UTC
16:38:55 KST

The Iran war, like so many that came before it, centers on energy's crucial role in geopolitics, according to Hebrew University historian Dr. Guy Laron, though international leaders often downplay or ignore it.
"Time and again, leaders speak in the language of values, security, justice, freedom, while chasing oil behind the scenes," Laron said, speaking on the Haaretz Podcast in a discussion of the increasingly complicated geopolitics of the ongoing regional conflict in the wake of February's U.S.-Israel attack on Iran and its effect on energy markets.
Historically, he added, even wars that don't begin with energy at the center of the conflict often evolve into 'oil wars' once countries fighting for domination and influence are impacted by the necessity of access to tremendous levels of fuel to power both land and naval military forces.
Speaking on the podcast, Laron, the author of the new book "Oil Wars: The Struggle for Control that has Shaped the Modern World," (Yale University Press) noted how Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu used "energy calculus" to sell President Donald Trump on the attack and discussed the missteps that have left the White House mired in the region after Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz - something that the U.S. president "was told that this is exactly what would happen, and he still took the risk," Laron said.
"Trump was dumb enough to think that what he did in Venezuela - in America's backyard - he can do in the Middle East in the same way."

In response to allegations regarding missing artifacts, Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Ersoy has cited outdated recording methods as the main cause of Turkish museum inventory discrepancies, while detailing new digital tracking and security enhancements.

The ministry’s broader MUES program standardizes museum records, including objects’ names, classifications, dates and production and decorative techniques. The program’s inventory work includes detailed photography and updates to existing records, providing a common framework for documenting and managing the country’s cultural assets.

====================================================================================================

Poor urban planning blamed for Istanbul flood damage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:37:00 UTC
16:37:00 KST

Experts have attributed extensive flood damage in Türkiye’s largest city to poor urban planning, saying construction along creek beds and concrete surfaces blocking rainwater from reaching the soil have increased the city’s vulnerability.
Former Environment Ministry Undersecretary Mustafa Öztürk said narrowing and covering waterways leaves surrounding buildings exposed to floods. “Rainwater always finds its way,” he said.
He called for wider creek protection zones, mandatory rainwater harvesting, roadside green spaces that collect runoff and rain gardens that let water soak into the soil. He urged checks on flooded buildings’ load-bearing systems, as water corrodes internal steel over time.
Landscape architect Hülya Dinç said 100-meter creek protection strips became 10-meter maintenance strips in 2013. She called for protection zones tailored to each creek’s basin, slope, geology and flood behavior.
“Urban planning decisions cannot be made without considering the integrity of creek systems,” she said.
Istanbul Water and Sewerage Administration (ISKI) 2023 data lists 2,772 creeks totaling 3,919 kilometers. Dinç’s research, based on 2007 maps, found 108 of 168 main creeks outside drinking water basins had lost their natural structure. Only 60 remained intact, while 33 of the 168 lay outside residential areas.
Dinç noted 31 percent of creeks flowing into the Golden Horn are encased in concrete. Waterways such as Ihlamur in Beşiktaş and Fulya in Şişli now lie beneath roads, as does Bayrampaşa beneath Fatih’s Vatan Avenue.
Urbanization accelerated after 1950, spreading to valley floors in the 1980s. Former industrial land along the Cendere creek gave way to housing, offices and malls.

After a year in turmoil, the Louvre faces uncertain future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
07:40:00 UTC
16:40:00 KST

After a year in turmoil, the Louvre faces uncertain future
PARIS – The Louvre is gradually plugging the security gaps exposed by the spectacular burglary of Oct 19, 2025, but its reputation has taken a battering and its creaking infrastructure is a growing source of concern.
The beloved Parisian museum, one of the most visited in the world, has spent a year as the subject of police investigations, government reports and parliamentary inquiries following the theft of eight crown jewels in broad daylight a year ago.
The heist exposed a string of failures, from old or non-existent CCTV cameras and a chronic shortage of equipment to the lack of a modern security control room and a security director.
“We still feel the trauma of the burglary,” Valerie Baud, a workers’ representative from the CFDT trade union, told AFP.
Parliament has heard how, in the run-up to the burglary, the institution had spent just €3 million (S$4.3 million) out of €83 million earmarked for a security masterplan because of administrative delays, management decisions and red tape.
The museum had “prioritised projects that were visible and attractive”, the French Court of Auditors found in one of many damning judgements.
That report and others, compounded by a staff strike and a spate of other incidents – including a water leak and a major ticket-fraud scandal – hastened the downfall of Louvre president Laurence des Cars, who resigned in February.
“The Louvre needs a change in security culture, which has yet to happen and will take several years,” said Laurent Lafon, who is monitoring the museum as chairman of the Senate’s culture committee.
“The Louvre’s leaders must embrace the idea that security is a priority, which wasn’t the case,” he told AFP.
‘Rapid progress’
New museum chief Christophe Leribault, who replaced des Cars in February, argues that change is taking place.
“The security masterplan is making rapid progress,” he told AFP in a written statement, while stressing the “complexity” of carrying out the work while keeping the museum open to the public.
The museum has pledged to invest around €20 million a year until 2032 and, since July, has a new dedicated security director.
Short-term worries about security are also giving way to longer-term questions about how to finance a palace-wide modernisation programme.
Every year, nearly nine million visitors walk the Louvre’s galleries, many unaware of the decrepit state of some of the rooms, the ageing plumbing and wiring, as well as poor ventilation in summer and non-existent heating in winter.
Leribault issued his most alarming warning yet earlier this week, telling Le Figaro newspaper “that if the Louvre is not repaired, updated, and transformed, it will very quickly fall behind and will eventually have to close its doors to the public”.
Money worries
French President Emmanuel Macron unveiled his vision – called “Louvre – Nouvelle Renaissance” – in January 2025 which included a new entrance and gallery for the Mona Lisa among other changes.
It came with an eye-watering proposed price tag of a billion euros – which now looks unrealistic for a country facing a severe budget crunch.
Unions accused him and Louvre management of prioritising grandiose plans for an architectural overhaul instead of more modest changes that would improve the visitor experience.
“We can step up security without going through with this project, which does not address the priorities and states as its goal an unsustainable increase in visitor numbers,” said Christian Galani, a representative of the hard-left CGT union.
Leribault remains committed to it, however.
Part of his task as Louvre head is finding new private sources of income from donors who will be invited to sponsor work – and earn public recognition and perhaps naming rights in return.
Other sources of income could come from further ticket price hikes.
The target is €360 million.
“It’s a huge challenge, and I don’t know whether I’ll succeed,” he said in June. AFP

China railway passenger trips hit record high in first three quarters
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
15:42:02 CST
16:42:02 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- China's railway network handled 3.71 billion passenger trips in the first three quarters of 2026, up 4.8 percent year on year, the highest for the period, according to the China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway).
During the period, the railway network operated an average of 11,511 passenger trains daily, up 5.3 percent from a year earlier.
Railway departments have actively responded to demand for sightseeing, wellness tours and red-themed study tours, according to China Railway. In the first nine months, a total of 2,860 tourist trains were operated across the country, up 25.5 percent year on year.
The railway network also operated 947 special trains for concertgoers and sports fans during the period, effectively boosting the catering, hotel and cultural tourism sectors.
Cross-border rail travel also continued to grow. The China-Laos Railway carried 265,000 cross-border trips, up 37.8 percent, while the Guangzhou-Shenzhen-Hong Kong high-speed railway handled over 25.8 million cross-border trips, up 11.8 percent, China Railway said.
China Railway also adapted to the inbound travel boom created by the country's visa-free transit policy. The railway network carried over 19 million foreign passenger trips in the first three quarters, up 33.4 percent year on year, the company said.
Behind the steady growth in passenger traffic is China's increasingly dense high-speed rail network.
By the end of 2025, the country's total operating railway mileage had reached 165,000 km, which included more than 50,000 km of high-speed rail.
On Sept. 28, China opened four high-speed rail sections, connecting Xiongan in north China's Hebei Province with Shangqiu in Henan Province in central China, Xi'an with Ankang in Shaanxi Province in northwest China, Yichang with Xingshan in central China's Hubei Province, and Harbin with Yichun in Heilongjiang Province in the country's northeast.
China's high-speed rail network is projected to hit 70,000 km by 2035, featuring eight north-south vertical lines and eight east-west horizontal lines. Once complete, the network will connect major cities, city clusters and key economic zones across the country. ■

Int'l biodiversity summit calls for stronger global action to protect nature
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
15:41:57 CST
16:41:57 KST

YEREVAN, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- The UN chief and government officials called for accelerated global action to protect biodiversity at a summit held here on Friday, urging countries to turn international commitments into concrete measures and strengthen cooperation to address biodiversity loss.
The Leaders' Summit on Biodiversity, themed "Leaders for Nature," brought together heads of state and government and representatives of international organizations ahead of the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17), scheduled for Oct. 19 to 30.
Representatives of governments, non-governmental organizations, experts and other stakeholders also attended the summit.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urged countries to show "more action, more speed, and more will" to protect biodiversity.
"Halfway to 2030, Yerevan is our moment of accountability," Guterres said at the summit, calling for assessing progress toward global conservation targets laid out in the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework adopted in 2022.
He warned that progress to halt biodiversity loss remained uneven and too slow, with financing and other support still falling short of what was needed.
Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan highlighted the links between peace and biodiversity conservation.
"Peace and biodiversity are of great significance, both domestically and across borders," Pashinyan said during a roundtable discussion held as part of the summit. He stressed that environmental challenges could not be addressed by any country alone, calling for greater international cooperation.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian also noted the importance of biodiversity conservation in the context of peace, security and sustainable development. He highlighted the environmental damage caused by armed conflicts and called for stronger international support for conservation efforts.
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for broad international cooperation to safeguard the world's natural heritage, stressing that "biodiversity sustains human well-being, economic resilience and long-term security."
Chinese Minister of Ecology and Environment Huang Runqiu said China had consistently participated in global biodiversity governance with strong political commitment and concrete action, helping promote the adoption of the landmark Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
Huang called for greater financial, technological and capacity-building support for developing countries to ensure the framework's comprehensive, balanced and effective implementation.
The summit adopted the Yerevan Declaration, entitled "Taking Action for Nature," which reaffirmed commitments to the Convention on Biological Diversity and to the effective implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, with its mission of halting and reversing biodiversity loss by 2030 and its vision of living in harmony with nature by 2050. ■

Interview: China plays significant role in global poverty reduction -- Kyrgyz economist
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
15:41:09 CST
16:41:09 KST

BISHKEK, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- The eradication of absolute poverty stands as one of China's most significant socio-economic achievements in recent decades, highlighting its important contribution to international poverty reduction efforts, a Kyrgyz economist said ahead of the International Day for the Eradication of Poverty.
China's success in lifting hundreds of millions of people out of poverty within a relatively short period was driven not only by government social support programs but also by large-scale industrialization, improved employment opportunities, and the development of infrastructure, education, and rural areas across the country, said Tolonbek Abdyrov, a professor of economics and vice rector of the International Higher School of Medicine in Kyrgyzstan.
"China's experience demonstrates that poverty cannot be overcome solely through the provision of welfare payments. Rather, it is necessary to create conditions in which people can earn a living on their own and improve their quality of life," he said, adding that this experience holds immense global significance.
"It proves that even in a nation with a vast population and significant regional disparities, a consistent economic policy can substantially transform people's standard of living," the expert noted.
Regarding China's remarkable role in international poverty reduction efforts, he said, "Through the Belt and Road Initiative, the Global Development Initiative, and cooperation with countries in Africa, Asia and other regions, China is involved in the construction of roads, energy facilities, and industrial plants, as well as the development of agriculture."
According to Abdyrov, China's contribution to global poverty reduction should be measured not simply by the scale of its investments or the number of facilities built, but by how effectively such cooperation enables other countries to develop their own drivers of economic growth, create jobs, and improve living standards.
"For Kyrgyzstan, this is particularly relevant. Cooperation with China can help us develop transport corridors, the energy sector, processing industries, and agriculture," he said. ■
